lawyer:
Md Habibur Rahman, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 

Debashish Bhattachayrya with Md Arifur Rahman with Md Khorshedur Rahman with Najmul Karim with Mohammad Rafiqul Islam and Md Mazharul Islam Advocates—For the respondent No. 2.
parties:
Mizanur Rahman (Md) and others ---------- Petitioners
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Dhaka and another --------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J : At the instance of the petitioner, this Rule under adjudication, issued on 24-2-2016, was in the following terms:

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 7 dated 10-9-2015 and order No. 14 dated 18-1-2016 (Annexure-'C' and `C-1') passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Artha Execution Case No. 441 of 2014 arising out of Artha Rin Suit No. 42 of 2014 should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or why such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper."

2. Needless to mention that this writ petition is in the nature of certiorari.

3. Background leading to the Rule, in short, is that the Respondent No. 2, Eastern Bank Ltd., Dhaka as the plaintiff on 6-2-2014 instituted Artha Rin Case No. 42 of 2014 before the Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as Adalat) against the defendant petitioner for recovery of outstanding dues of Taka 11,38,472.92 (Eleven lac thirty eight thousand four hundred seventy two taka & ninety two paisa only). The Suit was decreed ex-parte on 22-6-. 2014 and put into execution in Artha Execution Case No. 441 of 2014. Thereafter, the petitioners submitted an application on 10-9-2010 before the Adalat to adjust the deposited amount under section 19(3) of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as a Ain) by filing a Miscellaneous Case which was rejected by one of the impugned order and the plaintiff Bank also filed an application under section 34(7) read with section 57 of the Ain seeking warrant of arrest against the petitioner which was allowed by the second impugned order dated 15-4-2015 by issuing order of warrant of arrest against the petitioners and the petitioners deposited 25% equivalent to Taka 2,77,962 against decretal amount of Taka 11,38,472.95 in compliance with section 34(6) of the Ain and was enlarged on bail. The petitioner then filed an application to adjust the said deposit of 25% for treating the same as a deposit in terms of section 19(3) of the Ain and to register a Miscellaneous Case, which was of course rejected.

4. It is at this stage the petitioners moved against the aforesaid two impugned orders and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.

5. Mr Md Habibur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, after placing the petition, both the impugned orders and other materials on record mainly pressed his ground Nos. 5 and 6 of the petition and those grounds have been reflected in the factual matrices of the case as discussed above. He submits that the petitioners have already paid maximum amount against the principal loan amount, but the learned trial Court did not consider any of the submissions of the petitioners. The petitioners filed an application to adjust the money deposited during the time of obtaining bail asking to treat the deposit under section 19(3) of the Ain and to register the case as a Miscellaneous Case, but the trial Court did not consider this aspect and rejected the prayer, which is illegal in the eye of law.

6. Mr Debashis Bhattacaryya, the learned Advocate on the other hand appearing for the respondent No. 2, bank by filing vokalatnama entered appearance and opposed the Rule. His bone of contention is that the order of warrant of arrest which is order No. 7 dated 10-9-2015 (Annexure-C) does not suffer from any legal infirmity in as much as the same is absolutely in keeping with section 34 (9) and 10 of the Ain. There is no mortgaged property as it could be easily seen from the plaint of Execution case No. 441 of 2014 (Annexure-'A'). And in respect of second impugned order dated 18-1-2016 (Annexure-C1) the learned Counsel for the petitioner has submitted that the deposited 25% of the outstanding amount ought to have been treated as a legal deposit within the meaning of section 19(3) of the Ain but this aspect was not considered by the Adalat with positivity. The learned Counsel for the respondent, Mr. Debashis also candidly supported the submissions of the petitioner.

7. However, no forceful argument was advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner against the order of warrant of arrest (Annexure-C).

8. Mr. Bhattacharya assailed the arguments pressed into service by the petitioners mainly on the grounds that the order of warrant of arrest, when there is no property mortgaged securing the payment of loan, is well justified under section 34(10) of the Ain. Moreover, this order cannot be circumvent in any way since the provision under section 34 is independent and not a punishment. It is only an additional method of realizing the unsatisfied dues as held in the decision of Provat Kumar vs Agrani Bank, 15 MLR (AD) 96 = 15 BLC (AD) 96.

9. We have heard the learned Counsel of both sides and considered their submissions, we have perused the petitions, both the orders impugned against and other materials on records carefully, in respect of warrant of arrest we are of the view that by the order impugned against directing issuing warrant of arrest against the petitioner, no illegality  has been committed with in the provision of section 34 of the Ain.

10. With the introduction of the Ain a new provision under section 34 has been introduced under the Ain that makes an elaborate, exhaustive and independent provision for issuing warrant of arrest. It is well settled that the provision of special law shall override all other laws in force that includes the Code of Civil Procedure. The provision of section 34 of the Ain is absolutely independent and self-contained. In the decision of Provat Kumar vs Agrani Bank, 15 MLR (AD) 96 = 15 BLC (AD) 96, our Appellate Division maintained that the above provision of section 34 is exclusive, independent and exhaustive which cannot be subjected to or circumvent by other provisions of the Ain. The Appellate Division observed:

"It appears that the section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is clear and provides for ordering civil imprisonment up to 6 months against a judgment-debtor for compelling to satisfy the decree. Section-34 is not dependent upon section 33. In the instant case, the decree holder has taken step for auction sale of the property but there being no response, auction sale could not be held. Further it appears from the provisions of section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 that the law provides for simple civil imprisonment of the judgment-debtor to compel to make the payment for satisfaction of the decree and is not an alternative punishment in lieu of payment of the decretal amount. Civil imprisonment will not exempt payment of the decretal amount."

11. Further this Division observed that: "Be that as it may having regard to the reasons given by the High Court Division in discharging the rule as well as the submissions of the learned Advocate for the leave petitioner and the provisions of section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, we are of the view that the impugned judgment and order has been passed by the High Court Division in accordance with law and no interference is called for."

12. The Appellate Division thus upheld the decision of the High Court Division reported in Provat Kumar vs Agrani Bank Rajshahi, 15 MLR 122 = 15 BLC 180.

13. We are in respectful agreement with the decision of Provat Kumar's case and hold that the said decision fortified what we have already discussed on the issue.

14. Section 20 of the Ain 2003 has ensured in particular the finality of the order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. We have already mentioned that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 is a special law which will apply with all its trappings while dealing with each and every situation as contemplated under it.

15. The ratio of Provat Kumar's case by now has been applied in several subsequent decisions. In a recent decision of Manik K. Bhattachayrya vs Artha Rin Adalat, (16 BLC 195) High Court Division has elaborated principle of civil imprisonment under section 34 of the Ain after discussing several decisions including Provat Kumar's case.

16. Now the most vital question that comes for decision is whether the deposition of 25% under section 34(6) of the AM by the petitioners can also be held as a legal deposition within the meaning of section 19(3) of the Ain. In other words whether the deposit of 25% of the outstanding amount by the petitioner under section 34(6) of the Ain is a good deposit even under section 19(3) of the Ain.

17. For better understanding let us see what 34(6) and 19(3) enjoins:—

“(৩) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান অনুযায়ী দরখাস্ত দাখিলের ক্ষেত্রে বিবাদীকে উক্ত দরখাস্ত দাখিলের তারিখের পরবর্তী ১৫ (পনের) দিবসের মধ্যে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের ১০% এর সমপরিমাণ টাকা বাদীর দাবীর সেই পরিমাণের জন্য স্বীকৃতিস্বরূপ নগদ সংশ্লিষ্ট আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে, অথবা

জামানতব্বরূপ ব্যাংক ড্রাফট, পে-অর্ডার বা অন্য কোন প্রকার নগদায়নযোগ্য বিনিময়ে দলিল (Negotiable Instrument) আকারে জামানত হিসাবে আদালত জমাদান করিতে হইবে ।”

<u>18. Section 34(6) of the Ain states:—</u>

<u>“(৬) উপ-ধারা (৫) এর বিধান সত্বেও, দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক দায়িক যদি ডিক্রিদারের অপরিশোধিত পাওনার ২৫% এর সমপরিমাণ অর্থ নগদ পরিশোধ করিয়া এই মর্মে বন্ড প্রদান করেন যে, তিনি পরবর্তী ৯০ (নব্বই) দিবসের মধ্যে অবশিষ্ট পাওনা পরিশোধ করিবেন, তবে সেক্ষেত্রে আদালত দায়িককে মুক্তি প্রদান করিবে ।”</u>

<u>19. "Boni judicio est ampliare Jurisdictional" is a maxim which means it is the duty of a good Judge to extend Jurisdiction or in other words to enlarge his jurisdiction. But it does not necessarily mean that in course of interpretation a Judge would formulate any law but certainly a Judge can extend it's jurisdiction in a fit case.</u>

<u>20. On a plain reading of section 19(3) of the Ain we have found that for a registration of a Miscellaneous Case to set aside an ex-parte decree, it is required to deposit 10% of the decreetal amount either by cash or bank draft, pay order or by other method permissible under Negotiable Instrument Act as security. On the other hand the petitioner deposited 25% of the outstanding amount under section 34(6) of the Ain which is much more then the decretal amount. The petitioners for the purpose of releasing himself, under section 34(6) deposited 25% of the outstanding amount and was enlarged on bail. Therefore, by legal fiction we can hold that he has also deposited more then 10% as required under section 19(3) of the Ain. The law is clear that 10% of the decreetal amount is needed to register a Miscellaneous Case under section 19(3) of the Ain. Unhesitatingly, we can hold that it was absolutely a legal deposit to meet up legal necessity within the meaning of section 19(3) of the Ain. The deposit must be treated as a valid one under the same provision of law.</u>

21. Even when we act in 'Ex debito justitiae' it is well justified to hold that the deposit was a legal deposit and perfect in all respect and the petitioner was entitled to have the Miscellaneous Case registered under section 19 of the Ain to set aside the ex-parte decree.

22. That being the situation, we are of the view that this Rule should be made absolute in part. The order No. 14 dated 18-1-2016 Annexure-C1 refusing to register the Miscellaneous Case is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority having no legal effect and set aside. The Adalat is directed to register immediately the Miscellaneous Case of the petitioner and dispose of the same in accordance with law forthwith.

23. The first part of the Rule which relates to issuance of warrant of arrest is discharged. However, there will be no costs.

End.

lawyer:
Probir Neogi with MG Mahmud Advocates—For the Petitioners 

Khair Ezaz Masood, Advocate—For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Shimul Rani Saha and others --------- Petitioners
Vs.
Palash Chandra Saha and another ---------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 2-112004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Feni in Title Appeal No. 59 of 2002 affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-5-2002 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni in Title Suit No.31 of 2000.

2. The opposite party No.1 Palash Chandra Saha as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 31 of 2000 on 17-8-2000 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni for a declaration that he is the adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha father of the defendant No.1, Shimul Rani Saha.

3. The short facts, of the case, are that the plaintiff was born on 3rd Bhadra, 1375 BS. His natural parents were late Nishi Kanta Das and late Charubala Das. The plaintiff's natural mother died when he was six months old; that late Khitish Chandra Saha and his wife defendant No.4, Gouri Rani Saha had no child they decided to adopt the plaintiff and their offer to adopt the plaintiff was accepted by his natural father Khitish Chandra Saha. Accordingly late Nishi Kanta Saha handed over the plaintiff to defendant No.4 and her late husband Khitish; that on 15th Falgun, 1375 BS, the adoption ceremony of the plaintiff was held and since then he has been living in the adopted father house; that after adoption, the plaintiff had no relationship with his natural father and while he was raised in his adoptive parents' house, their only daughter defendant No.1 Shimul Rani Saha was born; that the plaintiff's adoptive father got him admitted in the Government Primary School and wrote his name as the father of the plaintiff in all his school documents. Subsequently plaintiff passed SSC examination in the year 1986 from Dagonbhuiyan KMC High School and HSC examination in the year 1989 from lqbal Memorial College. In the admission register of the School and all the certificate and testimonial the plaintiff's father name was recorded Khitish Chandra Saha. Moreover, in the voter list also plaintiff's father name was Khitish Chandra Saha. Due to misunderstanding between adoptive father during her life time, Khitish Chandra Saha instituted Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993 against the plaintiff and admitted him as his adopted son and after death of Khitish Chandra Saha on 15th Magh, 1402 BS, plaintiff performed all rituals as his son. After the death of Khitish Chandra Saha plaintiff allowed defendant No.1 and her family to temporarily stay with him and defendant No.4 in the same house. Khitish Chandra Saha died on 15th Magh, 1402 BS leaving behind present plaintiff as his adopted son and his wife, defendant No.4. According to Hindu law, the plaintiff inherited all properties of his adoptive father. In order to deprive the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 has been declaring that the plaintiff is not adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha. With these averments the plaintiff filed the present suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the said suit by filing written statement alleging, inter alga, that the suit is barred by limitation and not maintainable in the present form, the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the present suit and same is barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It is further stated that the plaintiff did not institute any suit against late Khitish Chandra Saha while he was alive seeking declaration that he is the adopted son Khitish Chandra Saha despite the fact that late Khitish Chandra Saha stated in his plaint of Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993 that the plaintiff neither his foster nor his adopted son; that the father of the defendant No.1 was rich man. He purchased huge land in his own name and also in benami of others. Apart from his landed property and business he had a  sweetmeat shop in Dagonbhuiyan Bazar and suit premises was owned by Dagonbhuiyan School Authority. Late Khitish Chandra Saha rented shop premises from one Sumanta Kumar Bhowmic, who was the original lessee of the premises. The house rent was in the name of Sumanta Kumar Bhowmic during the life time of Khitish Chandra Saha and after his death his wife defendant No.4 became the lessee. In order to avoid income tax, late Khitish Chandra Saha purchased property both his own name and in the benami of others including defendant No.4 and the plaintiff. The plaintiff was a cashier in the sweetmeat shop. When late Khitish Chandra Saha came to know that present plaintiff was about to dispose of the benami property in his name, he instituted Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993 against the present plaintiff for a declaration that the plaintiff was a mere benamdar of the said property.

5. After hearing the learned Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, declared that the disputed property was in the name of plaintiff. The appellate court upheld the decision of the trial court. Late Khitish Chandra Saha was the real owner of the property purchased in the benami of defendant No. 1 . Since they had no son late Khitish Chandra Shah purchased in his wife's name to secure her future and constructed building thereon. Since defendant No.1 had no brother she and her husband stayed in her father's house even after her marriage and has been living jointly in her father's house with her sons and husband. That late Khitish Chandra Saha left landed property purchased in his own name and in the benami of defendant No.4 and the building thereon, business and an account in Krishi Bank. According to Hindu Law defendant Nos. 2 and 3, sons of defendant No.1 inherited all moveable and immovable properties of late Khitish Chandra Saha. Since defendant Nos. 2 and 3 are minors and in order to withdraw money from Bank account defendant No.4 after consulting defendant No.1 's husband filed Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1996 in the court of First Sub-ordinate Judge, Feni to obtain succession certificate. In the said case deceased brother Narayan Chandra Saha was named as his near relative. In order to avoid obstacles in obtaining succession certificate, defendant No.1 husband deposed in favour of defendant No.4. Prior to obtaining succession certificate there was understanding that after bearing the funeral expenses and other debts of the deceased, defendant No.4 will return the rest of the money to defendant No.1, but in conspiracy with the present plaintiff and defendant No.4 misappropriated all the money. Since then the relationship between mother and daughter deteriorated. The plaintiff took advantage of this situation and told defendant No.4 that defendant No.1 would file suit for a declaration that the property in the name of defendant No.4 and the plaintiff was the benamder of late Khitish Chandra Saha. According to the plaintiffs advice defendant No.4 made two gifts in his favour about which neither defendant No.1 nor her father was aware. It is to be mentioned that had the plaintiff been Khitish Chandra Saha adopted or foster son no such gifts were necessary. The present plaintiff is neither the foster son nor the adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha. The plaintiff himself admitted in the plaint of the present suit that late Khitish Chandra Saha filed Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993 against him. It also stated that the father of the present plaintiff gave his son to late Khitish Chandra Saha in order to take care of his son and that Nishi Kanta Das natural father of the present plaintiff used to visit Khitish Chandra Saha house to look after his son. According to the written statement filed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 the relationship between the father and the son was never severed. The plaintiff did not claim himself to be the adopted son of Late Khitish in his written statement filed in Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993. Had it been true, he would have filed a declaratory suit during the life time of Khitish Chandra Saha. He filed the present suit long after the death of Khitish and after expiry of period of limitation.

6. In the suit plaintiff examined 7 witnesses including himself as PW 1 and defendant No.1 examined 3 d.ws and defendant No.4 examined 9 witnesses to prove their respective case.

7. The learned Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan by judgment and decree dated 29-5-2002 decreed the suit and declared that the plaintiff is the adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha.

8. Defendant Nos. 1-3 preferred Title Appeal No.59 of 2002 against the judgment and decree dated 29-5-2002 in the Court of District Judge, Feni eventually, same was transferred and heard by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Feni who by his judgment and decree dated 2-11-2004 dismissing the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

9. Mr Probir Neogi, with Mr MG Mahmud, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the appellate court failed to appreciate that the incidental finding of trial court in respect of Civil Suit No. 69 of 1993 to the effect that the plaintiff is the adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha is not binding upon the defendant-petitioners since the finding of the trial court in respect of Title Suit No. .69 of 1993 was not directly or substantially the issue in that suit. Thus such incidental findings in Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 in respect of adoption of Palash will not operate as res-judicata in the present suit. The former Title Suit was not for adoption but for Benami transaction and adoption was not really an issue in the Title Suit. So an incidental finding without any issue on the point of adoption, the principle of res-judicata will of course have no application. In support of his submissions, the learned Advocate relies on the following decisions reported in AIR 1941(Calcutta) 449, AIR 1989 (SC) 2290, AIR 2003 (SC) 4295, 10 DLR 277 and 1988 BLD 493. He further submits that the court of appeal below committed error of law in not holding that the present suit is barred by limitation having been filed long after 6 (six) years of accrual of cause of action. He finally submits that there is no giving and receiving of the plaintiff in as much as physical act of giving and receiving is absolutely necessary to the validity of adoption. Thus the appellate court below committed error of law in not setting aside the decision of the trial court wrongly relying on the incidental findings of the Title Suit No. 69 of 1993.

10. Mr Khair Ezaz Masod, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that although no specific issue was framed in the earlier Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 in respect of adoption of plaintiff but impliedly that issue was dealt with in the suit, which have been materially and substantially decided, same cannot again be the subject matter of issue in the present suit to be adjudicated upon. He further submits that the father of the plaintiff, Khitish did not file any appeal against the finding `Dattak' passed in previous Title Suit No.69 of 1993, although he was fully aware about "Dattak". In this connection, the learned Advocate refers two decision reported in AIR 1924 (PC) 144 and AIR 1932 (PC) 50. He next submits that the learned Advocate for the petitioner failed to show any misreading, misconstruction and non-consideration of any facts and evidence which was concurrently found by the courts below. The appellate court rightly affirmed the judgment and decree of trial court by holding that the plaintiff was adopted by the adoptive father Khitish Chandra Saha after complying the provision of Hindu law and completing the ceremony called "datta homam" for adoption as required under the Hindu law. In this respect learned Advocate refers Article 489 of Mulla Principles of Hindu Law, Sixteenth Edition, page 516 and accordingly prayed for discharge of the Rule.

11. Let me now consider the moot point and determine it as to whether incidental finding passed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 in respect of adoption of plaintiff as adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha will operate as res-judicata in the present suit or whether the principle of res-judicata under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has any manner of application in the instant suit.

12. It is well settled principle that, the principle of res-judicata has to be applied when all the conditions namely an identity of matter in issue, identity of parties, similar title, concurrence of jurisdiction and lastly the matter whether directly or substantially is in issue in the subsequent suit have been finally decided in the former suit or not.

13. It appears from the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 (Exhibit-6) that the suit was for a declaration as to benami transaction whether the defendant No.1 (present plaintiff) is the ostensible owner of the property described in the schedule of the said suit, Although it appears that the parties that is the present plaintiff is the defendant No.1 of the said suit are same but it appears that although in the plaint it was stated that-

ক্ষিতিশ চন্দ্র সাহা নিজেই দেওয়ানী ৬৯/১৯৯৩ ইং নং মোকদমায় স্বীকার করন যে, তার কোন পুত্র সন্তান না থাকায় তিনি অত্র মামলায় বাদী পলাশ কে অতি শৈশব কালে তার নিজ পরিবারে এনে নিজ পুত্রবৎ লালন পালন করে স্কুলে শিক্ষাদান এবং নিজ খরচে স্নাতক শ্রেণী পর্যন্ত শিক্ষাদান করান। পলাশের পৈত্রিক দেয়া নাম ও উপাধি পরিবর্তন করে তিনি ও তার স্ত্রী, অতিশয় স্নেহ ভালবাসা বশতঃ আপীলাধীন  মোকদমায় বাদীর  নাম রাখেন পলাশ চন্দ্র সাহা এবং পিতার নাম ক্ষিতিশ চন্দ্র সাহা  লিখান। It was also stated that ১নং বিবাদীকে হিন্দু সম্প্রদায়ের বিধান মতে পৌষ্য করেন নাই।

14. It is not disputed that the former title suit between the parties are suit for Benami declaration and in that title suit no issues was framed whether the present plaintiff is the adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha. In Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 decree finally conclude the case of Benami transaction not adoption of the present plaintiff. It is to be borne in mind that it is the matter in issue and not the subject matter of the suit that forms the essential part of res-judicata. The subject matter of two suits may be different, object of the suit, the relief asked for and the cause of action may also be different but if the matter in issue in them be identical, then the principle of res-judicata will of course have its application.

15. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that although no issues was framed in the earlier Title Suit No. 69 of 1993, but impliedly that issue were dealt with in the suit. So, according to him the principle of res-judicata is applicable. In support of his submission he relied upon the decision reported in AIR 1932 (PC) 50 wherein it has been held that where a point is not properly raised by the plaint, but both the parties have without protest chosen to join issue upon that point, the decision on the point would operate as res-judicata between the parties. In the case of Midnapur Zamindaty Co. Ltd vs Kumar Naresh Narayan Roy reported in AIR 1924 it has been held that where the plaintiff had excluded certain question by the statement of his pleader and the first court had therefore expressly stated that it could not decide it but the defendant, expressly urged in appeal that the judge was wrong in not deciding that question even though his action was based on the plaintiffs adviser's statement and he asked the lower appellate court expressly to decide it and the court did decide it, Held, that the question was necessary for the decision of the suit and therefore the decision thereon operated as res-judicata. It was immaterial that the court did not refer to that question in its judgment.

16. In reply, Mr Neogi, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that facts of the cited two cases are of no avail to the opposite party and there is no conflict with the case because of the fact, in the present case the parties have not join on the issue of adoption and, as such, the above contention advanced by the learned Advocate for the opposite party cannot be accepted.

17. In the judgment of Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 (Exhibit- 6 and A), it appears that in that suit no issues was framed in respect of adoption, but in the earlier suit the parties did not raise to frame any issues in this respect although the court can frame issue under the provision of Code of Civil Procedure before passing any decree. The argument on principle of res-judicata cannot be raised in the present suit because in the previous suit the question of adoption was not directly or substantially the issues but the issue was that whether the defendant No.1 that is the present plaintiff Palash was the benamder of plaintiff Khitish Chandra Saha. So, the contention as raised by the learned Advocate for the opposite party cannot be accepted. The principle of res-judicata under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is attracted where issues directly and substantially involved between the same parties in the previous and subsequent suit are the same.

18. In my considered opinion that both the courts below failed to appreciate this vital aspect of the case. The Trial Court is not justified in decreeing the suit in relying on the incidental findings passed in the judgment of the previous Title Suit No. 69 of 1993 between the parties and same was erroneously affirmed by the appellate court.

19. In the cited case of AIR 1932 (PC) 50 referred by the learned Advocate for the opposite party is not applicable since in the cited case both the parties have without protest chosen to join issue upon that point, the decision on the point would operate as res-judicata. But in the instant suit defendant did not join any issue regarding

adoption and, as such, it will not operate as res-judicata.

20. In the case of Nur Hossein Serang vs Tomijuddin reported in AIR 1941 Calcutta 449, a learned single judge of Calcutta High Court has held that the finding in the former suit that the remittances were not loan did not operate as res-judicata in the mortgage suit, inasmuch as the question whether the remittances were loan was not really an issue in the mortgage suit.

<u>21. In the case of Shivaraj vs Patil reported in AIR 2003, (SC) 4295, Supreme Court of India has held Res-judicata—Suit for partition—Issue directly involved in earlier suit for eviction filed against present plaintiff was claim of exclusive ownership of plaintiff to whole property left behind by deceased although eviction was sought by defendant from a particular portion of land on which he had built but for residence- It cannot be held that judgment in earlier suit can be held to operate as res-judicata between parties, only in respect of portion of the suit property which alone was subject-matter of dispute in earlier suit—Principle of res-judicata under section 11—is attracted where issues directly and substantially involved between same parties in the previous and subsequent suit are same-may-be in previous suit only part of property was involved when in subsequent suit whole property is subject-matter.</u>

22. In the case reported in 10 DLR (1958) 277 it has been held that Res-judicata—Execution proceeding—A question decided in an earlier execution case will operate as a res-judicata in a subsequent execution case arising out of the original decree between the same parties.

<u>23. When a party succeeds in a suit or a proceeding, an adverse finding against him cannot be made the foundation of a plea of res-judicata.</u>

24. The same view has also been taken in the case of Nasim Ali vs Sajina Bibi reported in 1988 BLD 493.

25. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions cited above. I find merit in this revision.

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the courts below are hereby set aside and the suit is dismissed.

27. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby affirmed.

Send down the lower court records expeditiously.

End.

Ahmed Nowshed Zamil, Advocate --------- For the Petitioner.

parties:
Abu Touhid --------- Petitioner
VS
House Building Finance Corporation (HBFC) and others --------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment dated 30-9-2014 passed by the learned District Judge, Khulna dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 136 of 2008 allowing the Auction held on 28-7-2005 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite party decree-holder filed Miscellaneous Case No. 181 of 1997 for recovery of loan amounting to Taka 8,86,859.99 from the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 before the District Judge, Khulna. The said Miscellaneous Case was decreed on 29-11-2001.

3. Being aggrieved, the petitioner judgment debtor filed appeal before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree of the learned District Judge. In appeal this Court directed the petitioner to pay Taka 50,000 instantly to the decree-holder opposite party and the rest amount by equal installments within the time fixed by the court. The judgment debtor petitioner did not comply with the order of this Court. Resultantly, the decree-holder opposite party filed Money Execution Case No. 28 of 2003 for recovery of the decretal money.

4. In the said execution case the mortgaged property was placed on auction for three times but no bidder participated in the bid. Finally, the decree-holder opposite party filed an application before the executing court seeking permission to participate in auction and purchase the property against the claim of the decree-holder. The executing court allowed the application and pursuant to that the decree-holder opposite party took part in auction and purchased the property and a sale certificate to that effect was issued by the court in favour of the decree-holder on 15-1-2006 which was duly registered with the Sub-Registrar, Khulna and delivered possession of the property to the decree-holder and disposed of the sale execution case with full satisfaction by order dated 25-4-2006. The petitioner then filed Miscellaneous Case No. 136 of 2008 under Order XXI, rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the sale on the allegations that the auction was held fraudulently by practicing fraud. Decree-holder opposite party contested the case by filing written objection. The court below upon contest hearing rejected the case by the impugned judgment and order dated 30-9-2013.

5. At this stage, the petitioner judgment-debtor moved this Court by filing this revision and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.

6. The opposite party decree-holder contested the Rule by filing a counter affidavit contending, inter alia, that the petitioner has mortgaged the property as security against loan to the decree-holder opposite party. They being failed to make repayment of the said loan the decree-holder filed Miscellaneous Case No. 181 of 1997 in the court of District Judge, Khulna which was decreed and the decree-holder put the said decree in execution by filing Execution Case No. 28 of 2003.

7. In the said execution case the property in question was placed on auction but no bidder found. Subsequently, the decree-holder opposite party purchased the property against their claim and the court duly issued sale certificate and delivered possession of the same. After purchase, the opposite party decree-holder published a tender notice for sale of the property inviting quotation from intending purchaser. In response to tender notice, opposite party No. 5 along with others participated in the said tender and among the bidders, offer of the opposite party No. 5 was found highest and the property was sold to the opposite party No. 5 by registered sale deed No. 3001 dated 22-12-2013.

8. The opposite party No. 5 contested the Rule by filing separate counter affidavit contending, inter alia, that the opposite party is a bonafide purchaser of the property who participated in open tender called by decree-holder opposite party and in the said auction the opposite party No. 5's quotation was found highest among the bidders and accepted by the opposite party No. 1.

9. It is also stated that the petitioner knowing fully well about execution proceedings and purchase of the mortgaged property by the decree-holder, after a long time filed miscellaneous case challenging the auction only to harass and deprive the bona fide purchaser-opposite-party No. 1. It is also contended that the miscellaneous case filed under Order XXI, rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure is hopelessly time barred under Article 166 of the Limitation Act, as the case has not been filed within 30 (thirty) days from the date of auction as alleged.

10. Mr. Ahmed Nowshed Zamil, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner at the very outset submits that the auction so far held by the court was in violation of Rule 69 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that where a suit is adjourned under Sub-Rule 1 of Rule 69 for a longer period than 30 (thirty) days a fresh proclamation under Rule 67 shall be made unless the judgment debtor concern to waive it. But in the instant case there was no such waiver of the judgment debtor and, as such, the court ought to have published proclamation a fresh for holding auction. He further submits that for non-compliance of the procedure as contained in Rule 69 the entire auction process has become irregular and questionable. Mr Zamil further argued that non-compliance of the provisions as contained in Rule 69(2), the petitioner has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularity. As such, the auction is liable to be set aside.

11. Mr. Imam Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the decree-holder opposite party submits that the property in question was placed on auction thrice but no bidder found. Subsequently, the decree-holder purchased the property against its due claim through court with expressed permission not by any auction. As such, a fresh proclamation under Rule 69 is not at all required to publish. It is also argued that an application under Rule 19 of Order XXI is maintainable where any fraud has been practiced in conducting auction sale but in the present case there is no allegation of fraud and the irregularity so have been raised on the part of the petitioner is not at all true. Moreover, he submits that proviso to Rule 19 provides that no sale shall be set aside on the ground of irregularity where the applicant has not sustained substantial injury.

12. In the instant case the applicant could not substantiate, by any means, what injury they have sustained. But it is established that even after publishing auction notice they did not come forward to pay the dues and also they utterly failed to make payment of the installments directed by the High Court Division in appeal preferred by them. Therefore, the decree-older had no other option but to purchase the property against their due claim. Accordingly, with the permission of the court the decree-holder purchased • the property and got delivery of possession. After purchase the opposite party decree-holder again sold the property in auction to the opposite party No. 5 being found highest bidder and delivered possession of the same to her. As such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

13. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, perused the application, impugned judgment and order along with other annexures annexed to the counter affidavit and supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner.

14. Admittedly, the petitioner along with two others mortgaged the property in question to House Building Finance Corporation ("HBFC") as security against loan. They failed to make repayment of the said loan as per terms and conditions of the sanction. HBFC instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 181 of 1997 before the District Judge, Khulna for recovery of the said loan. The said case was decreed against the petitioner judgment debtor who preferred appeal before the High Court Division which was ended with a direction to the judgment-debtor to pay the decretal amount by installments. But the judgment-debtor failed to pay the decretal amount to the decree-holder. The decree-holder opposite party then put the said decree in execution by filing Execution Case No. 28 of 2003. In the said case the property in question was placed on auction for three times but no bidder was found. Resultantly, the decree-holder opposite party filed an application before the court seeking permission to purchase the property against their dues under Rule 72 of Order XXI. The court allowed the application and sold the property to the decree-holder against their dues and delivered possession. Thereafter, the decree-holder opposite party again sold the property by auction to opposite party No. 5 and delivered possession of the same.

<u>15. From perusal of order sheet (Annexure-'C' series to the supplementary affidavit) it is found that the court permitted the decree-holder to purchase the property by its order dated 28-7-2005. Sale certificate was issued on 15-1-2006 and possession delivered to the decree-holder on 13-4-2006. Finally, the case was disposed of vide order dated 25-4-2006. After disposal of the execution case on satisfaction the judgment debtor petitioner came before the court with this application after near about 3 (three) years. Any application under Order XXI, rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure has to be filed within 30 (thirty) days from the date of auction under Article 166 of the Limitation Act. And, as such, the case is therefore, barred by limitation.</u>

16. I have gone through the order sheet of the execution case and it has been found that the executing court properly complied with all provisions of Order XXI in disposing mortgaged property in favour of decree-holder. The property in question was not sold in auction but the decree-holder purchased the property with the permission of the court against their claim. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner that a fresh proclamation was not published is not correct. From the papers available in record, this Court finds that no irregularity or fraud has been done in the execution process and disposal of the property in favour of the decree-holder.

17. In view of the above, I find no merit in the Rule and in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 18. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to cost. 19. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacate.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned at once.

End.

caseno: Civil petition For Leave To Appeal No. 902 of 2004
lawyer:
S. M. Zillul Hoque, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners.
Not represented ------ Respondents.
parties:
Anowarul Hoque being dead his heirs:- 
1 (a): Md. Ruhul Amin and others ------ Petitioners
Versus
Mohammad Tafazzal Mondal and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25th February, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 415 of 2005)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam, J.:- The defendants filed this civil petition for leave to appeal challenging the judgment dated 25.2.2004 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 415 of 1992 discharging the Rule Which was obtained against the judgment and order dated 2.2.1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge( now Joint District Judge), Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 29 of 1990 affirming the judgment dated 12.3.1990 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Kaligonj in Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1990 rejecting the application filed under Order 9 Rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 28.11.89 passed in the Title Suit No. 100 of 1989 of the Coat of Assistant Judge, Kaligonj, District Jhenidah.

2. The respondent No. 1, as plaintiff, filed the above Title Suit No. 100 of 1989 on 16.8.1989 for declaration of title and khas possession stating, inter alia, that his father late Mandar Mondal was the owner in possession of the disputed land measuring 2.07 acres and his name was duly recorded in S.A. khatians and he died leaving behind his wife and also the plaintiff who at that time was minor being aged about 3/4 months; subsequently the mother of the plaintiff transferred her entire share to the plaintiff by an oral gift and thereby the plaintiff become the owner of the entire property left by his father; on attaining majority the plaintiff came to know that the suit land is under the possession of the defendants who, on query, told the plaintiff that they purchased the suit land from one Afsar Ali Gazi who having no title and interest in the suit land, had no authority to sell the same and, in fact, the defendants, in connivance with Afsar Ali Gazi, used the death of the father of the plaintiff and also the minority of the plaintiff, as an opportunity to deprive the plaintiff of the suit land; the defendants, in spite of requests, declined to restore the possession to the plaintiff and hence the suit. The defendants, including the minor defendants, filed petition seeking setting aside of the ex-parte decree contending that not being notified about the filing of the above suit through proper service of summons, they could not appear in the suit and in the above circumstances the trial court on 29.11.89 decreed the suit ex-parte. The defendant/petitioner, after coming to know about the said ex-parte decree, filed application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 3 of 1990. The plaintiff contested the above miscellaneous case by filing written objection. The learned Assistant Judge, by judgment and order dated 12.03.1990, dismissed the above miscellaneous case. The defendant/ petitioners then preferred the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 29 of 1990 and the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Jhenidah, after hearing, dismissed the same more or less on the same findings arrived at by the learned Assistant Judge and also with the further finding that the said miscellaneous case was time barred. The petitioners then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 415 of 2002 and after hearing a Single Bench of High Court Division on 25.02.2004 discharged the Rule.

<u>3. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law by discharging the Rule in so far as to the appointment of Acting Nazir/Nazir as guardian in contravention of the provision of the Rule 843(1)(2) of Civil Rules and Orders and Rule 4(4) of Order 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure and such appointment being illegal and without jurisdiction, the Rule ought to have been made absolute for the protection of rights/ interests of the minors and also for ends of justice; in the case of Bhagoban Das vs. Mahadeb reported in A. I. R. 1923 Allahabad 298 it has been held that a vakil appointed as guardian of minors by court is an officer of that court for the purpose of Order 32 Rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such in Bangladesh, the learned Advocates are officers of the Court for the same purpose and so Acting Nazir/Nazir cannot be appointed as guardian of the minor.</u>

4. The above submissions merit consideration.

5. Leave is granted.

6. Security of Tk. 1000/- is to be deposited within one month.

7. Preparation of paper book is dispensed with as prayed for.

8. The petitioners are permitted to add additional grounds.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Fazlul Karim and Shahabuddin Ahmed, Advocates ------ for the petitioners 
M.A. Karim, Advocate ------ For the opposite parties
parties:
Ansar Ali & Ors
Vs.
Sundar Alt & Ors
full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J:—This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff U/S. 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Comilla affirming those of the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in a suit for permanent injunction.

2. Plaintiffs instituted a suit for permanent injunctions to restrain the defendants from disturbing their possession over the suit land and not to reap away their paddy there from alleging that the suit jote originally belonged to Hosenuddin and it was sold in Certificate Case No. 604/16-17 for arrears of rent and the landlord auction purchased the same and took possession therein and possessed it in khas. The land of the jote thereafter was settled with Safaruddin and Abdul Latif on the basis of a registered kabuliyat dated 16.3.1919. After the settlement Safaruddin and his brother Amjad Ali possessed the lands and after their deaths their heirs had been possessing the lands and paid rents to the landlords. Hosenuddin filed Title Suit No. 242/1919 against the land lord impleading as well Safaruddin and Abdul Latif as defendants for declaration of his raiyati-right in the suit jote and for getting a patta with respect to the suit joie and that suit was dismissed on contest. On appeal as well judgment of the trial Court was affirmed. Thereafter it has been alleged Hosenuddin through his fufatabhai Hasen Ali got instituted the suit for declaration and khas possession on partition being Title Suit No. 88/44 impleading Abdul Latif and Safaruddin, the predecessors of the plaintiffs as defendant nos. 1 and 2 and the landlord as defendant no. 3 and Hosenuddin as pro-defendant no. 4. The learned Munsif dismissed that suit. On appeal, the appellate Court reversed the decree of the learned Munsif and decreed the plaintiffs' suit so far as regards his 8/27th share in the land of schedule 2 except Settlement Plot no. 603. On further appeal to the High Court of Calcutta plaintiffs' right in 8/27th share in plot nos. 417 and 572 was declared and that he would be entitled to recover possession thereof jointly with the defendant. The plaintiffs of the present suit further alleged that heirs of Abdul Latif sold 2.86 acres of land to Noab Ali, son of Hosen Ali and Ansar Ali, son of Aftabuddin. Some of the plaintiffs filed the Misc. Case in Case No. 183/40 for pre-emption of the said kabala up to High Court it was decided in favour of the plaintiffs and the preemptors got pre-emption Dr the kabala land 'width was taken to the High Court in Civil Revision No. 1411/41. The plaintiff alleged that they also purchased some lands of the jote from the heirs of Abdul Latif by kabala dated 29.3.1944. It has been further alleged that subsequent to these kabalas further transactions by way of kabalas took place between the plaintiffs and their heirs. It has been alleged that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land which comprised the bhiti and nal lands and that the defendants have threatened the plaintiffs to dispossess from the suit land. The defendant opposite parties 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 filed written statements and contested the suit. They alleged that the suit land belonged to Hossenuddin and C.S. khatian was correctly recorded in his name and after the death of Hosenuddin his heirs had been possessing the lands. They further denied the certificate sale for arrears of rent of the suit land and delivery of possession in pursuance of the auction sale. They have alleged that the landlords did not lease out the lands to Safaruddin and Abdul Latif and that the kabuliyat was never acted upon if There was no sale of 2.86 acres of land the suit jote out of the jote by Noab Ali, son of Hosenuddin and Ansar All did not purchase 2.86 acres of land out of the suit jote from Abdul Latif Bhuiya and that the alleged pre-emption proceeding at the instance of Anser Ali son of Safaruddin was a collusive one. Defendants have alleged that Hosenuddin possessed the suit jote all through and paid rents to the landlord and after his death his heirs and successors-in-interest have been possessing the same. They have denied the story of auction sale of the jote in certificate sale and taking delivery of possession through Court. The defendants have further alleged that the suit land was unspecified and vague.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties dismissed the suit. On appeal, the learned Additional District Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the appeal. Hence the plaintiffs have obtained this Rule.

4. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff—petitioners has submitted that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law and failure of justice and that the Court did not consider certain material documents exhibited by the plaintiffs, namely, Ext. 4(a), 5, 5(a) and 5(b) which were relevant to determine the question of possession of the parties in the suit land. He has further submitted that the Court of appeal below committed error of law in arriving at his decision as to possession without referring to the aforesaid documents and those caused a failure justice in as much as that the judgment in Title Suit No. 88/1924, Ext. 5(a) and judgment of the High Court in Second Appeal No. 474/1927, Ext. 4(a), would show and indicate as to how the heirs and successors—in—interest of Safaruddin and Abdul Latif and for that matter Hosenuddin dealt with this land. He has further submitted that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in arriving at his decision on merit on the question of possession of lease out and parting to several kabalas, Exts. 1-8, relating to the suit land since long before the institution of the present suit. Mr. Fazlul Karim has further submitted that the decree in Title Suit No. 88/1924 (Ext. 5(a), and judgment of Pre-emption Case in Misc. Case No. 182/1940 Ext. 5(b) and judgment in Title Appeal No. 30/1921, Ext.5, in the suit filed by Hosenuddin for declaration of his raiyati right and for getting a patta with respect to the suit jote would operate as res judicata to the claim of the defendants as regards rights and possession of the suit land in as much as that the question of title and possession of the parties in this suit have been heard and finally decided in the previous suit. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the decision of the Court of appeal below as regards possession is tainted in serious error in as much as that the learned Additional District Judge misread the evidence of P.W. 2 in deciding the question of possession.

5. Mr. Abdul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant opposite parties has submitted that the judgment in the aforesaid proceedings would not operate as res judicata to the claim of title and possession of the defendants in the suit land in that Title Suit No. 88/1924 Hosenuddin was pro-defendant and that no relief was sought for in that suit and that the order of the pre-emption proceeding would not operate as res judicata against the defendants. He has next submitted that in terms of Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code the decision referred to above would not operate as res judicata against the defendants. He has next submitted that although the learned Additional District Judge has misread the evidence of P.W. 2 as regards possession of the defendant this solitary misreading of an innocuous portion of evidence of P.W. 2 has not affected the merit of the case and that the error has not affected the decision of the learned Additional District Judge. Moreover, the learned Additional District Judge, he has submitted, upon adverting to the other evidence of possession as adduced by the parties has found that the plaintiffs were not in exclusive possession of the suit land.

6. The suit jote originally belonged to Hosenuddin who held it in raiyati interest. The plaintiffs have alleged that the suit jote was put to certificate sale and it was purchased by the landlord on 26.4.1919 and the landlord went into possession through Court on 9.7.1918. This assertion of the plaintiff is supported by the plaint in Title Suit No. 242/1919 filed by Hosenuddin against the landlord impleading the heirs and successors-in-interest of Safaruddin and the judgment in appeal from that suit being Title Appeal No. 30/1921, Ext. 4, and the judgment of the learned Munsif in Title Suit No. 88/1925 (Ext. 5(a). From the plaint of Title Suit No. 242/1919 filed by Hosenuddin and judgment in Title Appeal No. 30/1921 in a suit for declaration of raiyati right of Hossenuddin and for getting a patta which was dismissed although, Hossenuddin after the aforesaid decree dismissing his suit had no title in the suit jote although his heirs were under certain possession. Hossenuddin having filed a suit for declaration of his raiyati interest and for getting a patta upon averment that the suit jote had not been sold in auction and that after the auction sale he approached the landlord for taking fresh settlement, and that suit having been dismissed the defendants' claim of title in the land cannot be based upon any raiyati right of Hossenuddin in the suit land.

<u>7. Be that as it may, the learned Additional District Judge ought to have adverted to all the judgments filed by the plaintiffs including the kabalas (Exts. 1 to 1(8) relating to the suit land. These transactions with regard to the suit land were relevant for the purpose of ascertaining the possession of the parties in the suit land. The question of present possession of the parties in the suit land ought to have been determined on consideration of all evidence both oral and documentary. The kabalas produced by the parties also indicate possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The learned Additional District Judge has committed an error of law in reaching his decision as to possession without adverting to these documents. He has also misread the evidence of P.W. 2 in that the learned Judge has stated that the defendant no. 2 had admitted that the defendants have their residential structures and tank in the suit land where as the deposition of the plaintiffs does not show that the plaintiff no. 2 admitted that defendants have their residential structures and tank in the suit land. It has been admitted by the defendants that plain-tiffs have possession in plot no. 696 wherein they have constructed their huts. If the plaintiffs have got possession in some plot of the suit land, the learned Judge ought to have granted injunction in so far as that plot is concerned. As regards the submission of the learned Advocate of the defendant opposite parties that the suit land was unspecified and indefinite no injunction ought to be issued in favour of the plaintiffs, Mr. Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff has taken us to the schedule of the plaint. Plaintiffs have prayed for injunction with respect to the specified portion either at the north or at the south of the plots and in that view it cannot be said that the suit land is unspecified and indefinite and no injunction could be granted with respect to the suit land and in our view were susceptible to specification and definition and as such there was no defect or hindrance in granting an order of injunction. With regard to the question of res judicata we are of opinion that except for the purpose of determining the question of possession and title of the parties so far as it would help in finding which of the parties had clear possession, in a suit for permanent in junction Court need not enter into a question of disputed question of title of the parties except to the extent as it would help the Court in finding which of the parties has clear possession (BCR 1982 AD 321). In this view we are of opinion that question of res judicata on the basis of the judgments in Title Suit No. 242/1919, Title Suit No. 88/1924 and the judgments of the Court of appeals thereof should not be adjudged at this stage to determine the question of res judicata. These documents, however, should be adverted to so far those would be felt necessary in arriving at the question of possession of the parties.</u>

8. The Court of appeal below has also misread Ext.2, rent receipt and held that it is of 1951. It is absolutely wrong. Ext. 2 and other Exts. namely, 2(a) to 2(e) begins from 1940 to 1955. The Court has also not considered, namely, the evidence of Ext. 7, writ of delivery of possession in Pre-emption Case of 1940 (Misc. Case 182/ 1940). The learned Additional District Judge has also misread the evidence of Ext. 2 series in as much as that the Ext. 2 series the date of the rent receipt began from 1940 and not 1950.

9. In our opinion the Court of appeal below has decided the question of possession without considering all material evidence necessary to arrive at its finding of possession and has misread some important evidence in reaching his finding of possession. The documents filed by the plaintiffs have a very important and direct bearing on the question of possession.

10. The learned Additional District Judge having omitted to consider the aforesaid documents on record having bearing on the question of possession and misreading the evidence of P.W. 2 and Ext. 2 series has committed an error of law affecting the merit of the case. In this view, we are inclined to remand the case to the Additional District Judge for re-hearing of the appeal in the light of the observations made by us.

11. In the result, this Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge is set aside and the case is remanded to his Court for re-hearing of the appeal and to dispose of the same in the light of the observations made by us and in accordance with law. The learned Additional District Judge is directed to dispose of the appeal within two months from the date of arrival of the records in his Court.

12. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3970 of 2018.
lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record -------- For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Baset Majumder, Senior Advocate (with Farid Ahmed, Senior Advocate) instructed by Md Ferozur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record -------- For the Respondents.
parties:
National Bank Limited and another ---------- Petitioner
VS
MR Trading Company and others -------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-10-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 13673 of 2017.)
full_judgment:
Delay in filing this petition is condoned.

2. In unprecedented circumstances, National Bank Ltd. and another have filed .this leave petition against the interim order dated 5-10-2017 passed in Writ Petition No. 13673 of 2017 inasmuch as Rule issued in the said writ petition was discharged as not being pressed within 42 days of issuance of the same.

3. On 1-3-2016, (1) National Bank Limited and (2) Agrani Bank Limited filed Artha Rin Suit No. 382 of 2016 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka against (1) Md. Mizanur Rahman and (2) Razia Rahman for recovery of loan of Taka 209,83,85,128.63 (two hundred nine crore eighty three lac eighty five thousand one hundred twenty eight and paisa sixty three) and, if so required, by selling the mortgaged property as described in the schedule to the plaint.

4. The defendant-respondent No.1 filed an application for getting a decree in the said suit in terms of a memorandum of understanding allegedly entered into on 30-8-2017 between National Bank Limited and Md Mizanur Rahman which was rejected vide order No. 19 dated 27-9-2017 by the Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka in Artha Rin Suit No. 382 of 2016. 14. Fraud and collusion are secret in its origin and inception. Collusion may be either apparent and patent or what is more common secret and covered by apparent show of honesty. A deliberate deception with the design of securing some unfair or undeserved benefit are elements of fraud and collusion which must necessarily be inferred from the circumstances, considering all the facts together. Let us examine the facts and circumstances of this case.

15. For our perusal, we brought the record of Writ Petition No. 13673 of 2017 from the record room of the High Court Division and perused the cause list dated 5-10-2017.
