parties:
Bangladesh .... Appellant.
Vs.
Babu Indu Bhusan Gupta & others .... Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya J.— This appeal is directed against a judgment and decree passed by the second court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal after an order of remand made by the High Court of. East Pakistan and was at the instance of the Province of East Pakistan, which was defendant No. 1 in the suit.

2. The plaintiff respondents brought this suit being Title Suit No. 42 of 1943 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Bakerganj for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and for mesne profits as well as for a permanent injunction against the Province of Bengal and others. The subject-matter of this litigation is a newly formed char measuring more or less 700 acres thrown up by a tributary of the Meghna at Bhola and the rival claimants are the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs who have been subsequently added as such on the one hand, and defendant No.1, which was originally Province of Bengal, subsequently after partition of the country was province of East Bengal, and now after the liberation of the country, Bangladesh. The basis of the claim made by the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs is that the disputed char is partly a reformation in situation of their lands of Osat Taluk and Howla in Char Ilsha which appertained to a permanently settled estate and partly accretions thereto.

3. This claim was contested by the Province of Bengal and thereafter by the Province of East Bengal, on the allegation that the disputed char was partly a reformation in situ of the lands of, Mouza Kalupura and Char Ananda Part III, which were Government estates, and partly accretions to the said estates.

4. The suit was decreed in part on contest against defendant No. 1 and export against the rest on 13.9.47. Of the said decree, the title of the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs to the lands of the whole of the dispute char excepting a certain portion was declared and they were also granted a decree for khas possession of the same. The learned Subordinate held, in course of his judgment, of the question of the plaintiff's title, that the southern portion of the Char was definitely a reformation in situ of the plaintiff's land and the northern portion excepting some lands was an accretion thereto. As regards the Government's claim that it was a reformation of the Government land in situ and accretion to the same it was held that as soon as the Char belonging to the Government was diluviated it had become a part of the bed of the river arid lapsed back into the public domain so fully and completely that the lands might be gained from it by gradual accession under clause (1) of section, 4 of the Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (Regulation XI of 1825).

5. The Province of East Bengal preferred an appeal against the said decree to the Dacca High Court being F A. No. 52 of 1948. This appeal was heard by a Division Branch of the said Court, (Murshed and Idris Ji), who, by their judgment dated 14-7-1960, allowed the appeal in part, holding that Char Ananda part III which was a Govt. Estate having reformed in the old site, the Government could claim by virtue of its title as the original owner and as such the fight of accretion could not be claimed by the plaintiffs in respect of such lands,. The learned Judges disposed of the appeal by the following orders:

“The result, therefore, is that the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, except as regards Char Ananda Part III, are firmed. The judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge, so fax as the said Char Ananda Part III is concerned are hereby set aside. In as much as there has been no demarcation of Char Ananda Part III, the case is tent back on remand to the learned Subordinate Judge with this direction that the Char be demarcated by the same Pleader Commissioner, namely, Mr. Surendra Nath Roy, if possible, and if not, by a competent pleader Commissioner to be appointed by the said Court; that the said court upon receipt of the Pleader Commissioner's report shall take such evidence, both oral and documentary, as the parties in order to determine the boundaries of the said Char Ananda Part III, and that after ascertaining the boundaries, he would pass a decree in favor of the said defendant No. 1 in respect of the said Char.”

6. There was no appeal against the said judgment and order of remand passed by the High Court of Dacca and the case went back to the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, Mr. Surendra Nath Roy, pleader Commissioner mentioned in the order of remand being not available Mr. Sultan Mollah was appointed Pleader Commissioner who prepared a case map and demarcated the land of Char Ananda as shown as in Ext G(4), a map prepared in 1895 B.S An objection being taken that Ext., G (II), the oldest available map of the entire Char Ananda Part III was not shown in the case map prepared by Mr. Sultan Mollah, Mr. Arnold Hossain was, thereupon appointed pleader Commissioner to superimpose Ext. G(II) on the case map prepared by Mr. Sultan Mollah. Mr. Amjad Hossain Superimposed the map, Ext. G(II) as directed and the map, report, field book etc. submitted by Mr. Amjad Hossain was accepted without any objection.

7. At the time of hearing, neither party adduced any oral evidence. The learned Subordinate Judge has disposed of the case by passing an order to the following effect:

“The lands of Char Ananda Part III as shown and depicted in the present case map, report and field book prepared by Mr. Sultan Mollah, Pleader Commissioner and supplemented by those of Mr. Amjad Hossain, Pleader Commissioner, be decreed in favor of the defendant. The Commissioner's map, report and field book to form part of the decree.”

As against this judgment the present appeal was filed by the Province of East Pakistan, which is now being prosecuted by Bangladesh.

8. Learned Attorney General who has appeared in this case in support of the appeal has placed before us the following additional ground which is sought to be urged in support of the appeal.

"That the order of remand passed by the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan so far as it related to demarcation and passing of a decree in favor of the defendant No. 1 was illegal, void and consequently all subsequent proceedings were of no legal effect."

9. Learned Attorney General has argued that in a suit brought by the plaintiffs there could not have been any decree in favor of a defendant who had not sought for nor could seek for such a decree under the law, and that the order of remand which was made by the Dacca High Court providing for such a decree was without jurisdiction and as such the decree which has been passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court of Barisal in pursuance of the said order of remand was also bad.

10. The Dacca High Court, by its judgment, affirmed the judgment and decree of the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal dated the 30th September, 1947 in part and set aside the said judgment and decree to the extent of the lands covered by Char Ananda Part III. In our opinion, no exception can be taken to this part of the judgment and decree of the Dacca High Court.

11. It is no doubt true that ordinarily it is the plaintiff who prays for certain reliefs in a suit according to the procedure laid down by law and the said reliefs may be granted in favor of such a plaintiff. It is only in exceptional circumstances that there can be a decree in favor of a defendant. As for instances in a suit for money, a defendant may be allowed to put in a claim according to law on payment of Court fees, by a way of set off or in a suit for partition, a defendant may make a prayer for a Saham in the suit and a decree may be made in favor of a defendant on the basis of such a claim or prayer. The defendant of course, shall have to put in necessary court fees and conform to other formalities for such a benefit. Apart from a decree for costs which can always be granted in favor of a defendant in any kind of suits, there may be a decree in favor of a defendant in a suit for specific performance of a contract or in a suit for preemption. It is, therefore, riot inherently incompetent for a Court to pass a decree in favor of a defendant. In the instant case it might not have been proper or regular for the Dacca High Court to make a decree in favor of Defendant No. 1 but it would be rather difficult, in our opinion, to maintain that such a decree being without jurisdiction was a nullity.

12. In the present case, however, what was really meant by the learned Judges of the Dacca High Court in the order of remand was that the plaintiffs would be granted a decree only in respect of the lands which were not covered by Char Ananda Part III and, as Char Ananda Part III was not properly demarcated and the extent of the lands covered by this Char could not be ascertained with any precision on the available materials, the learned Judges made an order of remand to the trial Court so that the extent of the lands of the said Char could be properly ascertained and demarcated and that after such demarcation the said lands could be excluded from the land covered by the decree passed in favor of the plaintiffs. There seems to be nothing wrong so far as, this part of the decree in favor of the plaintiffs is concerned. It is no doubt true that the part of the decree which was in favor of Defendant No. 1 does not appear to be strictly regular, and was rather unusual, but we can notice that this order was obtained by the appellant, namely, the Province of East Pakistan in their own appeal and it was to their benefit and that they did not object to this part of the judgment. We rather find that all the parties submitted to the same. More than one Pleader Commissioner were appointed, who initiated appropriate proceedings for repayment of various maps and all the parties participated in the said proceedings on the basis of which the decree under appeal has been passed. It seems to be rather too late in the day to come and say that the decree of the Dacca High Court, and all these proceedings based thereon are without jurisdiction, and should be set aside. Having regard to the substance of the judgment and order made by the Dacca High Court, we have no manner of doubt that the said judgment and order cannot be said to be without jurisdiction. The High Court gave effect to the contention of Defendant No.1 in the appeal and set aside the part of the decree as related to the lands of Char Ananda Part III, but affirmed the decree of the trial Court, so far as they related to the other lands in the suit. Even if the part of the decree which was in favor of Defendant No.1 is taken to be a nullity, that does not detract from the effectiveness of the judgment of the High Court which really affirmed the decree of the trial Court in respect of the lands in suit, excepting the lands of Char Ananda Part III, and remanded the suit to the trial Court for excluding the area of lands covered by the said Char from the decree passed in favor of the plaintiffs. This action of demarcation for the purpose of ascertainment of the exact extent of the decretal lands is sanctioned by the law and no exception can be taken to the same.

13. Learned Attorney-General has next contended that the learned Subordinate Judge misconstrued the order of remand and failed to notice that the contention of the Government was that the plaintiffs cannot claim any title in respect of the land of Char Ananda Part III as well as the accretions thereto and that the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge was bad because in declaring title in favor of the Government in respect of the lands of Char Ananda Part III the accretions to the said Char were not taken in to consideration.

14. We have been taken through the judgment of the Dacca High Court and in our opinion, there is hardly any room for doubt as to what was really meant by the said High Court in this regard. It is clear from the operative part of the judgment, which has been quoted above, that what was directed to be demarcated was the Char Ananda Part III as has been shown in the previous Surveys. It may be pointed out that, the learned Judges, in course of their judgment, have referred to the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge, that Char Ananda Part III which formed in 1941 covered the entire site of the Char formed in 1895 as well as the Char formed in 1920-21, and has stated thereafter that this is Char Ananda Part III. We do not think that any other meaning can be attached to the expression 'Char Ananda Part III', as has been used in the Paid judgment. On a careful reading of the judgment it does not appear to us to be the intention of the learned Judges of the Dacca High Court that when they have referred to the name, 'Char Ananda Part III, they have meant not only the Char reformed on its old site but also the accretions thereto, and that by the direction contained in the operative part of the judgment they wanted that not only Char Ananda Part III, but also the accretions to the said Char should be excluded from the decree passed in favor of the plaintiffs. We, therefore, do not find any substance in this contention of learned Attorney General.

15. The next contention of the learned Attorney General has been that on reference to the map of the disputed land as well as of Char Ananda Part III it would be clear that if Char Ananda Part III is excluded from the decretal lands of the plaintiffs, in that case the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III, as has been depicted in the case map, cannot be conceivably claimed by the plaintiff's as accretions to the Char Ilsha claimed by them as reformation in situ, which is lying to the south or south east of Char Ananda Part III, because there is no physical continuity between the lands of the plaintiffs appertaining to Char Ilsha and the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III. It is no doubt true that the plaintiffs have come to the Court for a declaration of their title to the disputed land as reformation of their own lands in their old site as well as accretions to the said lands and if the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III, which are separated from the lands of Chair Ilsha by Char Ananda Part III itself, cannot be claimed as accretions, it is difficult to conceive that such lands having no physical contiguity with Char Ilsha can be regards as accretions to the lands of the plaintiffs. It seems to us, however, that it is not open to this Court to interfere with the said judgment and order of the Dacca High Court even if we are of the view that if Char Ananda Part III is to be excluded from the decree of the plaintiffs on the ground that it was a reformation of the Government lands in situ, the lands lying to the north of the said Char which are completely separated from the lands of the plaintiffs cannot be acquired by the plaintiffs as accretion to their lands. The defendant having preferred no appeal against the judgment of the Dacca High Court they cannot question the validity of the said judgment at this stage and this Court which is of co-ordinate jurisdiction is not, in our opinion, competent to sit in appeal over that.

16. Learned Attorney General has contended that section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure which precludes a party from disputing the correctness of an order of remand is not applicable to the present case as the order of remand passed by Dacca High Court was not appealable and in support of his contention reliance has been placed by learned Attorney General on the decision of Indian Supreme Court in the case of Satyadhran Ghosal and others Vs. Smt. Deorajin Debi and another, reported in A.I.R. 1960 (S.C.) 941. In that case, an application under section 26 of Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act was dismissed by a Munsif and on an application under section 115 of code of civil procedure against the said order the High Court of Calcutta set aside the order of the learned Munsif and remanded the case for its disposal to the said Court. After remand the learned Munsif rescinded the decree Obtained by the landlord against the Thika tenant under section 128 of the Thika Tenancy Act. Thereafter the landlord moved the High Court against the said order of the learned Munsif, challenging the correctness of the Order of the learned Munsif. The High Court took the view that in view of the order of remand passed previously by the High Court this question was res judicata between the parties. On an appeal to the Supreme Court of India, the Supreme Court pointed out that no question of res judicata did arise in the said case as the order of remand as not a final order determining the rights of the parties and it was also observed that the provision of section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable to such a case as no appeal lay under the code against such an order of remand and expressed their view in the following Words.

“It is clear therefore that an interlocutory order which had not been appealed from either because no appeal lay or even though an appeal lay an appeal was not taken could be challenged in an appeal from the final decree or order. A special provision was made as regards orders of remand and that was to the effect that if an appeal lay and still the appeal was not taken the correctness of the order of remand could not later be challenged in an appeal from the final decision: If however an appeal did not lie from the order of remand the correctness thereof could be challenged by an appeal from the final decision as in the cases of other interlocutory orders. The second sub-section did not apply to the Privy Council and can have no application to appeals to the Supreme Court, one reason being that no appeal lay to the Privy Council or lies to the Supreme Court against an order of remand.”

<u>17. This case is an authority for the proposition that an order of remand which has been made by the High Court but has not been appealed against, may be challenged in an appeal from the final order of the High Court to the Supreme Court, but this is not an authority for the proposition that the High Court can sit in judgment over an earlier judgment of the said Court when it came back to it after the disposal of the case in accordance of the order of the remand. It is no doubt true that subsection (2) of section 105 has no application to an appeal which may be taken against the final judgment of the Court to a superior court and the superior court may in such an appeal examine the correctness of the earlier order leading to the final judgment which comes before the said Court in appeal. But it is not for this Court to review an earlier order made by this Court when the case comes back to this Court in an appeal from the judgment of the Subordinate Court passed after the remand.</u>

18. In this connection we may refer to a Bench decision the Patna High Court of the Indian Jurisdiction, namely, in the case of Sundar Ahir and others Vs. Phuljharia and another, reported in A.I.R. 1957 Patna page 534, which relying upon the Privy Council decisions in the case of Rahimthoy Hibibhoy Vs. Turner, reported in 155 (P.C.) and Muzhar Husein Vs. Bodha Bibi reported in 22 I. A. 1, same case I.L.R. 17 All. 122 (P.C.) has expressed a similar view. Raj Kishore Prasad, J in delivering the judgment of the Bench has expressed this view in the following manner:

“If a Bench of the High Court remands a case to the lower Court under its inherent powers, the matters finally disposed of by the order of remand cannot, any of them, be reopened, when the case comes back from the lower court but, if at the time of remand no final decision is given on a point, though some observations only are made in respect of it, it is open to another Bench, a Court of co-ordinate jurisdiction, when finally determining the case, to come to its own conclusion on it.”

19. The same view was expressed in another judgment of the said Court in the case of Smt. Lalbati Kuer Vs. Satchitananda Verma and others, reported in A.I.R. 1960 Patna 418 in which it has been held that if the High Court in a Second Appeal remands a case to the lower Court, the matter finally disposed of by an order of remand cannot be reopened when the case comes back from the lower Court on the principle of constructive res judicata.

20. In the instant case the judgment of the High Court affirmed the decree of the trial Court with respect to the lands claimed by the plaintiffs as reformation in situ i.e. all the lands in the suit excepting the lands covered by Char Ananda Part III and by the said judgment, as we have already held, the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III, were included in the decree in favor of the plaintiffs in addition to the lands of Char Ilsha reformed in the old site. This was the final order made by the Dacca High Court. If any of the parties want to dispute the correctness of the said judgment and order as to whether the High Court was correct in excluding the lands covered by the lands of Char Ananda Part III from the land decreed in favour of the plaintiffs or in including the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III in the decree passed in favour of the plaintiffs, he cannot do so in this Court when the same matter; has come back to it after disposal of the case in accordance of the order of remand.

21. In this connection, it may be mentioned that a possible argument may also be made that the High Court was not correct in holding that the Government, just like a private owner of land, was entitled to claim right to alleviated lands as reformation in situ in preference to a private owner's claim of accretion and that the right of accretion to which a private individual was entitled, was not available in respect of the lands which the Government could claim as reformation in situ. This view appears to be clearly opposed to the principle as enunciated by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Felix Lopez Vs. Muddun Mohan Thakoor and others reported in 13 Moore's Indian Appeals 467. The Judicial Committee in interpreting section 4(1) of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (Regulation XI of 1825) laid down the law in the following words:

“It is to be observed, however, that the clause refers simply to cases of gain, of acquisition by means of gradual accession. There are no words which imply the confiscation or destruction of any private person's properly whatever. If a regulation is to be construed as taking away any body's property, that intention to take away ought to be expressed in very plain words or be made out by very plain and necessary implication.

* * * *

“It would certainly seem that something more than mere reference to the acquisition of land by increment, by alluvion or what other term may be used, would be required in order to enable the owner of one property to take property which had legally vested in another. In truth, when the whole words are looked at, cot merely of that clause but of the regulation, it is quite, obvious that what the then legislative authority was dealing with was the gain, which an individual proprietor might make in this way from that which was part of the public territory, the public domain not usable in the ordinary sense, that is to say, the sea belonging the State, or public river belonging to the State; this was a gift to an individual whose estate lay upon the river or lay upon the sea, a gift to him of that which by accretion, became valuable and usable out of that which was in a state of nature neither valuable nor usable.”

22. This classical exposition of the law has, in the words of Chief Justice Munir of Pakistan Supreme Court, as expressed in the case of Surendra Lal De Pal Vs. Satya Tamas Ghosal, reported in 12 D.L.R. (S.C.) 214 same case P.L.D. 1960 S.C. (Pak.) 179, "remained unshaken during the last century and has been repeatedly re-affirmed by the Board."

<u>23. The bed of a public navigable river or sea is the property of that State and a private owner of land can exercise the right of accretion in respect of such lands only. A char or an island thrown up in the midst of a public navigable river out of its bed becomes the property of the State, according to third clause of section 4 of the said Regulation if it is separated from the lands of the riparian owners by non-fordable streams. If such a char or island goes under water, it becomes again a part of the bed of the river and lapses back into the public domain. If the land of this bed reappear by a slow and gradual process by the side of the land of a private owner, it is, according to the line of decisions referred to above, a case of acquisition of the right by way of accretion by the said private owner and there is no question of accrual of any Government right on the basis of reformation in situ. None of the cases referred to in the judgment of the Dacca High Court, namely, Lope Vs. Muddun Mohan 13 Moor's Indian Appeals 467, Maharaja Bahadur Keshora Prosad Singh Vs. Secretary of State,  A.I.R. 1927 P.C. 89 same case 54 I.A. 156, same case 31 C.W.N. 717, Rahimuddin Matabbar Vs. Naimuddin Howladar 31 C.W.N. 751 same case  A.I.R. 1927 Cal. 565 and Surendra Lal Depal Vs. Satya Tamas Ghosal, 12 D.L.R. 214 same case P.L.D. 1960 S.C. (Pak.) 179, is an authority for the proposition that the Government can claim title to alleviated lands as reformation in situ in preference to a private claim of title by accretion.</u>

24. Relying upon this line of reasoning, it may be argued that the Dacca High Court was not possibly correct in excluding the lands of the Char Ananda Part III from the claim of accretion made by the plaintiffs. But such an argument, as we have indicated above, is not available to the affected party, in this Court. The correctness of the decree or the order of made by the High Court of Dacca remand cannot be raised in this appeal.

<u>25. In order to meet this situation, learned Attorney General has contended that the judgment of the Dacca High Court which was an institution attached to the State of Pakistan has no binding effect upon this Court, as it is a Court of the sovereign state of Bangladesh, which is not a successor to the State of Pakistan. This argument of the learned Attorney General has failed to take notice of the provision of Article 6 of the High Court of Bangladesh Order (President's Order No. 5 of 1972), read with paragraph 6(3) of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution according to which a judgment, decree, order or decision passed, made or given by the High Court of Dacca before the commencement of the said Order shall be enforceable in Bangladesh, notwithstanding the cessation of the High Court of Dacca, as if it were a judgment, decree, order or decision, passed, made or given by the High Court of Bangladesh, and so by this Division. The Constitutional pre-eminence, as granted by Article 111 of the Constitution to the law declared by the appellate Division or the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh does not, of course, attach to such a declaration of law made by the Supreme Court of Pakistan or the High Court of Dacca, but by virtue of the above-mentioned provision of the High Court of Bangladesh Order read with the relevant provision of the Constitution, a judgment of the High Court of Dacca has, the same force and effect, as between the parties, as that of this Division. We are, therefore, unable to accept this contention of the learned Attorney General as correct.</u>

26. No argument has been addressed to us on the question as to whether Char Ananda Part III has been properly demarcated or delineated in the Commissioner's report nor any contention has been raised before us as to the correctness of the order of the learned Subordinate Judge made on the basis of the commissioner's report excepting the question of accretion to Char Ananda Part III as has been dealt with by us.

27. We, therefore, do not find any substance in this appeal and the appeal is dismissed. Under the circumstances of the case there shall be no order as to costs in this appeal. Civil Rule No. 924(f) of 1968 has been obtained by as many as 85 petitioners for their addition as respondents to the present appeal on the ground that they are subsequent lease holders from the Government with regard to the disputed properties. By an order of the Court it was directed that this Rule should be heard along with the appeal. The petitioners claim to be tenants under the Government in respect of Char Ananda Part III and as such they claim to be interested in the subject matter of the suit. The statement on the basis of which the petitioners lay their claim has been made apparently during the pendency of the suit. The appeal, as was filed by the Government, is being properly prosecuted. We do not think that there is any necessity in impleading these petitioners as party respondents to this appeal. The Rule is, therefore, discharged without any order as to cost. There is another Rule being Civil Rule No. 1764(f) of 1968 which was obtained by the plaintiff respondents as against Defendant No. 1. The appeal having been disposed of the rule stands discharged without any order as to costs.

S. M. Mohsen Ali J.—I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud with H. Fazlul Karim  ------ For the petitioners. 
S.C. Das ------ For the opposite parties 1 & 2.
parties:
S Joga Maya Debi & ors ------Petitioners
Vs.
S. D. D. Singh Hazari & ors ------Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J.—This Rule at the instance of the 3 petitioners (who are pre-emptors in Misc. Case Nos. 82, 83 and 84 of 1982 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949) was issued calling upon the plaintiff opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 of Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong to show cause why Order No. 6 dated 24.4.82 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in the said Other Suit No.. 37 of 1982 rejecting the prayer of the 3 petitioners to be added as defendants should not be let aside and the prayer he allowed.

2. Petitioners Sreemati Joga Maya Debi, Sreemati Lilabati Debi and Sree Sunil Baran Deb instituted Misc. Case Nos. 82, 83 and 84 of 1982 on 20.2.82 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 alleging that plaintiff opposite party Nos. to 3 Sree Din Dayal Singh Hazari, Sree Durga Prasad Singh Hazari and Sree Arun Kumar Singh Hazari sold the suit land by five registered documents to opposite party No. 4 Sreemati Kalyani Biswas, opposite party No. 5 Sreemati Parul Rani Chowdhury and opposite party No. 7 Sreemati Geetasree Das Gupta and claiming as co-sharers by purchase. The seller opposite parties 1 to 3 Sree Din Dayal Singh Hazari, Sree Durga Prasad Singh Hazari and, Sree Arun Kumar Singh Hazari thereafter filed Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 on 53.82 praying for a degree declaring that the transfer of the suit property by the five deeds to defendants 1, 2 and 3 i.e. opposite party No. 4 Sreemati Kalyani Biswas, opposite party No. 5 Sreemati Parul Rani Chowdhury and opposite party No. 7 Sreemati Geetasree Das Gupta with the held of defendant Nos. 4, 5, and 6 i.e. opposite party, No. 9 Sree Shambhu Prasad Biswas, opposite party No. 6 Sree Ranjit Kumar Chowdhury and opposite party No. 8 Sree Nripati Bhusan Das Gupta is in fact a benami transaction and was created by plain-without any consideration whatsoever. In the said suit i.e. Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 the pre-emptor petitioners filed an application on 23.3.82 under Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. that the plaintiffs of the said suit in connivance with the defendants have collusively filed the said suit with a fraudulent design to defeat the claim of pre-emption of the petitioners, that the plaintiffs are not the real plaintiffs and are merely name lenders, that the petitioners have legal right to pre-empt, that in the facts and circumstances of the case the petitioners are vitally interested in the result of the suit and that for the ends of justice in order to avoid multiplicity of judicial proceedings, the preemptor petitioners should be added as defendants in the suit with a view to give an opportunity to them to con-test the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the parties passed the following order:—

"Both parties have filed haziras. Petitioners' petition dated 23.3.82 under Order l Rule 10 C P.C. is put up for hearing. Heard the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs and reply to that from the petitioners Perused the petition and the record. In view of the materials on record I do not think it proper to allow the prayer of the petitioners. Therefore the prayer is rejected."

Being aggrieved by the said order the petitioners have obtained this Rule.

3. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that with a fraudulent design to defeat the claim of pre-emption of the petitioners Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 has been collusively filed by the plaintiffs in collusion with the defendants, that the plaintiffs are not the real plaintiffs and are merely name lenders, that the petitioners have a legal right to preempt the suit land, that the presence of the petitioners as parties in Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 is necessary in order to enable the Court to effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in this suit, that the petitioners are vitally interested in the result of the suit and as such are proper parties and that for the ends of justice and with a view to avoid multiplicity of judicial proceedings the petitioners should be allowed to be added as defendants.

4. Mr. S. C. Das, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties I to 3 (the Sellers) submits that the suit is essentially between the plaintiff opposite parties 1 to 3 and defendant opposite parties 4 to 9, that the main issue is the question of benami, that under provision of Order 1 Rule 10 C.P.C. the petitioners are strangers who are not entitled to be made parties in the suit and that the petitioners are neither necessary parties nor proper parties to suit.

<u>5. In the case Ashwini Kumar Karmaker and others Vs. Hari Mohan and others, 36 DLR (AD) 1 it has been held:—</u>

<u>"The question of benami cannot be gone into in a summary proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The facts of the cases of 6 DLR 589 and 51 C.W.N. 644 are altogether different from that of the instant case.......... If a pre-emption is sought to, be resisted on the ground that no transfer took place under the relevant kabala in that the vendor did not part with his possession but simply made a show of transfer for any purpose such as to put away his creditors, as in the case reported in 51 C.W.N 644, then such a transaction, whether it is called 'Benami' or colourable may be gone into."</u>

<u>In the instant case it is obvious that if the plaintiff opposite parties 1 to 3 succeed in getting the decree prayed for in Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 then the transfer will be treated as no transfer and in the said 3 aforesaid Misc. Case Nos. 82, 83 and 84 of 1982 the said decree may be used as evidence to show that there was no transfer under the impugned 5 registered deeds. The petitioners are thus vitally interested in the result of the aforesaid suit. Further in the event the plaintiff opposite parties succeed in obtaining the decree as prayed for. The pre-emptee for petitioners may be required to file another suit to set aside that decree. In the interest of justice and in order to avoid multiplicity of judicial proceedings it is fit and proper that the preemptor petitioners Sreemati Joga Maya Debi, Sreemati Lilabati Debi and Sree Sunil Baran Deb should be added as defendants in the said suit i.e. Other Suit No. 37 of 1982.</u>

6. At the time when the present Rule was issued all further proceedings in Other Suit No. 37 of 1982 was stayed. It also appears that on the prayer of opposite party No. 1 Sree Din Dayal Singh Hazari and opposite party No. 2 Sree Durga Prasad Singh Hazari proceedings in all the 3 Misc. Case Nos. 82, 83 and 84 of 1982 were stayed by the trial Court till disposal of Other Suit No. 37 of 1982.

7. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. We direct that the petitioners Sreemati Joga Maya Debi, Sreemati Lilabati Debi and Sree Sunil Baran Deb be now added as defendants in Other Suit No. 37 of 1982. The order of stay passed in this Rule is vacated and it is directed that Misc. Case No. 82, 83 and 84 of 1982 be heard analogously with Other Suit No. 37 of 1982.

Syed Mohammad Ali, .J.—I agree.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition For Leave to Appeal No. 930 of 1997.
lawyer: None appears-- For the Parties
parties:
Red Sun Limited & Others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Uttara Bank ------ Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment arid order dated April 29, 1997 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in FMA No. 62 of 1989).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal, C.J.: Plaintiff-respondent-Bank instituted Title Suit No. 40 of 1986 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj for recovery of money and realisation of securities from the defendant-petitioners. Summons were duly served upon the petitioners and several adjournments were taken for filing written statement but they did not file the same. The suit was ultimately decreed ex parte on 30-3-1987.

2. The defendants filed an application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Misc. Case No. 104 of 1987, for setting aside the ex parte decree, taking the ground that defendant No.3 wife of defendant No.2, was suffering from cancer from before and that defendant No.2 had taken her abroad for treatment and as such steps could not be taken in the suit in time which resulted in the ex parte decree. Defendant No. 2 came to learn about the ex parte decree for the first time on 2-7-87 and then filed the miscellaneous case for restoration of the suit. The decree-holder Bank opposed the prayer for restoration.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge while dismissing the Misc. case, by order dated 19-1-89 observed that the defendants failed to prove by any evidence, i.e., passport, visa etc. that at the relevant time defendant No.2 and his wife defendant No.3 were staying abroad. It was also observed that the decree was for a big amount of money and no irregularity was found in obtaining the said decree.

4. The defendants took an appeal to the High Court Division, F.M.A. No. 62 of 1989, against the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge. A Division Bench, by its judgment and order dated 29 April, 1997 dismissed the appeal observing that since no evidence was adduced in support of the defendant-appellants' case for not being able to be present when the suit was called on for hearing, the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in dismissing the Misc. case. The learned Judges further observed that it was an old case having been filed in 1986 and because of an order of stay the plaintiff-respondent was restrained from putting the decree into execution; we add, for an unconscionably long time.

5. Shafique Ahmed, learned Counsel for the petitioners, has filed some papers now after about 10 years for showing that the defendants had gone abroad for treatment and defendant No.3 died of Carcinoma breast with Metastasis very recently.

<u>6. The decree obtained by the Bank for realisation of money from the defendants has been put in cold storage for more than 10 years because of the miscellaneous proceedings taken by the petitioners. It will be wholly inequitable to permit the defendants to prove their facts in this Court after 10 years. The defendants must take the consequence for their own laches. Moreover there is nothing specific either to show that the defendants were absent from the country on the date of passing of the ex parte decree.</u>

The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
None appears-------For the Petitioner 
Md Omar Farouq Advocate-------For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Jobeda Begum and others--------Defendant-Respondent-Petitioners
Vs
Jahangir Hossain Mollah-------Plaintiff-Appelant-Opposite-Party
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-8-2016 (decree signed on 22-8-2016), passed by the learned Special Judge-cum-Bicharak, Jana-nirapatta Bighankari Aparadh Daman Tribunal, Barisal, in Title Appeal No.175 of 2015, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 20-8-2015, passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Uzirpur, Barisal, in Title Suit No.08 of 2009, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of this Rule, in brief, are that, the plaintiff Jahangir Hossain Mollah, the seller of the suit property, had filed Title Suit No.8 of 2009 before the court of Assistant Judge, Uzirpur, Barisal against the defendant late Hosen Ali Bepari (purchaser of the suit property), seeking a decree for redemption oi the suit property, under the provisions of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT Act). The defendant Hosen Ali Bepari appeared and filed a written statement. Subsequently he died during pendency of this suit and his wife along with their 3 sons were substituted as defendant Nos. 1 (Ka) to 1 (Gha) and they have contested in the suit. The plaintiff had produced 4 witnesses, who were cross-examined by the other side. Besides, the plaintiff had adduced and proved certain documents which were marked as exhibits 1-6(1). On the other hand, the defendants produced 3 witnesses to support their case, who had deposed as DWs No. 1-3 and were cross-examined by the plaintiff's side. The defendants had produced and proved a registered deed No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001, marked as exhibit "Ka", which was, admittedly, executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant and they had also proved the certified copy of the SA Khatian No.270, marked as exhibit "Kha".

3. However, the trial Court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the evidence on record, dismissed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 20-8-2015 (decree signed on 26-8-2015). In the result, the suit for redemption of the suit property treating the sale as an usufracutory mortgage, had failed.

4. Against the said judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Party (i.e. the seller) preferred Title Appeal No.175 of 2015 before the learned District Judge, Barisal, which was heard by the Special Judge-cum-Bicharak, Jananirapatta Bighankari Aparadh Daman Tribunal, Barisal, who being the Appellate Court, has passed the impugned judgment and decree, allowing the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court, vide its judgment and decree dated 14-8-2016 (decree signed on 22-8-2016), consequently the plaintiff has succeeded to get a decree for redemption of the suit property.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the Plaintiff-appellant-Petitioner has filed and moved this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule.

6. None has appeared on behalf of the petitioner to press the Rule, although this matter has been appearing in the cause list for more than 7 (seven) consecutive dates with the name of the learned Advocates.

7. Learned Advocate Mr. Md Omar Faruqu has appeared on behalf of the opposite party No.1 . He having placed the petition and other materials on record, first of all submits that, the plaintiff had transferred the suit property to Md Hosen Ali Bepari (the original defendant and the predecessor of the present petitioners) by a registered sale deed No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit Ka). He also submits that, the purchaser Hosen Ali Bepari had agreed to recovery the suit property, upon receiving back Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand), from the plaintiff-seller, within 7 (seven) years, vide a separate unregistered agreement dated 25-9-2001 (exhibit 6). Therefore, he maintains that, the transaction evidenced by the sale deed No. 2475 (Exhibit Ka) was not an out and out sale, but an usufracutury mortgage redeemable under section 95A of the SAT Act. The plaintiff had accordingly requested him to execute a deed of re-conveyance to return the suit property, he next submits, but the defendant did not pay any heed to it. Therefore, the plaintiff had issued a legal notice on 20-10-2008 (Exhibit 4), requesting the defendant to return the suit property within seven days from the date of the receipt of the legal notice. But, the said request was not complied with by the defendant, therefore, the plaintiff had to file this suit for getting the suit property redeemed, as per provisions of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (SAT Act). The learned Advocate also submits that, the agreement dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit 6), has been filed and proved by the witnesses No. 2, 3 and 4, who are witnesses to the said deed of agreement (Exhibit 6), which was executed on the same date of kabala deed (Exhibit-Ka). Therefore, he reiterates that, this sale deed accompanied by a separate unregistered agreement to re-convey the suit property tantamount to an usufructuary mortgage as per provisions of section 95A of the SAT Act and the plaintiff is entitled to get the suit property redeemed in his favour and the appellate court has rightly decreed the suit accordingly. But, the trial court had misread and misinterpreted the evidence, placed before it, as well as it has failed to properly appreciate the provisions of law applicable in this case. He next submits that, the trial court has, therefore, erred in law and of facts in dismissing the suit. He next submits that, being aggrieved, the plaintiff had to prefer Title Appeal No.175 of 2015, which has been rightly allowed by the appellate court, upon proper appreciation of law and evidence on record, by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and that the appellate court has lawfully decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has cited a decision reported in 16 BLD (1996) 165 = 1 BLC 202: between Md Osman Gani Talukder @ Sujat Ali Talukder vs Md Osman Ali Mondal, and submits that, even an unregistered agreement for re-conveyance is enforceable in law and the provision for registration of such an agreement, as required under section 95(2)(3) of the SAT Act, does not bar enforcement of such an unregistered agreement and the same is enforceable in law. He has also relied upon a decision reported in 20 BLC (AD) 4, between Asek Elahi vs Jalal Ahmed, and concludes that, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court suffers from no illegality and that does not call for any interference by this Court and he has prayed for discharging the Rule with cost.

8. I have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner, perused the application for revision, lower Court's record as well as the evidence, both oral and documentary, the judgments of the Courts below and other materials in the record.

9. The fact that the plaintiff has executed a deed of sale No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit Ka) is not disputed and this deed has been relied upon by the plaintiff, while the defendant has adduced and proved this deed, marked as exhibit "Ka".

10. Having perused the deed No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit Ka), I find that, it has been admitted by the plaintiff (as the seller) in the said deed, that,

“আমার ভোগ দখলিয় নিম্ন তফছিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি সাফ বিক্রয় করার প্রস্তাব ঘোষণা করিলে তাহা আপনি গ্রহিতা উহা জানিতে পারিয়া বর্তমান বাজার দর যাচাই মতে সর্বোচ্চ মূল্যে উহা খরিদ করিতে একান্তে যত্নবান হইলে আমি আপনার নিকট হইতে উহার মূল্য বাবদ মং ৫৪,০০০(চুয়ান্ন হাজার) টাকা সম্যক নগদ এককালীন বুঝিয়া পাইয়া অত্র কবলা দ্বারা জমি সাফ বিক্রয় করত জমির দখল আপনাকে বুঝাইয়া দিয়া সম্পূর্ণরূপে নিস্বত্ত্ববান হইলাম।”

As such, I find from the contents that this deed is an out and out sale deed or saf-kabala. On the other hand, PW 1 during his cross-examination made on 2-2-2015, admitted that, “দলিলটি সাফ কবলা” i.e. the deed (Ext-Ka) is an out and out sale deed.

11. The provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872, stipulates that, when the terms and conditions of a grant, or of any other disposition of property have been reduced to the form of a document, and in all cases in which any  matter is required by law to be reduced to the form  of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract, grant or other disposition or property, or of such matter, except the document itself, or secondary evidence of its  contents in cases in which secondary evidence is admissible.

12. This section 91 of the Evidence Act, occurring under Chapter VI of the Evidence Act, excludes, in the circumstances stipulated in that section, all oral by the documentary evidence.

13. In view of the fact that, this deed No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001, being a deed required by law to be in writing and registered, neither the so-called agreement dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit-6), nor any other oral evidence, given to modify, supplement or vary the terms, conditions and the contents of the registered sale deed (Exhibit Ka), were admissible, or relevant, since excluded by section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872. This provision of law is so clear that one need not run after the legislative intent. Provisions of section 91, in effect, fortifies the sanctity of a deed which is undisputed and this section gives finality to a transaction, between the parties to it, in terms of the deed itself.

14. The only means to prove any case of redemption, contemplated under section 95A of the SAT Act, is to rely upon the very registered sale deed dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit-Ka). If there were any agreement or condition to re-convey the property sold on 5-9-2001, then such agreement or condition to re-convey could have been and ought to have been incorporated in that very sale deed. Thus, the so-called agreement dated 25-9-2001, said to have been executed (unilaterally) by the purchaser Hosen Ali Bepari, was not only irrelevant and inadmissible in evidence, but the same is not believable at all. There is no earthly reason, nor any other difficulty, to execute, on the same date, a separate unilateral agreement (Ext.-6) by the purchaser, to re-convey the purchased property, which the parties could have incorporated in the sale deed, if that were their intention.

15. As such, it is evident from the materials on record that, the findings of the appellate court are not based on any admissible or relevant evidence. The evidence on record clearly leads to draw an inference that, the unilateral document dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit-6), was a fabricated one created before or after death of the purchaser Hosen Ali Bepari, by culpably gaining over the deed writer, who is described as an witness to the said document, Exhibit 6.

16. A mere perusal of the deposition, quoted below, proves the falsehood of the evidence relied upon by the appellate court to arrive at a hugely perverted findings by flouting the clear evidence and the provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Ac, 1872.

17. I have also taken notice of the fact that, the PW 1 (plaintiff) has neither produced, nor proved the unilateral agreement dated 25-9-2001. This unilateral and unregistered deed of agreement was engrossed on an stamp paper of Taka 150 (one hundred and fifty). But, it was produced by an witnesses named, Farid Hossain, who had deposed as PW 2, describing himself as a witness to the said agreement dated 25-9-2001. On his admission, this deed of agreement dated 25-9-2001 has been marked as Exhibit 6.

18. 1 find nothing in his deposition to explain from whose custody the said deed dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit-6) has been produced or how and why it has come into and produced from the custody of the PW 2.

<u>19. It is to be kept in mind by all court of law that, the courts must be satisfied about the proper custody of the deed before admitting the same into evidence. The Courts must ascertain as to who is entitled to the custody of such document and whether it has been produced by its proper custodian. If the deed is not produced from its usual custodian then the court must satisfy itself as regards the explanation offered about the custody and production of a deed by any person other than the one who ought to have the custody of the deed in the ordinary course of business and had the obligation to produce such a deed.</u>

20. But, in this particular case, PW 2, was neither the beneficiary of the document, nor he was an heir of the plaintiff, nor he was otherwise entrusted to keep the document in his custody. The plaintiff was not asked to explain why he had filed the photo copy of this agreement dated 25-9-2001, instead of the original that was supposed to be lying with him, and why he had failed to file the original deed of agreement dated 25-9-2001, that he claims to be a genuine one.

21. Be that as it may, PW 3, who is described as another witness to the said document (Exhibit 6) has admitted during his cross-examination, on 25-1-2015, that, “দাতা গ্রহিতার সাথে ৭ বছরের মধ্যে দলিল দিয়ে জমি ফেরত দেয়ার কথা বলেছিল কিনা জানিনা” Therefore, this PW 3 supported nothing of the plaintiff's case.

22. On the other hand, PW 4 the writer of the deed No. 2475 dated 25-9-2001, has deposed as  an witness to the said agreement (Exhibit 6).  During his examination in chief, this PW 4 has  asserted that, “এই চুক্তিতে ইসাদি হিসেবে আমার স্বাক্ষর আছে। চুক্তিটি লেখার পর উভয় পক্ষকে পাঠ করে শোনানো হয়েছে। আমার সামনে উভয় পক্ষ সই স্বাক্ষর দিয়েছে।” But, having examined this so-called deed of agreement dated  25-9-2001, I find that, it bears illegible signature of only one person (said to be defendant-purchaser), although PW 4 in his deposition has asserted that, “উভয় পক্ষ সই স্বাক্ষর দিয়েছে.”

23. Therefore, it is clear that, the PW 4 did not tell the truth before the court and has given false evidence on oath and his false deposition leads this Court to conclude that this so-called agreement dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit-6) was a fabrication by the plaintiff and his accomplices, whether done before or after the death of Hosen Ali Bepari.

24. In view of the falsity found in the deposition of the PW 4 and such falsity being so vital that cuts at the very foundation on which the plaintiff has designed, built and raised his case, I am constrained to hold that, the legal maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' should apply in this particular case and, I hold that, the entire case of toe plaintiff is false. If the falsity found were severable from other facts or had not destroyed the very foundation of the plaintiff's story, then the court should sift the truth from the falsity and arrive at its finding on the basis of the facts that the court considers as true and reliable. But, the appellate court, as the last court of fact, has not only failed to appreciate this vital defect in the plaintiff's case, it has also utterly failed in its duty to arrive at the correct findings in the dispensation of justice in accordance with law.

25. It is to be recorded here that, the purchaser Hosen Ali Bepari died immediately after filing of this case and his heirs were substituted and as regards the said agreement dated 25-9-2001 (Exhibit 6) there was none amongst the heirs of Hosen Ali Bepari who have ever witnessed his signing any such agreement. However, a son of the deceased-purchaser was examined as DW 1. He has categorically denied the existence of any such agreement and has stated, during his examination in chief, that, “আমার বাবা বিগত ২৫-৯-২০০১ ইং তারিখে মোঃ জাহাঙ্গীর এর নিকট থেকে রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত দলিল মূলে খরিদ করেন। ফেরত দেওয়ার কোন চুক্তি বা রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত একরারনামা ছিলনা.”

26. Therefore, judicial precaution, in my considered opinion, requires that, the genuineness of any document bearing signature of a dead person should always be looked with doubt when the attending facts and circumstances do not inspire confidence regarding genuineness of such signature, or when, in the production of such document or otherwise, the usual course of events appears to have been deviated from, at a stage, as has been found in this case.

27. Besides the reasons mentioned above, the plaintiff deposed as PW 1, who himself was an interested witness, while the other witnesses of the plaintiff were not credible and found to have lied on oath. Therefore, the appellate court ought not to have believed the case of the plaintiff and ought not to have allowed the appeal.

28. I have next turned my attention to the submission of the learned Advocate that, even an unregistered agreement (requiring transfer or re-transfer of an immovable property) is enforceable in law and also to the decision reported in 16 BLD 165 = 1 BLC 202: between Md Osman Gani Talukder @ Sujat Ali Talukder vs Md Osman Ali Mondal, referred to by the learned Advocate, in order to support this very contention.

<u>29. In view of the falsity of the plaintiff's case, having been proved and as noted above, disposal of this Rule does not require any discussion of the 16 BLD 165 = 1 BLC 202 case. Yet, to clarify the legal position, it is pertinent to record here that, clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, requires registration of all non-testamentary instruments that purport or operate to create or extinguish any  right, title or interest, whether vested or contingent, to any immovable property. Any deviation from the provisions of this law, allowing enforcement of any unregistered document, which is required by law to be registered (for instance, the registration of a deed as required by section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 or registration of a Memorandum of Association as required under the Companies Act, 1994) will be ineffective, and will definitely lead to fatal consequences, chaos and disputes in the society and shall open a flood gate, for the unscrupulous persons, to create false, forged and fabricated documents. The Single Bench decision, reported in 16 BLD 165 = 1 BLC 202, has been given by overlooking the clear and mandatory provisions of clause (b), sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908. Therefore, the judgment, reported in 16 BLD 165, has been given per incuriam and it should not be treated as a law as meant under Article 111 of the Constitution.</u>

30. I have also examined the legal notice (Ext. 5), but nowhere the plaintiff's witnesses had claimed that they had ever met the defendant or his heirs to refund Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand), with request to execute a deed of re-conveyance. If the agreement dated 25-9-2001 (Ext. 6) were genuine and if the plaintiff had believed that the terms and conditions of it were true then the plaintiff must have approached the defendant to re-convey upon receiving back Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand). Rather, the DW I has stated in his examination in chief that, “বাদী টাকা নিয়ে জমি নেওয়ার জন্য কখনও আমার বাবার নিকট আসতে দেখি নাই।”

31. Therefore, from the forgoing facts and conducts of the plaintiff, only one conclusion is possible, and that is that the entire story of sale of the suit property with condition to re-convey is false.

32. The decision reported in 20 BLC (AD) 4: between Asek Elahi vs Jalal Ahmed, submitted by the plaintiff-opposite party, is binding on this Court and that has laid down a very clear and sound principle of law. But, in that case, the deed of mortgage was for a period of 5 years. The consideration money shown as Taka 1,000 (one thousand), was indeed a loan secured by that registered deed. Since, in that case there was, in the registered deed itself, a clear stipulation for re-convey the suit property and that deed was a clear deed of usufructuary mortgage, as found by the Appellate Division. This 20 BLC (AD) 4 decision is liable to be distinguished from the facts and circumstances of this case of a saf-kabala deed (out and out sale deed).

33. In view of the forgoing deliberation, recorded above, I find that, the judgment and decree passed by the trial court is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record, but the appellate court has committed grave error of law and has utterly failed to appreciate the evidence as well as the relevant law in their proper perspective. The appellate court's judgment and decree (impugned in this case) has resulted in error in its decision and has occasioned failure of justice.

34. Before parting off, it may be pointed out here that, very surprisingly, none has appeared on behalf of the petitioner, although the litigants usually believe that their learned Advocates are properly looking after their cases, would advise them and would keep them informed whenever need be, while the learned Advocates owe a fiduciary duty to their client, until they withdraw them from the case concerned, by following proper procedure. This conduct of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, in this particular case, is a prima-facie violation of a lawyer's duty to his/her client as well as to the court. Therefore, the Supreme Court Bar Association/ Bangladesh Bar Council may take up this instance for educating the learned lawyers (particularly the newly enrolled ones) about their professional duties mentioned in their code of conduct and may arrange seminars on this and other related issues that would enhance the quality and proper understanding of the services and role of this honorable profession as well as their duties to assist the court (as officers of the court).

35. This Rule has merit and the same should be made absolute.

Order

In the result, the Rule is made absolute.

The impugned judgment and decree dated I 4- 8-2016 (decree signed on 22-8-2016), passed by the learned Special Judge-cum-Bicharak, Jana-nirapatta Bighankari Aparadh Daman Tribunal, Barisal, in Title Appeal No. 175 of 2015, is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 20-8-2015 (decree signed on 26-8-2015), passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Uzirpur, Barisal, in Title Suit No.08 of 2009 is hereby affirmed.

The order of injunction granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

No costs.

Let copies of this judgment be sent to the Secretaries of Supreme Court Bar Association and Bangladesh Bar Council, to take notice of the observation and recommendation made in paragraph No. 34 herein above.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down to the concerned Courts at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant-appellant-petitioner is directed against the judgment and decree dated 12-11-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur in Title Appeal No. 18 of 2012 dismissing the appeal in affirming the judgment and decree dated 27-11-2012 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Shariatpur in' Title Suit No. 36 of 2008 decreed the suit.

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed the above suit for declaration of title in the suit land along with a prayer for a declaration that SA Khatian No. 6 and BRS Khatian No. 6 of the suit land are wrong. Subsequently plaint was amended and prayer for partition was added. The specific case of the plaintiff, is that the suit land appertaining to PS Khatian 5 of an area of 1.56 acres of Mouza Kashta Shagar, PS Palong, District formerly Faridpur now Shariatpur belonged to Ismail Howlader who also belonged 44 decimals of lands of PS Khatian No. 17 of the same Mouza Kashtoshagor and 42 decimals of land of plot No. 49 of PS Khatian No. 3 of the same Mouza and by these way total 2.42 decimals of lands were belonged and possessed by Ismail Howlader who died leaving behind his legal heirs; wife Rahila Begum who got 30 (thirty) decimals of land, one son Nawab Ali got 1.41 acres and one daughter Bona Bibi got 71 decimals of land. Rahila Begum died leaving behind her one son Nawab Ali and one daughter Bona Bibi wherein amongst. 30 decimals of land, her son Nawab Ali inherited 20 decimals of land and daughter Bona Bibi got 10 decimals of land, and in this way, Nawab Ali's father of the plaintiff Lal Mati Bibi got 1.41 acres + 20 acres = 1.61 acres, daughter Bona Bibi got 71 decimals + 10 decimals = 81 decimals; Nawab Ali died leaving his only daughter plaintiff Lal Mati Bibi who acquired 1.61 acres of land as inheritance from her father Nawab Ali; Bona Bibi died leaving her one son Munshi Aynal Hossain and Ainuuddin Munshi defendant No. 1 who inherited 27 decimals, 4 (four) daughter (1) Shaju Bibi wife of late Abdul Wahab Madbar defendant No. 2 who inherited 13'4, decimals of lands, (2) Shonai Bibi wife of late Wazed Sardar defendant No. 3, who inherited 131/2 decimals of land, (3) Kuni Bibi wife of late Ead Ali Munshi defendant No.4 who inherited 13'/2 decimals of land; and (4) Kuti Bibi wife of Wazed Ali Howlader defendant No. 5 who inherited 131/2decimals = 81 decimals of land. That of 15th March 2008 defendant No. 1 Munshi Aynal Hossain disclosed that SA and BS records are prepared in his name and showed fear. That SA records were prepared partly in the name of her predecessor Nawab All but subsequently wrongly prepared in the name of the defendant No. 1. That the BRS record also wrongly prepared in the Khatian No. 6 in the name of the defendant No. 1 and hence the suit.

3. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statements stating that the suit is barred by limitation, defect of parties and has been filed against the dead persons. The land of PS Khatian Nos. 61, 62 and 67 of Cable Nagor Mauza is also the joint property of Ismail Hawlader, part of which has been already sold out by the said Ismail Hawlader, have not included the suit, so the suit is barred by the principle of hutch-pot. The further case of the defendant is that the CS recorded owner the suit land is late Rajjab Ali, which was recorded in his name in CS Khatian Nos. 23 and 24 and there is no basis for recording the PS Khatian in the name Ismail Hawlader and the PS record was not prepared actually measuring the land in the field. The SA and SRS records have been prepared correctly and the plaintiff in not possessing the suit land on payment of rents, so the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. In order to dispose of the suit, the trial court framed necessary issues and both parties adduced several witnesses and documents to prove their respective case. After conclusion of the trial the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Shariatpur (Sadar) by the judgment and decree dated 27-11-2012 decreed the suit in part with finding that the suit does not defect of parties, not barred by the principle of a hotchpotch and BRS record regarding 75 decimals of land are not binding upon the plaintiff.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 27-11-2011 the defendant-petitioner as appellant preferred Title Appeal No. 18 of 2012 in the Court of District Judge, Shariatpur. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur who by the judgment and decree dated 12-11-2012 dis-allowed the appeal and affirmed those passed by the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved thereby, the defendant as petitioner filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court and obtained the instant Rule.

7. Mr Alal Uddin the learned counsel for the petitioner upon taking me to the revisional application impugned judgment and Decree, Order No. 1 dated 18-5-2008 to order No. 40 dated 27-11-2011 of the trial court record and the materials on record vehemently submits that the defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 5 were died before filing of the suit, which is apparently clear from the decree of the appellate Court below and in the ground No. 12 of the petition of appeal a specific point was raised stating that the summons of the registered post of the defendant No. 2 Shaju Bibi was returned un-served on 9-5-2018 with a remark of “মারা গেছে তাই ফেরত” which is laying in lower court file No. C-2 page 35 and in the ground No. 11 of the petition appeal a specific ground was taken stating that the defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 5 had died long before the filing of the suit; that plaintiff-opposite party filed the suit writing the wrong nickname of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 as Shaju Bibi and Shonai Bibi but their real names are Hazera Bibi and Shonaban Bibi and the defendant-petitioner furnished 2 death certificates of the said defendant Nos. 2 and 3 which have been marked as exhibits "জ and জ (১) but the trial court illegally passed the decree against the dead man rather the appellate court failed to discharge his duties as per provision of section 107(2) and Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned decree against dead men is nullity. Mr Alal Uddin apart from his submission on other points raised a law point that deserves consideration. In support of his argument, he referred to the case of Abdul Khair Mia vs Abdul Latif Sarder reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 and Hari Bondhu Pal vs Hari Mahan Shah reported in 34 CWN 36.

8. In the case of Abdul Khair Mia vs Abdul Latif Sarder reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 wherein their Lordships observed that—

"This fact as disclosed by the evidence is that the decree-holder by suppressing summons obtained the ex-parte decree fraudulently and this finding of fact has been arrived at both by the appellate Court below and the High Court Division. Such decree obtained fraudulently is a nullity in the eye of law."

9. In the case of Hari Bondhu Pals case (Supra), a division bench of the Calcutta High Court held as follows —

"The question is what would happen if a person carrying on business in the name of a firm dies during the pendency of the suit. It cannot be disputed that if a man dies before any suit instituted against him, the suit would be infractions as having brought against the dead man who used to every on business under an alias. As I understand it, the position of a person carrying on business in a firm name is only that of a person who has got an alias and a plaintiff desiring to sue him in his other name. If during the continuance of the suit that person dies, it is necessary, in my opinion to bring his legal representative on the record to have a proper decree made in the suit. If the plaintiff fails to do so, then the decree is made against a dead man, having a different name from his own proper name, and in that case, the decree would be an absolute nullity.

<u>10. From a glance through the aforementioned decision what emerges as a point of law is that before proceeding ex-parte the court must be satisfied that there is due service of summons upon the defendant. The court cannot proceed for ex-parte without being satisfied that summons had been duly served upon the defendant and if the court proceeds for an ex-parte decree the same will suffer from the patent error of law. On the other hand when a decree has been passed against a dead person, as there is no doubt that any decree passed against a dead man in a nullity. I find myself in full agreement with the principle laid down in the cases cited before me.</u>

11. I have considered the submission of the learned Advocates, perused the impugned Judgment and Decree, and material evidence on record, and on perusal of the whole order-sheet up to date of the trial court it cannot be held that summons was duly served upon the defendants 2 and 5 either by the process server or by registered post rather summon was returned un-served from the defendant No. 2 due to her death but the plaintiff did not take any steps for bringing the heirs of that said defendant No. 2 on record and instead of that, obtained a decree by concealing the aforesaid facts from the court.

12. In view of all the discussions made above I am of the considered view that the judgments of the courts below cannot be allowed to be maintained. The Rule got merit and the Rule, therefore, succeeds.

13. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree dated 12-11-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur in Title Appeal No. 18 of 2012 disallowed the appeal in affirming the judgment and decree dated 27-11-2012 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Shariatpur in Title Suit No. 36 of 2008 is hereby set-aside.

14. Let the order of stay granted at the time of issuing of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment and send down Lower Court Records at once.

End.
