case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-3-2012 passed by the 1-ligh Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3108 of 2011).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain CJ : This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-3-2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3108 of 2011 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this civil appeal, in a nutshell, are: The appellant herein as the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 11 of 2005 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Gazipur for specific performance of contract, stating, inter alia, that Al-haj Mohammad Noor was the owner of 49.08 acres of land. SA and RS records were published in his name. Mosammat Rana Noor became the owner by way of inheritance and oral gift made by Alhaj Mohammad Noor by swearing affidavit dated 14-1-1971. Mosammat Rana Noor entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff on 16-5-2002. The sale price was fixed at Taka 6,00,000 (six lac) per bigha. The defendant took an amount of Taka 1.25 crore as baina from the plaintiff through pay order No. 0540179 dated 16-5-2002. The plaintiff made further payment of Taka 23,00,000 (twenty three lac) on 8-9-2002 and Taka 30,00,000 (thirty lac) on 1-12-2002. In total, the plaintiff paid Taka 1.78 crore to defendant No. 1. The vendor could not execute the deed due to want of mutation in her name because the Government refused to mutate her name. The vendor filed Writ Petition No. 770 of 2004 for getting mutation with the financial aid of the plaintiff-petitioner. The High Court Division issued Rule and subsequently, the Rule was made absolute on 9-11-2004 directing the ADC (Rev), Gazipur to mutate the name of Rana Noor. The plaintiff requested the defendant to execute deed pursuant to the bainapatra dated 16-5-2002. Defendant No. 1 kept silent and, as such, the plaintiff served legal notice on 21-3-2005 asking for execution and registration of sale-deed which was received by the defendant on 22-3-2005. Defendant No. 1 tried to sell the land elsewhere and the plaintiff published public legal notice in "The Daily Ittefaq" and "The Daily Jugantor" on 23-3-2005 and, thereafter, filed the above suit for specific performance of contract.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that present respondent Nos. 1-3 were made party to the suit as the pro-forma defendants. Moreover, they were party to the earlier Writ Petition No. 770 of 2004 and direction was given upon them by the High Court Division on 9-11-2004 to mutate the name of defendant No. 1 and the Government did not challenge the said order and as such, the order of the High Court Division has become binding upon them and they cannot deny the title of the vendor, i.e. defendant No. 1 and the respondents cannot claim any right over the self-same properties. Respondent Nos. 1-3 were party as pro-forma defendants only for the purpose of mutation and payment of rent in future and the plaintiff made specific statements in paragraph-2 to the plaint of Title Suit No. 11 of 2005.

4. The suit was decreed on contest against defendant No. 1, and ex-parte against the pro-forma defendants. Respondent Nos.1-3 received the notice/summons on 2-4-2005 by putting seals and signatures. The main relief was directed against the principal defendant seeking specific performance of contract dated 16-5-2002 executed by and between the parties for sale of 49.08 acres of land.

5. The plaintiff-petitioner deposited the balance consideration of Taka 7,14,36,324 through treasury challan in compliance with the decree dated 29-4-2008. After that, the decree was modified vide order No. 67 dated 31-7-2008 by reducing the quantum of land to 28.77 acres from 49.08 acres on the ground that defendant No. 1 had no valid title over the remaining portion of the suit land. Accordingly, the plaint, judgment and decree were modified in order to correct the price of the suit-land and the Court below directed the judgment-debtor to take the balance consideration money of Taka 3,45,09,091 after deduction of baina money of Taka 1,78,00,000 vide order No. 71 dated 19-10-2008. Meanwhile, the judgment-debtor applied to the Court for withdrawal of the entire deposited amount of Taka 7,14,36,324 from the Court fraudulently without giving the entire land and such kind of mala fide prayer was rejected by the Court itself vide order No. 70 dated 6-10-2008.

6. Defendant No. 1 being the judgment-debtor filed First Appeal No. 6 of 2009 on 07-1-2009 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree of the original suit passed on 29-4-2008 and modified on 31-7-2008.

7. Meanwhile, the appellant being the decree-holder filed Title Execution Case No. 21 of 2008 on 20-11-2009 and the judgment-debtor applied to the High Court Division for staying all further proceedings of the execution case till disposal of the appeal, which was allowed by order dated 20-1-2009.

8. Respondent Nos.1-3 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 455 of 2008 before the trial Court on 20-10-2008 under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29-4-2008 passed in the original suit.

9. The principal defendant No. 1 being respondent No. 2 to the miscellaneous case appeared in the case and informed the Court that she had filed appeal before the High Court Division. The appellant being opposite party No. 1 to the miscellaneous case filed written objection on 9-11-2008. Due to stay order passed by the High Court Division on 20-10-2009, the appellant did not contest the case in good faith. After that, the miscellaneous case was taken up for ex-parte hearing and ultimately, the application-was allowed on 25-4-2011 by setting aside the decree of the original suit dated 29-4-2008.

10. Being aggrieved by the said order dated 25-4-2011, the appellant preferred revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 3108 of 2011. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties concerned discharged the Rule directing the Joint District Judge, second Court, Gazipur to dispose of Title Suit No. 11 of 2005 within 1 (one) year from the date of receipt of a copy of the judgment of the High Court Division.

11. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff as the leave-petitioner has filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1534 of 2013 before this Division, in which, leave was granted on 6-8-2015, resulting in Civil Appeal No. 404 of 2015.

12. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the High Court Division has failed to consider that orders of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 2008 dated 4-2-2009, 19-2-2009 and 23-11-2009 show that the Government as well as the trial Court had the knowledge about the appeal pending before the High Court Division and the trial Court had no jurisdiction to set-aside the judgment and decree dated 24-9-2008 (decree signed on 3-5-2008) passed in Other Class Suit No. 11 of 2005. He further submits that the High Court Division has failed to consider that the trial Court failed to decide the question of limitation in filing the miscellaneous case, or the date of knowledge for filing the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was apparently barred by limitation. He then submits that the High Court Division has failed to consider that the appellant as the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract without praying for any relief against the Government and the summons were duly served upon defendant Nos. 2-4 and that the decree was obtained on contest against defendant No. 1, Rana Noor, and then execution case was started against defendant No. 1 only, not against the Government. He continues to submit that summons of the original suit were served upon the Government on 2-4-2005, who received the summons by seal and signatures and the suit was decreed on 29-4-2008, and the miscellaneous case was filed on 20-10-2008 on a false plea long after 171 days of passing of the decree instead of 30 days, without any explanation or prayer for condonation of delay and the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division should be set-aside. He lastly submits that the claim of the Government in respect of 4.64 acres of land out of 49.08 acre of land is vague, unspecified and misleading and the trial Court committed illegality by setting aside the judgment and decree as a whole and as such, interference of this Division is required.

13. Mr Momtaz Uddin Fakir, learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-3, on the other hand, submits that defendant No. 2, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur, was designated as proforma-defendant but in the plaint the plaintiff stated that proforma-defendant No. 2 is a necessary party to the suit for specific performance of contract in view of the provisions of law and that the plaintiff in order to confuse defendant No. 2 made it proforma-defendant No. 2 and that the trial Court and the High Court Division rightly considered this aspect of the case and the trial Court set-aside the judgment and decree dated 25-4-2011 and as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the trial Court came to a finding that summons were not duly served upon defendant Nos.2-4 and as such, they could not take proper step in the suit and this finding of the trial Court has been affirmed by the High Court Division and as such, no interference is called for.

14. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No. 4, on the other hand, supported the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division.

15. We have considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocate for the appellant and the learned Additional Attorney-General for respondent Nos. 2-3 and the learned Senior Advocate for respondent No. 4, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

16. It is necessary, to quote the grounds, on which, leave was granted as under: "The High Court Division has failed to consider that orders of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 2008 dated 4-2-2009, 19-2-2009 and 23-11-2009 show that the Government as well as the trial Court had the knowledge about the appeal pending before the High Court Division and the trial Court had no jurisdiction to interfere. The High Court Division has failed to consider and decide that the trial Court failed to decide the question of limitation in filing the miscellaneous case, or the date of knowledge for filing the case. The miscellaneous case was apparently barred by limitation for filing the case after 171 days from the decree and such important issue of law has been totally overlooked by the Courts below.

The High Court Division has failed to consider that the petitioner as plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract without praying for any relief against the Government and the notices were duly served upon the defendant Nos. 2-4 and decree obtained on contest against defendant No. 1 Rana Noor and then execution case was started against defendant No. 1 only, not against the Government and the Government had nothing to do, and the miscellaneous case was unwarranted.  The High Court Division has failed to consider that the Government received the notices of appeal and could have contested the appeal instead of proceeding in the miscellaneous case.

The High Court Division has failed to consider that the summons of the original suit were served upon the Government on2-4-2005, who received the summons by seal and signatures and the suit was decreed on 29-4-2008, and filed the case on 20-10-2008 on a false plea long after 171 days of the decree instead of 30 days, without any explanation or prayer for condonation of delay and the trial Court allowed the miscellaneous case most illegally, and the High Court Division committed gross illegalities, which requires interference.

The High Court Division has failed to consider that defendant Nos.2-4 have not given any specific description of their claimed land measuring 4.64 acres out of 49.08 acres of land; though the decree was modified by reducing the suit land to 28.77 acres and the Government is not affected by the decree. There is no specific schedule of the claimed land and the claim is vague, unspecified and misleading and the trial Court committed illegalities by setting aside the judgment and decree as a whole, which requires interference by this Division."

17. Defendant-respondent Nos.1-3 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 455 of 2008 in the Second Court of the Joint District Judge, Gazipur under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The miscellaneous case was allowed by the judgment and order dated 25-4-2011 setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29-4-2008.

18. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record set-aside the ex-parte decree dated 29-4-2008 passed against defendant Nos.2 to 5 holding that the miscellaneous case was filed on 20-10-2008, that is, within 30 days from the date of knowledge of the judgment and decree and as such, the case was not barred by limitation. The trial Court noticed that defendant Nos.1-3 were profroma-defendants in the suit and that the properties appended in the schedule to the plaint are properties belonging to the Government although defendant-respondent Nos.1-3 were not made principal-defendants and they were confused in such a situation and could not contest the suit. Therefore, the trial Court was of the opinion that there were sufficient reasons for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree passed against defendant Nos.2 to 5. The High Court Division also affirmed the aforesaid findings of the trial Court. The High Court Division came to a finding that Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure speaks about satisfaction and this satisfaction is the satisfaction of the Court and that the Court found that the Government satisfactorily explained the cause of non-appearance of defendant-respondent Nos.2 to 5 when the suit was called on for hearing.

19. Having gone through the record, we find that defendant Nos.2-4 were designated as profroma-defendants in the suit who claimed in the miscellaneous case that the properties appended to the schedule of the plaint belonged to the Government. The plaintiff stated that summons were duly served upon defendant Nos.2-4. As defendant Nos.2-4 were designated as proforma-defendants, they were confused when summons of the suit were served upon them. The plaintiff though did not pray for any relief against defendant No. 2 but it prayed for passing direction upon defendant Nos.3, 4 and 5 for taking necessary action in respect of mutation, execution and registration of the sale-deed in its favour. The plaint was drafted in such way which created confusion among defendant Nos. 2-4. Therefore, the trial Court and the High Court Division were completely justified in holding that summons were not properly served upon defendant Nos.2-4.

20. Defendant Nos.2-4 by adducing evidence both oral and documentary could prove that they came to know about the ex pate decree on 16-10-2008 and that the miscellaneous case was filed on 20-10-2008. Since the miscellaneous case was filed within 30 days from the date of knowledge of the impugned judgment and decree, it is within the statutory period of limitation and it was not barred by limitation.

21. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that defendant Nos.2-4 had not given any specific description of their claimed land measuring 4.64 acres out of 49.08 acres of land.

<u>22. In the application filed under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, there is no scope for giving any schedule. The questions to be decided in such a case is whether summons were duly served upon the defend-ants or whether they were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the suit was called on for hearing.</u>

23. It is also contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court Division failed to consider that orders of Execution Case No. 21 of 2008 dated 24-2-2009 show that the Government as well as the trial Court had the knowledge about First Appeal No. 06 of 2009 pending before the High Court Division and as such, the trial Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decree.

<u>24. A defendant against whom an ex-parte decree has been passed can either file an appeal against the decree, or file an application for review or pray for restoration of the suit under Order IX Rule 13. These remedies are all concurrent and independent. An application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be heard notwithstanding the pendency of the appeal arising out of the same decree. It makes no difference that the application is made by one defendant and the appeal has been filed by another defendant. But it is to be mentioned here that where the ex-parte decree has been confirmed or otherwise disposed of on appeal, the Court passing the decree ceases to have jurisdiction to hear the application for restoration even though the application was filed before the appeal was filed as its decree merged in the appellate decree. The same principle will hold good even if the appeal has been preferred by a party other than the defendant against whom the decree was passed ex-parte.</u>

25. In this connection reliance may be placed on the case of Md Wasiq Khan vs Md Sakib Khan, 31 DLR (AD) 57, it has been held in paragraph-18 as under:

18. On a review of the decisions and the discussion on the question set out, the following propositions seem to be well settled:

1. Where a defendant against whom an exparte decree is passed applies under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set it aside and at the same time prefers an appeal from it, the Calcutta High Court has held that notwithstanding the pendency of appeal the original court may proceed with the application. Damodar vs Sarat Chandra, 13 CWN 846 and Kumud Nath vs Jathindra Nath, 38 Calcutta 394. The Allahabad High Court has also taken the same view. Mathura vs Ram Charan, 37 Allahabad 208; Gajaraj vs Swaminath, 39 Allahabad 13: Humani vs Azizuddin, 39 Allahabad 143. The extreme position taken by Madras High Court in Sankar vs Subdrajan, 30 Madras, 535 has not been followed by other High Courts.

2. Where the exparte decree has been confirmed or otherwise disposed of on appeal the court which passed the exparte decree has no longer any power to entertain an application to set it aside, even though the application was made before the appeal was filed. Mathura vs Ram Charan 37 Allahabad, 208.

3. The same principle will hold good even if the appeal has been preferred by a party other than the defendant against whom the decree was passed exparte provided the decree was one and indivisible. Dhonai Sikder vs Tarak Nath, 12 CU 53.

4. But it will not affect the case of the defendant against whom ex-parte decree was passed and whose claim was not subject matter of appeal although he might be made party as respondent in the appeal. Abdul Jalil Bhuiyan vs Majibar, 12 DLR 581.

<u>26. The remedy under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not available if the appeal is disposed of prior thereto. But before disposal of the appeal trial Court which passed the ex-parte decree against defendant Nos.2 to 5 is competent to hear and dispose of an application filed under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

27. President Order No. 142 of 1972 in unequivocal terms stated in Article 6 that no person shall, without joining the Government which shall be a necessary party, file or proceed with any suit for specific performance of contract relating to transfer of immoveable property or for declaration of title to, or assertion of ownership of any such properly.

28. In the case in hand, defendant No. I, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur was impleaded in the suit as proforma-defendant No. 2 in violation of President's Order No. 142 of 1972.

In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any substance in this appeal. Accordingly, this civil appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Dr Naim Ahmed with Khandaker Shahriar Shakir, Advocates------For the Petitioner. 
Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate------For the OP Nos. 1-3.
parties:
Tara Bibi-----Defendant-Respondent-Petitioner
VS
Md Majed Mridha and others-------Plaintiffs-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-1-2006 (decree signed on 24-1-2006), passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari, in Title Appeal No.40 of 2005, allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2005 (decree signed on 12-5-2005), passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Baliakandi, Rajbari, in Title Suit No.16 of 2006, should not be set-aside, and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of this Rule, in brief, are that, one Md Majed Mridha and others, as plaintiffs, had filed Title Suit No.16 of 2004, before the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Baliakandi, Rajbari, against Tara Bibi others, being the defendants, seeking declaration of title and joint possession with the defendants and also prayed for declaration that, the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, registered in the office of Sub-Registrar, Baliakandi, Rajbari, is forged, without consideration, ineffective and was obtained by false personification, as stated in the plaint, as well as in the petition for amendment of the plaint. The defendant No. 1 had appeared in that suit and contested by filing written statements. The defendant No. 1 had also filed additional written statements in view of the amendment of the plaint. The defendant's case is that, she is owner of the suit property, as purchaser and that the plaintiffs are neither co-sharers, nor they have any inheritable interest in the suit property.

3. The plaintiffs adduced 4 witnesses to prove their case who have deposed as PW Nos. 1-4 and produced certain documents marked as exhibits 1 to 4, to support their case. On the other hand, the defendant No. 1 has examined himself as DW 1 and also produced DW Nos. 2-4. Besides, the defendant No. 1 has produced certain documents, marked as exhibits Ka, Kha and exhibit -I to prove her case.

4. The Trial Court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the oral and documentary evidences on record, dismissed the suit by her judgment and decree dated 10-5-2005 (decree signed on 12-5-2005).

5. Against the said judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the plaintiffs-Appellants-Opposite Parties preferred Title Appeal No.40 of 2005 before the District Judge, Rajbari, which was heard by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari, who, being the Appellate Court, has passed the impugned judgment and decree, allowing the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court dated 17-1-2006 (decree signed on 24-1-2006).

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the defendant-Respondent No. 1-Petitioner has filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and obtained the present Rule.

7. Learned Advocates Mr Naim Ahmed and Mr Khandaker Shahriar Shakir appeared for the petitioner. Mr Shakir, having placed the petition, judgments of both the courts below, the evidence adduced by the parties and other materials on record, first of all submits that, the admitted position is that, Md Majed Mridha was the owner of the suit property. The plaintiffs further case is that, Md Majed Mridha died leaving his 2(two) sons, one daughter and his 2nd wife i.e. the petitioner Tara Bibi (defendant No. 1), as his heirs in the suit property. On the contrary, he next points out that, the defendant's plain case is that the plaintiffs and the defendant are neither in joint possession, nor are they co-sharers by inheritance in the suit property. Rather, by a registered deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, the defendant-petitioner Tara Bibi has purchased the suit property from Md Majed Mridha (her husband and father of the plaintiffs). He then submits that, the trial court has framed proper issues and meticulously discussed the evidence on record and has come to a correct finding that, before his death, Md Majzed Mridha had transferred the suit property, vide deed No. 999 dated 08.03.1997 (Ext. Kha) to his 2nd wife, the defendant No. 1 Tara Bibi. He further submits that, although the plaintiffs had managed to produce the attesting witness Bashiram Das, as PW 2, to support their case, however, the trial court has compared the signature of the said witness Bashiram Das, that he had put on the kabala deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha), with his admitted signature made in another deed No. 4788 dated 5-11-1995, in which, the said Bashiram Das and his wife Sreemoti Kalitara Das were the sellers/executants. He proceeds on that, the trial court, after comparison of these signatures, has rightly arrived at the finding that, the signature put on the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) was that of the attesting witness Bashiram Das. The learned Advocate further submits that, the DW 2 Moslem Biswas, who is maternal uncle of the plaintiff, has admitted that he was present at the time of writing the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) and that the attesting witness Bashiram Das has put his signature on the said deed in his presence. He next pointed out that, Bashiram Das (PW 2) has also put his signature below the affidavit annexed to the said deed, as required by PO 92 of 1972. Therefore, the trial court has rightly arrived at the finding that, since Md Majed Mridha has transferred the title and possession of the suit property, vide deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, in favour of the defendant No. 1 Tara Bibi, therefore he left nothing in the suit property (schedule Kha) to be inherited by two sons and one daughter of the deceased Md Majed Mridha. But, the appellate court has not properly assessed the evidence on record placed before it and, as such, it has wrongly reversed the judgment of the trial court. Therefore, he concludes that, the appellate court has committed grave error of law, resulting in error in the impugned decision, occasioning failure of justice. Hence, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is liable to be set aside, and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court may kindly be upheld.

8. Learned Advocate Mr Md Khurshid Alain Khan appeared on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-3. Mr Khan submits that, admittedly the suit property belonged to Md Majed Mridha, who died leaving the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 Tara Bibi, his 2nd wife, as his heirs. He further submits that, there was no reason for Md Majed Mridha to transfer the suit property to his 2nd wife, as alleged, by depriving his two sons and one daughter. He also submits that, the entire case of the defendant No. 1 is concocted and the transfer was not done for any consideration. The PW 2 has also testified that he did not sign the impugned deed as the attesting witness, he also submits. But, the trial court has failed to find that there was no consideration for the alleged impugned sale to the defendant No. 1, nor the execution of the deed has been properly proved. Hence, the finding of the trial court is based on no evidence. He next argues that, the appellate court has rightly passed the impugned judgment and decree by setting aside the judgment of the trial court, upon proper appreciation of evidence on record and that, this Rule has no merit and the same is liable to be discharged.

9. I have heard the learned Advocates for the contending parties, perused the application for revision, lower Court's record as well as the judgment of both the Courts below and other materials in the record.

10. It is admitted position that Md Majed Mridha was the owner of the suit property, who later died leaving his 2 (two) sons, one daughter and the 2nd wife i.e. the petitioner Tara Bibi (defendant No. 1). It also appears that, the trial court has framed proper issues and meticulously discussed the evidence on record, and has come to the finding that, before the death of Md Majzed Mridha, he had transferred the suit property, vide deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) to his 2nd wife, the defendant No. 1 Taba Bibi.

11. It further appears that, the defendant has produced one Bashiram Das as PW 2, who denied his signature, as an attesting witness to the sale deed dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) and thus he had deposed to disprove the execution of exhibit Kha.

12. However, the trial court has compared signatures of Bashiram Das, PW 2, one being put on the impugned kabala deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) with his another signature, admittedly made on a deed No. 4788 dated 5-11-1995, in which Bashiram Das and his wife Sreemoti Kalitara Das had signed as the sellers/executants. The trial court has, thus rightly arrived at the finding that, the signature on deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) was put by Bashiram Das as attesting witness. The DW 2 Moslem Biswas, who is the maternal uncle of the plaintiffs, admitted that he was present at the time of writing of the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 (Ext. Kha) and he has categorically narrated, during his testimony, that Bashiram Das (PW 2) had put his signature, on the said deed, as an attesting witness, in his presence.

13. Thus, it has been properly proved before the trial court that, the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, executed by Md Majed Mridha and thereby the entire suit property was transferred to the defendant No. 1, Tara Bibi, and the said deed was produced before the trial court in original and Bashiram Das PW 2 has also put his another signature at below the affidavit annexed to the said deed, as required by PO No. 92 of 1972.

14. Therefore, the trial court has rightly arrived at the finding that, since Md Majed Mridha had transferred his entire title and possession in the suit property, vide deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, in favour of the defendant No. 1 Tara Bibi, therefore, he left nothing in the suit property (schedule Kha) to be inherited by two sons and one daughter of the deceased Md Majed Mridha.

15. The comparison of signature made by the trial court with that of exhibit "Kha" and exhibit-I are very much correct and is corroborated by DW 2 as per provision of section 71 read with the explanation to section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872.

16. But, the appellate court has failed to properly assess and interpret the evidence on record placed before it and, as such, it has erroneously reversed the judgment of the trial court.

<u>17. It should be mentioned here that, section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872 requires that when the execution of a registered document is disputed then it must be proved by at least one attesting witnesses, if alive, who is subject to the process of the court and capable of giving evidence. However, if the execution of the document is denied by the attesting witness then it should be proved by other evidence, as stipulated in section 71 of the Evidence Act, 1872. Therefore, it was within the competence of the trial court, as authorized by section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872, to compare the signature of the attesting witness Bashiram Das with his admitted signature made in another deed No. 4788 dated 5-11-1995 (Ext. I) and to record finding upon such comparison.</u>

<u>18. Besides, it has been adequately proved before the trial court that, the DW 2 Moslem Biswas was physically present at the office of the Sub-Registrar, Baliakandi, Rajbari, at the time of registration of the said deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997. As such, as clarified in the explanation to the section 47 of the Evidence Act, 1872, DW 2 was a person acquainted with the signature of the executants of deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997, and his deposition that Bashiram Das has signed the deed No. 999 dated 8-3-1997 was relevant and admissible in evidence as per provisions of section 71 of the Act, and that also corroborates the finding of the trial court, arrived at as per provisions of section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872.</u>

19. So far as the issue of payment of consideration is concerned, the DW 2 has positive case that Md Majed Mridha took loan and, in order to repay the same, he sold the suit property to his 2nd wife Tara Bibi. The PW 1 admitted that, Md Majed Mridha had bank loan which he could not repay. But PW 1 could not reply during his cross examination, as to what was the amount of loan and how much money he had repaid. Therefore, the case of the defendant No. 1 Tara Bibi that, Md Majed Mridha had bank loan and that was repaid by his 2nd wife, is proved by the preponderance of evidence. The finding of the trial court that, the suit property was transferred by the deceased Md Majed Mridha in order to repay the loan has thus been proved.

20. The trial court has also considered the deposition and noticed the demeanor of the DW 1 Tara Bibi and recorded that she was a simple village woman, and there was no reason to suspect that she wasn't telling the truth, telling lie, or to believe that she had forged the document in order to grab the suit property.

21. Hence, I am of the opinion that, the appellate court has misread the evidence on record and has committed grave error of law that has resulted in error in his decision occasioning failure of justice. Hence, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is liable to be set aside, his findings be reversed and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court should be upheld.

22. This Rule has merit and the same is to be made absolute.

Order

In the result, the Rule is made absolute.

The impugned judgment and decree dated 17-1-2006 (decree signed on 24-1-2006), passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari, in Title Appeal No.40 of 2005, is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2005 (decree signed on 12-5-2005), passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Baliakandi, Rajbari, in Title Suit No.16 of 2006 is hereby affirmed.

The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

No costs.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down to the concerned Courts at once.

End.

Purmindu Bikash Das with Dipayan Shah Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
None appears—For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Abdul Gafur and others ------ Pre-emptee- Petitioners
VS
Hazi Abdul Bashor and others ----- Pre-emptor-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman J : On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure the instant Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite Party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 11-2-2016 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2013 rejecting an application filed under Order VII, rue 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the application of pre-emption case should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The material facts, relevant for disposal of the instant Rule, in short, are that the Opposite Party No. 1 as pre-emptor filed a case being Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2013 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong praying for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of the land described in the schedule to the application for pre-emption.

3. One Habibur Rahman, the predecessor of the pre-emptor was the co-sharer of the khatian in question i.e. BS Khatian No. 1161. Habibur Rahman died leaving behind one son, the pre-emptor had 4 daughters, the opposite party Nos. 44 to 47. Another co-sharer Abdul Salam died leaving behind one son, the opposite party Nos. 15 and 5 daughters, the opposite party Nos. 10 to 14 the vendors. One co-sharer Siddique Ahmed died leaving behind the opposite party Nos. 16 and 17. The opposite party Nos. 18 to 20 are the co-sharers of the Khatian. Obaidul Haque, Syed Ahamed, Nawsha Miah, the co-sharer of the Khatian died leaving behind the opposite party Nos. 20 to 24, 26 to 29, 30 to 32 respectively. Another co-sharer Amir Hamja died leaving behind two sons, Abut Hasem and Abul Kalam who sold their shares to the opposite party No. 33. Other co-sharers of the Khatian Sufia Khatun, Ajahar Miah, Abdul Alem died leaving behind the opposite party Nos. 34 to 36, 38 and 39 to 43 respectively. Another co-sharer Parija Khatun is the opposite party No. 37. The pre-emptor is the co-sharer of the suit jama. The pre-emptee opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 and 6 are the strangers, not the co-sharers. The pre-emptee opposite party No. 5 was the co-sharer. The pre-emp tee No. 5 out of misunderstanding with pre-emptor has purchased the case land by the pre-emptees from the vendor-opposite party Nos. 7 to 14; no notice has been served upon the pre-emptor. The vendor sold the case property very secretly to the pre-emptee. On 30-12-2012 the pre-emptees came to the land under pre-emption for measuring the said land. The pre-emptees at that time disclosed to the pre-emptor that they purchased the suit land from the opposite party Nos. 7 to 14; thereafter through searching on 2-1-2013 the pre- emptor obtained the certified copy of the deed in question and definitely came to know in respect of the sale in question. The suit land is very much necessary to the pre-emptor hence, the pre-emptor has been compelled to file the instant pre-emption Miscellaneous Case.

4. The pre-emptees entered into appearance and contested the case by filing written objection denying all the materials allegation made in the application for pre-emption.

5. During the pendency of the case the pre-emptees filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Hereinafter referred as Code) for rejection of the application for pre-emption on two grounds, one the pre-emptor at the time of filing of the case did not deposit the requisite money as required by law and another is the pre-emptor prayed for partial pre-emption which is barred by the principles of pre-emption.

6. The pre-emptor filed written objection against the application for rejection of the application for pre-emption.

7. The learned Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong upon hearing both the learned Advocates of the respective parties considering the pleadings and relevant law by his judgment and order dated 11-2-2016 rejected the application for rejection of the pre-emption application.

8. The pre-emptees having aggrieved with the order dated 11-2-2016 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2013 passed by the Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong preferred the instant revisional application and obtained the instant Rule with an order of stay.

9. Mr Purmindu Bikash Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner took us through the sub-section 3 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Hereinafter referred as the Act) and pointed that the pre-emptor did not deposit money required as per sub-section 3(a), (b) and (c) of the Act however, according to their calculation deposited Taka 233.33 less than total money.

10. He has further pointed that point of less deposit was not detected at the instance of the pre-emptor however, this point has been agitated by the pre-emptees in their application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

11. 2nd Point raised by Mr Purmindu Bikash Das according to the pre-emptor he prays for partial pre-emption. Therefore, Mr Purmindu Bikash Das took us through the prayer Ka of the application of pre-emption case which are runs as follows:—

তপশীল

জিলা-চট্টগ্রাম, থানা/উপজেলা-সাতকানিয়া, মৌজা-জনাব কেওচিয়া, জে,এল নং-৩৯ আর,এস খতিয়ান নং-২৭৩ বি,এস খতিয়ান নং-১১৬১ দাগ নং আর, এস ৩৩২৯ বি,এস দাগ নং-৫২৩২, দাগ আন্দর ১/১৩ (এক গন্ডা এক কান্তি তের) তিল নাল জমির মধ্যে ৫নং খরিদ্দার জিয়াউল হকের হিস্যা বাদ দিয়ে বাকী জমি ১ গন্ডা ১৩ তিল। এক গন্ডা তেল তিল থানা- সাতকানিয়া সাব-রেজিষ্ট্রি অফিসে রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত বিগত ২৪-১২-২০১২ ইং তারিখের রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত ৫১৭০ নং কবলার অমি বিরোধীয়।

জমির চৌহদ্দি বিবরণঃ__

উত্তরে-ছিদ্দিক আহামদ দক্ষিণে-নুরু মেম্বার ।

পূর্বে-জিয়াউল হক পশ্চিমে-আবদুল হক গং।

এই চৌহদ্দির মধ্যে ১-১৩ (এক গন্ডা তের ভিল) জমি মাত্র ।

12. He also referring the schedule of the application pointed that the land which has been transferred through the deed No. 5170 dated 24-12-2012 belong to more then one parties however, the pre-emptor in the schedule has mentioned that except share of purchaser No. 5 Ziaul Haque rest land 1 No 13 cam (sic) is under the pre-emption. However, in the schedule of the application the pre-emptor did not specifily the land of pre-emptee No. 5 and rest of the land which sought pre-emption by the pre-emptor. Therefore, in such unspecified and undivided land partial pre-emption cannot be allowed.

13. The opposite party No. 1 entered to the revisional application by filing power through one Abdul Momen Chowdhury on 2-1-2017 however, he never appeared before us although this item has been appearing in the cause list with the name of the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 for few weeks.

14. The pre-emptee called in question the legality and propriety of the impugned order dated 11-2-2016.

15. Therefore, we are of the view that we must address the first question raised by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee-petitioner. In view of the legal question as raised by the . learned Advocate we must look into the provision of sub-sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows:-

"96. Right of Pre-emption—(1) If a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is sold to a person who is not a co-sharer tenant in the holding, one or more cosharer tenants of the holding may, within two months of the service of the notice given under section 98, or, if no notice has been served under section 98, within two months of the date of the knowledge of the sale, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be sold to himself or themselves:

Provided that no application under this section shall lie unless the applicant is—

(a) a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance; and

(b) a person to whom sale of the holding or the portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under section 90: Provided further that no application under this section shall lie after expiry of three years from the date of registration of the sale deed.

(2) In an application under sub-section (1), all other co-sharer tenants by inheritance of the holding and the purchaser shall be made parties.

(3) An application under sub-section (1) shall be dismissed unless the applicant or applicants, at the time of making it, deposit in the Court—

(a) the amount of the consideration money of the sold holding or portion or share of the holding as stated in the notice under section 89 or in the deed of sale, as the case may be;

(b) compensation at the rate of twenty five per centum of the amount referred to in clause (a); and

(c) an amount calculated at the rate of eight per centum simple annual interest upon the amount referred to in clause (a) for the period from the date of the execution of the deed of sale to the date of filing of the application for preemption."

16. On perusal of the above provisions of law it is apparent that the pre-emptor must deposit the amount as prescribed in clause (a), (b), and (c) of sub-section 3 of section 96 of the Act at the time of filing the pre-emption application. However, on perusal of the application for pre-emption and impugned order it is patently visible that the pre-emptor and the learned Judge of the Court below clearly admitted amount deposited less than the required amount. So, the submission advanced by the learned Advocate regarding the less deposit is sustainable which by now is not a disputed question. However, the learned Judge of the trial Court has further opined that the pre-emptor filed a petition to deposit the due amount as calculated by the pre-emptee. The Court has passed an order to deposit the said less amount. The learned Judge of the Court below further opined that there is no bar to deposit the rest amount during the pendency of the case. So we have to now answer whether the opinion of the learned Joint District Judge is correct and acceptable.

17. Mr PK Das, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has categorically pointed that the period of time for filing of the pre-emption as stipulated in the provision of sub-section 1 of section 96 of the Act is 2 (two) months from the date of registration or from the date of knowledge. The pre-emptor has filed the application under section 96 on 29-1-2013 however, the question of depositing the rest amount has arisen while the pre-emptee filed application on 24-4-2015 and the learned Judge by his order dated 11-2-2016 allowed the pre-emptor to deposit the rest amount from the date of calculation and order.

18. The requirement of the law is that the deposit must be given at the time of filing of the application under section 96 of the Act. According to provision of the sub-section 4 of section 96 of the Act the deposit requires money is a condition precedent. So, we are of the view that the sub-section 4 of section 96 of the Act be reproduced for ready reference which runs as follows:—

"On receipt of such application accompanied by such deposits, the Court shall give notice to the purchaser and to the other persons who made parties thereto under sub-section (2) to appear within such period as it may fix and shall require the purchaser to state what other sums he has paid in respect of rent since the date of sale and what expenses he has incurred in annulling encumbrances on, or for making any improvement in respect of the holding, portion or share sold."

19. On perusal of the provision of sub-section 4 of section 96 of the Act it's become crystal clear that the Court cannot register the application as pre-emption case without taking deposit of the require amount as described in clause (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section 3 of the section 96. So, in view of such condition precedent as provided in the provision of law the learned Joint District Judge directed the pre-emptor to deposit the rest due amount on 11-2-2016 which should not but must opine that such direction is not within the purview of the provisions of sub-sections 3 and 4 of section 96 of the Act. So, we are of the considered view that the opinion of the learned Joint District Judge regarding the deposit of the rest amount by the pre-emptor is not only illegal but also flagrant violation of the provisions of sub-sections 3 and 4 of section 96 of the Act.

20. We find support of our view to the case of Mojibar Rahman Mondal (Md) vs Khoteza Khatoon reported in 2 BLC (AD) 170.

21. It has been held in Mojibar Rahman case that the application for deposit of the rest of the amount was allowed by the Court below and on revision the High Court Division also upheld that order however, the Appellate Division found that legal proposition of section 96 of the Act does not allow to deposit the rest of the amount beyond the period of limitation. Therefore, we cannot but to opine that the direction for deposition of the rest of amount beyond the statutory period is clear violation of the provision of law of sub-section 3 of section 96 of the Act.

22. In the impugned order the learned Joint District Judge further opined that there is no impediment to allow the partial pre-emption.

23. He has also opined that there is no such law which impede the pre-emptor to pray for the partial pre-emption. We have to give answer whether the opinion of the learned Joint District Judge is sustainable in accordance with law or not.

24. It has been held in the case of Arifan Nessa vs Haroon-or-Rashed reported 2 BLC 76 that State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1951, section 96—

"Partial pre-emption cannot be allowed-Although all the pre-emptees were brought on record except one who was impleaded-in the pre-emption case after the statutory period of limitation, a valuable right has already accrued in favour of the pre-emptees for which the case must fail as partial pre-emption is not allowed under section 96 of the Act. "

25. It has been held to the case of Hatem Ali Mollah vs Hayet Khan reported 1986 BCR (AD) 237:

State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, section 96—

"Partial pre-emption is not permissible." Deposit of entire consideration money stated in the kabala was made but pre-emption of only 54½ acres of land out of 1.14 acres was sought- When the prayer for pre-emption was for a part of the entire land sold, the prayer cannot be read in respect of the whole when the entire consideration money stated in the kabala was deposited by the appellants. The Court is not required to make deduction otherwise in respect of the prayer.

26. Therefore, in view of the above authorities we are of the opinion that learned Joint District Judge in an imperceptible manner totally misconceived regarding the settled principle enunciated by the apex Court in respect of partial pre-emption which cannot be sustained in law. So, we are unable to accept the opinion expressed by the learned Joint District Judge as well it is deprecated.

27. The pre-emptees filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure to reject the plaint. Now, legal question is whether the application of pre-emption case is plaint or not ? So, we are of the view that the provisions of Rules 1 to 9 and 11 Order VII of the Code be reproduced herein below which runs as follows

1.	The plaint shall contain the following particulars:—

(a) the name of the Court in which the suit is brought;

(b) the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff;

(c) the name, description and place of residence of the defendant, so far as they can be ascertained;

(d) where the plaintiff or the defendant is a minor or a person of unsound mind, a statement to that effect;

(e) the facts constituting the cause of action and when it arose;

(f) the facts showing that the Court has jurisdiction;

(g) the relief which the plaintiff claims;

(h) where the plaintiff has allowed a set-off or relinquished a portion of his claim, the amount so allowed or relinquished; and

(i) a statement of the value of the subject-matter of the suit for the purposes of jurisdiction and of court-fees, so far as the case admits.

2.	Where the plaintiff seeks the recovery of money, the plaint shall state the precise amount claimed:

But where the plaintiff sues for mesne profits, or for an amount which will be found due to him on taking unsettled accounts between him and the defendant, the plaint shall state approximately the amount sued for.

3. Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers.

4. Where the plaintiff sues in a representative character the plaint shall show not only that he has an actual existing interest in the subject-matter, but that he has taken the steps (if any) necessary to enable him to institute a suit concerning it.

5. The plaint shall show that the defendant is or claims to be interested in the subject-matter, and that he is liable to be called upon to answer the plaintiffs demand.

6. Where the suit is instituted after the expiration of the period prescribed by the law of limitation, the plaint shall show the ground upon which exemption from such law is claimed.

7. Every plaint shall state specifically the relief which the plaintiff claims either simply or in the alternative, and it shall not be necessary to ask for general or other relief which may always be given as the Court may think just to the same extent as it had been asked for. A the same rule shall apply to any relief claimed by the defendant in his written statement.

8. Where the plaintiff seeks relief in respect of. several distinct grounds, they shall be stated as far as may be separately and distinctly.

9. (1) The plaintiff shall endorse on the plaint, or annex thereto, a list of the documents (if any) which he has produced along with it; and, if the plaint is admitted, shall present as many copies on plain paper of the plaint as there are defendants, unless the Court by reason of the length or the plaint or the number of the defendants, or for any other sufficient reason permits him to present a like number of concise statements of the nature of the claim made, or of the relief claimed in the suit, in which case he shall present such statements.

(2) Where the plaintiff sues, or the defendant or any of the defendants is sued, in a representative capacity, such statements shall show in what capacity the plaintiff or defendant sues or is sued.

(3) The plaintiff may, by leave of the Court, amend such statements so as to make them correspond with the plaint.

(4) The chief ministerial officer of the Court shall sign such list and copies or statements if, on examination, he finds them to be correct.

11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:—

(a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b)where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.'[:]

[Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days].

2j(e) Where any of the provisions of rule 9 (1A) is not complied with and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to comply therewith within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so.]"

28. On perusal of the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code it is clearly divulged that the provision can only invoke on an application only to reject the plaint. The application filed in the Miscellaneous Case which is not a plaint, now the question is in the instant Miscellaneous Case the pre-emptee as applicant can invoke the Rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure.

29. To determine the question whether Miscellaneous Case under section 96 of the Act can be rejected through such an application under Rule 11 of Order VII of the Code.

30. To draw the differences between the plaint and the application of pre-emption case we must refer to the provisions Rule 1 to 9 of Order VII of the Code because the legislator codified the requirements of the plaint for different class of suit as quoted in Rules 1-9 in the Order VII, of the Code but we do not find any such provision of law for the application under section 96 of the Act.

31. Besides the above legal proposition another prescribed form has been laid down in Sub-Rule 44 of Rule 774 of the Civil Rule's and Order for filing application of pre-emption case. In the referred sub-rule it has been shown that any application under section 96 of the Act, 1950 would be registered as Miscellaneous Case. Therefore, it is crystal clear that such an application cannot be treated as suit and description given in the application cannot be treated as pleading of plaint.

<u>32. Moreover, in pre-emption case never drawn up a decree after its disposal but, if the suit is disposed of in either way decree must be drawn up to that effect. So, it is crystal clear that the final order passed in a pre-emption case it is an order not decree.</u>

33. Now to determine the difference between the decree and order we must look into the provision of section 2 of the Code wherein the definition of order and decree has been given. We are of the view that it would be profitable to reproduce the definition of the decree and order which runs as follows:—(2) "decree" means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. It shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within.

(14) "order "means the formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree:

34. From the above definition we can conclude the difference between the decree and order, since in the pre-emption case no decree would be drawn up after disposal but if the application for Miscellaneous Case is rejected under Order VII, rule 11 in that situation decree must be drawn up because in the definition of the decree it has been clearly opined that Court itself be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint as decree. It is, therefore, crystal clear that the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code cannot invoke in the case in hand, because an application under section 96 of the Act is disposed of finally by an order, obviously not by a decree.

35. However, Mr Purmindu Bikash Das advanced his submission referring section 141 of the Code wherein it has been enacted by the legislature that the provision of section 141 would be applicable in the proceedings of the Miscellaneous Case in the Court of civil jurisdiction therefore, it would be noteworthy to reproduce the provision of section 141 herein below which runs as follows:-

141. The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of civil jurisdiction.

36. On perusal of the provision of section 141 it is our considered view that this section would be applicable only for procedural matter so far it can be made applicable. Therefore, we are of the opinion that section 141 of the Code cannot be invoked at the time of passing the substantive justice. From the above discussion in respect of order and decree which determine substantive justice or any of the party in a proceeding resolving the controversy in between the parties through decree but not by order. In a present case it appears that the learned Advocate filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code and impleading the said provision of law and resorted to reject the plaint but we find no plaint in the present case rather, it is an application which has been registered as Miscellaneous case (Pre-emption).

<u>37. So, it is obvious that an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act does not come in the category of a suit. It just an application for the purpose of pre-emption as prescribed by the special law which cannot, therefore, be equated with a suit because none of the requirements of a suit such as regular plaint, Court fees, written statement and decree etc is attracted to such an application. On the aforementioned discussions it is crystal clear that the application for Miscellaneous Case cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

38. Mr Purmindu Bikash Das further advanced his submission referring section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that miss-quoting and non-quoting of provision of law by the learned Advocate on an application cannot be the sole basis for passing the appropriate order, if from the contentions of the application it appear that any question of law has been raised in respect of any proceedings for ends of justice and to protect abuse of process of law the Court. The Court himself can invoke the inherent jurisdiction of under section 151 of the Code for exercising the jurisdiction for ends of justice.

39. He very candidly submitted that the learned lawyer of the trial Court filed application under Order VII, rule 11 instead of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure only for this reason a illegal proceedings cannot be proceeded since it has clearly been mentioned in the application under Order VII, rule 11 that the proceeding is illegal and if such illegal proceeding going on that would be tantamount abuse of process of the Court as well as both the parties in the litigation could not get any result after the conclusion of the trial because the future result of the instant proceeding is as clear as day light therefore, such unfounded proceedings must be buried in its inception.

40. In view of the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner we find support from the principles enunciated in the case of Abdul Jain vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12 wherein the apex Court has held that—

"It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

41. It has been further held that-- "As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light such a suit must be hurried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation."

42. In the case in hand regarding the legal provision as to the maintainability we have already discussed elsewhere in the judgment. Our such view is supportive to the case of Mojibar Rahman Mondal (Md) vs Khoteza Khatoon reported in 2 BLC (AD) 170 wherein the apex Court himself found that the principle of accepting the rest amount of the deposit to file an application under section 96 of the Act, 1950 beyond the statutory period is not maintainable.

43. We have also find support of our view from the discussion regarding the partial pre-emption to the case of Hatem Ali Mollah vs Hayet Khan reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 237.

44. In view of the discussions hereinabove and legal proposition has been cited hereinabove we are of the view that the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code cannot be invoked as discussed hereinabove. However, we are inclined to exercise the Court's inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Because in the impugned order it has been admitted that the application was filed for less deposit and further prayed for in the prayer Ka of the case for partial pre-emption. We are of the considered view that it is a fit case to invoke the jurisdiction of section 151 and exercise the inherent power of the Court to resist abuse of process of the Court for ends of justice.

45. Thus, the Rule having merit, in exceptional circumstances it's succeed.

46. In the result, the Rule is made absolute.

47. The impugned order dated 11-2-2016 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2013 is hereby aside.

48. It is further declared that proceedings of pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2013 now pending in the Court of Joint District Judge, Satkania, Chittagong on an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 at the instance of the pre-emptor is not maintainable hence, the application for pre-emption is rejected.

The office is directed to communicate this judgment and order at once.

End.

lawyer:
M Qumrul Haque Siddique with Runa Iqbal, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Md Monowar Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General, with Md Mojibur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Abdul Kuddus Shah Chowdhury………Petitioner
VS
Government of Bangladesh............Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This revision under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 20-7-20111, passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Naogaon, in Civil Revision No.6 of 2010, preferred under section 115(2) of the Civil Procedure Code against the judgment and order dated 18-11-2009, passed by the Assistant  Judge, Sapahar, Naogaon, in Miscellaneous Case No.22 of 2005.

2. The fact necessary for disposal of the Rule in brief, that the petitioner obtained an ex-parte decree dated 28-5-1988, in Other Class Suit No.115 of 1985 from the Court of Assistant Judge, Sapahar, Naogaon. In that suit the Government was the sole defendant. Since the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the Government the petitioner as plaintiff instituted that suit. After 17 years from that decree in 2005 the Government/opposite party filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code being Miscellaneous Case No.22 of 2005 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sapahar, Naogaon for setting aside that ex-parte decree alleging that it was obtained by the petitioner without serving any notice or summon upon the Government. On 3-5-2005 the petitioner went to the local Tahshil office for payment of rent of the suit land and therein disclosed that regarding the suit land he obtained the aforesaid ex-parte decree, and thereafter the Government/opposite party on 25-5-2005 instituted the instant proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code. The petitioner opposed that application stating that the summon or notice was properly served upon the Government, but having no interest over the suit land the Government did not contest the suit, and accordingly it was decreed ex-parte. It is further stated the suit was decreed before long 17 years and after obtaining the decree the petitioner got the suit land mutated in his name and has been paying rent to the Government. Even after receiving the rent for long time some of the Government officials instituted the instant Miscellaneous Case with false statements, and the same is barred by limitation.

3. After hearing the parties the Assistant Judge allowed the said Miscellaneous Case, and set aside the aforesaid ex-parte decree finding that the Miscellaneous Case is not barred by limitation, and apparently the summon was not treated as served, but on perusal of the postal receipt the summon sent by post was treated as served.

4. Against the said judgment and order the petitioner preferred Civil Revision No.6 of 2010, in the Court of District Judge, Naogaon under section 115(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, and on transfer the same was heard by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Naogaon who by the impugned judgment and order rejected the said revision and affirmed the judgment and order of the Assistant Judge.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and order the petitioner preferred this revision under section 115(4) of the Civil Procedure Code and obtained the Rule.

6. Ms Runa Iqbal, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner submits that the Assistant Judge committed illegality in allowing the Miscellaneous Case in an arbitrary manner though he himself found that from the postal receipt it appears that the notice was served only by post. Service of notice by post is enough to find that the notice of the suit was served upon the defendant. That since the defendant did not contest the suit the suit was naturally decreed ex-parte. She further submits, that after obtaining the ex-parte decree against the Government the suit land was mutated in the name of the petitioner in 1988 and since then he has been paying rent to the Government, and after receiving rent from him the Government has no scope to say that there was no information about the decree against the Government, and, as such, the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code is time barred. That Additional district Judge also committed illegality by affirming such illegal judgment and order by the impugned judgment and order passed in a telegraphic manner without discussing the provision of law or the fact of the case.

7. To oppose her such submission Mr Md Monowar Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing for the opposite party submits that the Assistant Judge, as well as the Additional District Judge rightly passed the impugned judgments and orders, and there is no harm to decide the suit on contest after setting aside the ex-parte decree obtained by the petitioner.

<u>8. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and on perusal of the impugned judgments and orders alongwith the deposition of the witness which are annexed to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner it appears to me, that the Assistant Judge committed illegality in allowing the prayer of the judgment debtor made under Order IX, rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code. I hold the view that it is unnatural that a suit was decreed ex-parte without serving any notice upon the Government. I find no reason for the Government machinery not to know about any suit instituted against the Government. Moreover, the suit was decreed long before 17 years. After obtaining the decree the petitioner by filing a Miscellaneous Case corrected the khatian and got it prepared in his name in 1988, and since then he has been paying rent to the Government. After correction of the khatian by the responsible Government officers and after receiving rent from the petitioner I find no scope to say that the Government was not aware of the ex-parte decree passed long before 17 years. Apparently, the judgments of the Courts below are illegal.</u>

9. Accordingly, the Rule is hereby made absolute. In the result, the judgment and order dated 20-7-2011, passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Naogaon, in Civil Revision No.06 of 2010 and those dated 18-11-2009, passed by the Assistant Judge, Sapahar, Naogaon, in Miscellaneous Case No.22 of 2005, are hereby set aside.

10. However, there is no order as to costs.

Send down the lower Court's records immediately.

End.
