full_judgment:
In this revision Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 1-11-2001 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh in Other Appeal No. 99 of 1998 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and order dated 18-2-1998 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No. 200 of 1997 rejecting the plaint in suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that predecessor of the petitioners named Md Sirajul Islam filed Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 against one Apurba Kumar Majumder and Government of Bangladesh for Specific Performance of Contract. Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue), and Assistant Custodian Enemy Property Mymensingh, representing the Government of Bangladesh contested the suit by filing written statement. The suit was decreed, thereafter, said 2 of 1979. The Additional Deputy Commis-sioner and Assistant Custodian Enemy Property preferred First Appeal No. 41 of 1980 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree of the trial court and obtained an ad-interim order of stay in Civil Rule No.1287 (F) of 1980. Subsequently, the order was vacated when the rule was discharged. First Appeal No. 41 of 1980 was finally dismissed by this Court. Additional Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Custodian Enemy Property filed CPLA No 474 of 1997 before the Appellate Division which was also dismissed on 12-6-1997. Thereafter, the plaintiff in suit got the sale deed executed and registered through court, but before effecting delivery of possession, Government of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner Mymensingh filed Other Suit No. 200 of 1997, in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Mymensingh against the present petitioners, as defendant, praying for setting aside the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977. Present petitioners appeared in suit and filed an application under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint. The trial court allowed the application and rejected the plaint by order No. 24 dated 18-2- 1 998. Against the judgment and order of the trial court, the government preferred Other Appeal No. 99 of 1998 before the District Judge, Mymensingh which was subsequently, transferred to the court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, for disposal, who upon hearing by the impugned judgment and order dated 1-11-2001 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and order of the trial court. At this juncture, the petitioners moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present rule. Subsequently, by filing an application for injunction obtained an order of status quo. 

3. One Md Akkas Ali by filing an application added as opposite party No. 9 in this revision. 

4. Mr Abdul Haque, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977, Deputy Commissioner and Additional Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh were defendants who contested the suit by filing written statement claiming that the owner of the property left the then East Pakistan for India leaving the property uncared for and denied that the owner executed any agreement for sale with the plaintiff in suit. The suit was decreed and the decree was upheld upto the Appellate Division. Thereafter, Md Wahid Box and another tried to create obstruction and execution of the decree by filing several applications and pro-ceedings which were also ended unsuccessfully upto the Appellate Division maintaining the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977. In all the proceedings, it has been established that the plaintiff in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 acquired the property on the basis of bainanama and subsequently, by a registered sale deed through court and the dispute between the parties have been set at rest finally by the highest court of the country. As such, again the defendants in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 cannot agitate the same matter already settled earlier, by filing an independent suit for setting aside the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977. 

5. He further submits that, considering all the facts and circumstances of the case, the trial court rightly rejected the plaint in suit, but the Appellate Court on misconception of law and facts allowed the appeal holding that the present suit cannot come within the purview of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the question of res-judicata is a mixed question of facts and law which can be determined on evidence only. 

6. It is also argued that it is apparent on the face of the record that in earlier suit, claim of the present plaintiff-government was settled finally and the government could not prove and establish that owner of the property left for India and he did not execute bainanama in favour of plaintiff in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977, as such, the judgment and order of the appellate court is liable to be set-aside. 

7. Mr Md Taherul Islam, learned Deputy Attorney-General with Ms. Umme Masumun Nesa, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 submits that the plaintiff in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 could not produce any bainanama before the court to prove that owner of the property entered into any contract for sale with him and in the said suit the government of Bangladesh was not made party and obtained the decree by suppressing the real fact. He further submits that the appellate court rightly observed and held that question of res-judicata is a mixed question of fact and law and it can be settled only on evidence, as such, the judgment and order of the appellate court is not liable to be interfered with. 

8. Mr Md Jashimuddin, learned Advocate appearing for the added opposite party No. 9, Akkas Ali submits that the opposite party No. 9 entered into a contract with the owner Apurbo Kumar Majumder on 8-3-1958 at a consideration of Taka 11,000 out of which he paid Taka 7,000 as advance, but Apurbo Kumar Majumder did not execute and register the sale deed within 3 (three) months. He further submits that the opposite party No. 9 continued in possession of the property on the basis of bainanama. Subsequently, he paid Taka 4,000 to Apurbo Kumar Majumder when he wanted to go to India and thereafter, Apurbo Kumar Majumder could not come back to the then East Pakistan because of some legal complications. The opposite party No. 9, as possessor of holding No. 40 obtained lease from the government and continuing possession of the same. It is also submitted that plaintiff in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 knowing fully well about possession of the opposite party No. 9 did not make him party in the suit and obtained decree in the absence of the opposite party No. 9 and proceeded with execution case for recovery of possession. The opposite party No. 9 after coming to know about the decree obtained in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1997 instituted Other Class Suit No. 45 of 1997 for declaration of his title by adverse possession and for cancellation of the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 which is now pending for disposal. 

9. It is also submitted that the government filed the instant suit for cancellation of the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 and knowing about filing of this revision by the petitioner, the opposite party No. 9 by filing an application, added in this revision and got an order of status quo in respect of possession and position of the suit property. The opposite party No. 9's possession is protected under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and the decree obtained by Sirajul Islam in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 is not at all binding upon him. As such, unless evidences are led in the suit it cannot be decided whether the suit is barred by any law. Hence, the rule is liable to be discharged. 

10. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, have gone through the revisional application, plaint in Title Suit No. 200 of 1997, application for rejection of plaint, judgment passed in earlier Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 and judgment in appeal before this Court as well as Appellate Division and judgment and order of both the courts below passed in Title Suit No. 200 of 1997 and other Appeal No. 99 of 1998. 

11. Admittedly, the property in question originally belonged to Apurbo Kumar Majumder. Predecessor of present petitioner, Sirajul Islam obtained a decree for Specific Performance of Contract in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977. In the suit Additional Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Custodian Enemy Property as well as Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh representing the government were defendants. They contested the suit by filing written statement contending that the owner of the property left this country for India leaving the property uncared for. Resultantly, the property entered into the census-list and declared by the government as enemy property now vested and non-Resident property. The contention of the defendants was not sustained, consequently, suit was decreed. Thereafter Additional Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Custodian Enemy Property preferred First Appeal No. 41 of 1980 before this Court against the judgment and decree of the trial court which was also dismissed on merit. Thereafter, preferred CPLA No. 474 of 1997 before the Appellate Division which was also dismissed on 12-6-1997. Then, decree holder by virtue of the sale deed executed and registered through court on 22-9-1979 started the Execution Case No. 2 of 1979 for recovery of possession. After final adjudication of the matter in dispute starting from trial court upto Appellate Division, Government of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) filed Title Suit No. 200 of 1997 on the following prayer: 
“(ক) উপরোক্ত অবস্থা ও বৃত্তান্ত মূলে এবং আইন ইকুইট মতে এবং ন্যায় বিচারার্থ জেলা ময়মনসিংহের অতিবিক্ত সাব জজ আদালতের ৭/১৯৯৭ সন অন্য প্রকার মোকদ্দমার বিগত ইংরেজি ১৪-১-১৯৭৯ তারিখের রায়ও ডিক্রি বাতিল করিয়া বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে এবং বাদীর অনুকূলে প্রয়োজনীয় ডিক্রী দিতে ।”

12. Heirs of plaintiff in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 appeared in suit and filed an application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaintiff on the ground that in the earlier Suit No. 7 of 1977, the present plaintiff, Bangladesh Government and Additional Deputy Commissioner were defendants who contested the suit by filing written statement on the same averment made in the present plaint which was finally adjudicated upon by the court and upheld upto the Appellate Division. As such, there is no earthly reason for the plaintiff, government to re-agitate the matter by filing the instant suit challenging the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 which was tested in appeal by the High Court Division and thereafter by the Appellate Division. 

13. The trial court by order dated 18-2-1998 allowed the application and rejected the plaint in suit. Rejection of plaint in suit is a decree and appealable before the appellate court, but from the record it appears that the trial court did not draw any decree pursuant to rejection of the plaint. 

14. However, the government preferred appeal against the order of rejection of plaint. The appellate court heard the appeal and by its judgment and order dated 1-11-2001 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and order of the trial court, but the appellate court also did not draw any decree after disposal of the appeal. Both the courts below committed error of law and illegality in not drawing up any decree in both the occasions of rejection of plaint as well as allowing the appeal. 

15. However, the present petitioners moved this Court by filing this revision against the judgment and order of the appellate court without any decree. I have gone through the judgment passed by this Court in First Appeal No. 41 of 1980 and CPLA No. 474 of 1997. From perusal of both the judgments it appears that present plaintiffs were party to Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 and they contested the suit by filing written statement averring same contentions made in the plaint in suit. 

16. In the earlier suit all the Courts starting from Subordinate Judge to Appellate Division, concurrently observed and held that the owner of the property entered into an agreement for sale with Sirajul Islam and decreed the suit as well as dismissed both the appeal by the High Court Division as well as by the Appellate Division and Sirajul Islam got the sale deed registered through court by filing Execution Case No. 2 of 1979. Thereafter, one Wahid Box and another tried to challenge the execution case by filing miscellaneous proceeding which was ultimately went to the Appellate Division, wherein CPLA No. 2473 of 2009 was dismissed by judgment and order dated 20-4-2014. Not only the government, but opposite party No. 9, Akkas Ali also tried to obstruct execution process claiming to be the owner of the property on the basis of a bainanama and adverse possession. 

17. This Court is not concern with the proceeding initiated by opposite party No. 9, but concern with the present proceedings and suit filed by the government challenging the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977. The claim of present plaintiff-government has been finally settled by the Appellate Division in the earlier suit. On the same averment and same claim, the government has filed the present suit for setting aside the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1977 in which the government fought upto the Appellate Division unsuccessfully. 

18. It is true that question of res-judicata is a mixed question of law and facts necessitating evidence and investigation upon trial of the suit. But the present dispute is a clear case to come into a definite conclusion without evidence, because of the fact that the matter raised in the instant suit has raised in the earlier suit which was finally adjudicated upon and in that suit the government utterly failed to establish their claim that the owner of the property left the country for India without executing any deed of agreement for sale in favour of any person, consequently, the property in question was entered into the census-list as enemy property now vested property, as such, the present suit is barred by res-judicata. 

19. In view of the above, this Court finds that the trial court rightly rejected the plaint in suit but the appellate court wrongly held that the suit is not barred by any law and set-aside the judgment and order of the trial court. 

20. Taking into consideration of the above, this Court finds merit in the Rule as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

21. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. 

22. The judgment and order of the appellate court is hereby set-aside and the judgment and order of the trial court is hereby restored. 

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned and send down the lower court records at once. 

End.

caseno: Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016. with Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3203 of 2015.
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney-General (with Biswajit Debnath, Deputy Attorney-General) instructed by Mahmuda Begum, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellants. [In CA No.187/2016] 
Abul Kalam Chowdhury, Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. (In CP No.3203/2015)
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate (with MA Jabbar, Advocate) instructed by Md Toufique Hossain, Advocate-on-record—For Respondent Nos.1-12. (In CA No.187/2616)
Abul Kalam Chowdhury, Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No.13. (In CA No.187/2016)
None Represented—For Respondent No.14. (In CA No.187/2016)
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate instructed by Md Toufique Hossain, Advocate-on-record—For the Respondents. [In CP No.3203/2015]
parties:
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform, Dhaka and others -------- Appellants [ln CA No.187/2016]
Jalal Uddin College, represented by the Principal, Jalal Uddin College, Begumgonj, Noakhali -------- Petitioner [In CP No.3203/2015]
VS
Mazharul Huq Khan and others -------- Respondents [In both the cases]
case_source: From the judgment and order dated 16-9-2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2622 of 2010).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, CJ: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 16-9-2015 passed by High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2622 of 2010 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this civil appeal, in a nutshell, are: Respondent No. 1 herein, predecessor of respondent Nos.2 to 7 and respondent Nos.8 to 12 as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.27 of 1986 before the then Court of Upazila Munsif, Begumgonj on 3-2-1986 impleading the appellant Government of Bangladesh, respondent Nos.13 to 18 and Jalal Uddin, father of present respondent No.19 as defendants for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession.

3. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that their grandfather Moulvi Serajul Hoq Khan was the owner of the suit land. The then Government acquired more than 600 acres of land at Begumgonj, including 13 acres of land of Serajul Hoq Khan in LA Case No.6 of 1941-42. Serajul Hoq Khan took part of the compensation money on 15-2-1943 under protest and did not take the balance money which remained as revenue deposit. The Government did not evict the owners from the acquired land and said Serajul Hoq Khan remained in possession of his 13 acres of land, including dwelling house, garden, tanks etc. The Government ultimately did not use the land for the purpose of which it was acquired and by order dated 10-6-1955 ordered that the acquired lands including 'Ka' schedule land be given by way of lease to the former owners or their heirs on year to year basis upon executing an agreement for the same. Accordingly, all the ex-owners and their heirs including Makbul Hoq Khan, the father of the plaintiffs took year to year lease upon executing an agreement for 'Ka' schedule land. In 1975 the Government decided to return the acquired lands on condition that the former owners or their heirs would refund the compensation money which they took from the Government. This decision was communicated by the Land Ministry to defendant No.3-Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in Memo No.6-38/75 dated 31-1-1975. Accordingly, Mukbul Hoq Khan, father of the plaintiffs filed a petition dated 05-4-1975 addressed to defendant No. 2-Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali for return of the 'Ka' schedule land to him. Defendant No. 3 by Memo No. 2749 SA dated 23-9-1975 reported to the Ministry of Land that 'Ka' schedule land might be returned to Mukbul Hoq Khan upon refund of the compensation money taken by Serajul Hoq Khan. Ultimately, the land having not been returned to the plaintiffs, they were compelled to file the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1 to 4 and 5 to 8 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that after completion of the process of acquisition the suit land vested in the Government and the plaintiffs as year to year lessees have been in possession of the suit land, but the lease has not been renewed for many years. It was further contended that the `Kha' schedule land was leased out on the application of defendant No. 5 for establishing Jalal Uddin Mohila College.

5. The trial Court upon consideration of the evidence and materials on record by the judgment and decree dated 23-7-2005 dismissed the suit. Against the said judgment and decree, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 156 of 2005 before the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Noakhali, who by his judgment and order dated 06-5-2010 dismissed the appeal.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the appellate Court, the plaintiffs then preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.2622 of 2010. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 16-9-2015 made the Rule absolute.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the defendants as the leave-petitioners filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3202 of 2015 before this Division and obtained leave on 21-1-2016 resulting in Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016.

8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that admittedly, the suit land was acquired in LA Case No. 06 of 1941-42 by the Government and the plaintiffs failed to prove that their grandfather, Serajul Hoq Khan, was owner of the suit land or the suit land was acquired from his possession. He further submits that the plaintiffs claim that their grandfather "উক্ত ভুমি অর্জন করিয়া" constructed homestead but no piece of paper in support of it could be produced by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs' grandfather could not prove title to and possession in the acquired suit land and their grandfather could not withdraw the entire assessed compensation money. He continues to submit that there were as many as five prayers in the plaint without any prayer for declaration of title and that the suit land as shown in 'Ca' schedule for recovery of khas possession was vague and unspecified. He then submits that the definite case of the defendants is that the suit was not maintainable as it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the High Court Division fell into error as it failed to consider the aforesaid legal and factual aspects of the case. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He then submits that the High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and erred in reversing concurrent decisions of the Courts below without adverting to the findings of the Courts below. With reference to the letter dated 9-2-1987 (Exhibit-15), he submits that High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the aforesaid letter of the Ministry of Land which is a inter-ministerial correspondence and decision for de-requisition of acquired land can be taken only in cabinet meeting. He then submits that admittedly the suit land was acquired and it completely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances.

9. In respect of the college, the learned Attorney-General, submits that it was established on 'Kha' schedule land and defendant No.5 paid Taka 4,01,497 as lease money and possession was delivered by the Government to the college and lease deed could not be registered as the suit is pending and the Board of intermediate and Secondary Education, Cumilla, on being satisfied that the college fulfilled the required criteria gave affiliation to the college and the National University also gave recognition to the college.

10. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-12 of Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016 and the respondents of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015, on the other hand, submits that admittedly, the suit land belonged to the plaintiffs' grandfather, Serajul Hoq Khan and that as the property was not used for the purpose for which it was acquired the Ministry of Land by Exhibit-15 directed to release the suit land from acquisition and to handover possession thereof to the plaintiffs and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the acquisition was made by the then Government under the Land Acquisition Act No. I of 1894 and, as such, the trial Court and the appellate Court fell in error as both the Courts below considered the case with reference to (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act,1948 and, as such, no interference is called for.

11. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.13 of the Civil Appeal No.187 of 2016 and leave-petitioner of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015, supports the arguments advanced by Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Senior Advocate.

12. Before addressing the conflicting contentions of the learned Attorney-General for the appellants and the learned Senior Advocate for respondent Nos.1-12, it would be pertinent to quote the following grounds, on which, leave was granted: "Admittedly the suit land was acquired in LA Case No. 06 of 1941-42 by the Government. The plaintiffs failed to prove that their grandfather Serajul 1-loq Khan was owner of the suit land or the suit land was acquired from his possession. And in the plaint it was claimed that their grandfather "উক্ত ভুমি অর্জন করিয়া" but no piece of paper in support of it could be produced by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs' grandfather could not prove title and possession in the acquired suit land and their grandfather could not draw the entire assessed compensation money as he had no title in the suit land. And there are five prayers in the plaint without any prayer for declaration of title. And the suit land as shown in 'Ga' schedule for recovery of khas possession was vague and unspecified and in this connection defendant-opposite party referred Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and decision in the case of Nazrul Islam Babal vs Shanti Rani Dhupi and others reported in 12 MLR (AD) 105 = 12 BLC (AD) 36, and the definite case of the defendant that the suit was not maintainable as it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the High Court Division fell into error as it failed to consider aforesaid legal and factual aspects of the suit and, as such, the impugned judgement and order is not legally tenable. The High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and erred in reversing concurrent decisions of the Courts below without controverting the findings of the Courts below. The High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the letter of the Ministry of Land dated 9-2-1987, i.e. Exhibit-15 which is inter-ministerial correspondence and decision for de-requisition of acquired land can be taken only in cabinet meeting and not by any person and in this connection decision in the case of Haji Aftab Liddin vs Bangladesh reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 1 was cited, but the High Court Division overlooked the same and thus committed error of law resulting miscarriage of justice. Admittedly the suit land was acquired land and it completely vested to the Government free from all encumbrances and the plaintiffs had no legal right to claim release of the properties unless the right is conferred on them by any statutory provision and the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land when it was leased out and possession was delivered to the college, and the defendants including the Deputy Commissioner rightly and legally passed the orders and findings of the High Court Division to the contrary are against materials on record and erroneous. Admittedly the college was established on 'Kha' schedule land and defendant No. 5 paid salami money amounting to Taka 4,01,497as lease money and possession was delivered by the Government to the college and lease deed could not be registered as the suit is pending and the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Cumilla, on being satisfied that the college fulfilled the required criteria gave affiliation to the college; National University also gave recognition to the college. The Government legally and rightly enlisted the college for Monthly Payment Order (MPO). The Government constructed multi-storied building of the college and thousands of students have been studying there but findings of the High Court Division to the contrary ignoring the counter affidavit filed by opposite party No. 7 are unwarranted and legally erroneous."

13. Admittedly, for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali District, the suit land and other lands were acquired by the Government but the Government shifted the establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali from the suit land and other acquired lands to Maijdee. The acquired suit land was stated to have been in possession of the plaintiffs. Normally the Government took possession of acquired land but in the instant case, possession has not been taken over and compensation money has not been fully paid. The Government claimed that after acquisition the suit land vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and the title, if any, of private individuals of acquired land extinguished.

14. In the plaint, the plaintiffs admitted that the suit property was acquired in LA Case No.06 of 1941-1942 as shown in schedule-Ka to the plaint for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali. The plaintiffs also claimed that their grandfather Moulavi Serajul Hoq Khan was the owner of the 'Ka' schedule land.

15. The trial Court came to a finding that defendant No.4, Upazila Revenue Officer submitted a report to defendant No.3, Additional Deputy Commissioner, stating that the 'Ka' schedule land measuring 8.10 acres of which 4.75 acres of land were used by the plaintiffs for their dwelling houses, garden, tanks etc. and that the remaining land was nal land and that the plaintiffs' predecessor-in-interest was the owner of that land and that the said report (Exhibit-16) was filed by the plaintiffs before the Court. The trial Court also found that the written statement of defendant Nos.1-4 and Exhibit-16, reveal that the suit land belonged to the plaintiffs' predecessor-in-interest. The trial Court also found that the plaintiffs obtained lease of the suit land from the Government on year to year.

16. After acquisition, the ownership of the suit land devolved upon the Government and the Government would decide whether they would lease out the suit land to anybody or not. The trial Court noted that if the Government decides to settle the suit land, then settlement should be given to previous owner of the suit land. But the plaintiffs could not claim that the Government was bound to settle the suit land to the plaintiffs.

17. The appellate Court concurred with the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court. The appellate Court came to the finding that the decisions taken pursuant to Exhibits-12 and 15 are Administrative decisions and if anybody neglected in implementing those decision then the plaintiffs could seek redress to the higher authority but unless higher authority took any action the civil Court did not have the jurisdiction to give any relief to the plaintiffs.

18. The High Court Division came to a finding that the specific prayer of the plaintiffs is for declaration that the order dated 26-1-1986 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, was illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction and also for implementation of the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 9-2-1987 (Exhibit-15). The High Court Division further came to a finding that it was an admitted position that the plaintiffs were in possession from before acquisition of the suit land which was acquired in LA Case No.06 of 1941-1942. The High Court Division held that apart from the so-called lease of 1959, there was no paper to show that the plaintiffs were lessees of the Government and rather the plaintiffs were in continuous and uninterrupted possession for more than 60 years and the Government did not take any step to evict the plaintiffs and, as such, on this score also the plaintiffs acquired title to the suit land. The High Court Division also came to the finding that from the records, it appeared that till date admittedly no lease deed had been executed and registered by the concerned authority in favour of the college and, as such, recognition of the college by the Education Board and inclusion of the college in the MPO and construction of the building under development project of the Government were illegal and collusive.

19. Admittedly, the plaintiffs in clear terms stated that the suit land along with other land was acquired for development of District Headquarters of Noakhali in LA Case No.06 of 1941-1942. The plaintiffs also admitted in the plaint that as per decision of the Government, the then Collector, Mr Pana Ullah Ahmed on 10-5-1955 passed an order that the property acquired for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali be given lease to the original owners or their legal representatives on year to year basis. The plaintiffs also admitted that from 1956 the plaintiffs' father stated obtaining lease of the 'Ka' schedule land from the Government and that they have been in possession thereof on payment of lease money and also by executing agreement.

20. It is contended that the order dated 26-1-1986 (Exhibit-12) passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, proposing lease in favour of the college was illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction and that the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 9-2-1987 for releasing the suit land form acquisition be implemented. Admittedly, the suit land was validly acquired in LA Case No.06 of 1941-1942. Unless the suit land is released from acquisition no right, title and interest of the plaintiffs accrued in that land and, as such, the plaintiffs are not entitled to obtain a decree declaring the order dated 26-1-1986 (Exhibit-12) issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, proposing lease in favour of the college to be illegal and without jurisdiction.

21. Since the property was validly acquired and vested in the Government free from all encumbrances the plaintiffs do not have any right to pray for implementation of the decision of the Ministry of Land dated 9-24987. The High Court Division came to a finding that the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land from before acquisition and that they continued to possess thereof and that the plaintiffs pursuant to their uninterrupted possession of the suit land for more than 60 years acquired title to the suit land. The High Court Division, however, did not mention that the plaintiffs acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession. But the above finding implies that the High Court Division tried to mean that the plaintiffs acquired title by adverse possession. Admittedly, the suit land was validly acquired by the Government in A Case No.06 of 1941-1942 and the suit was filed in 1986. Therefore, it appears that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land from the date of acquisition for a continuous period of 60 years. Therefore, the above finding is erroneous and patently based on wrong calculation.

22. The trial Court and the appellate Court decided the case based upon the (Emergency) Requisition of the Property Act, 1948 but the acquisition in the disputed case property was made under Land Acquisition Act No.I of 1894. In this connection, it is pertinent to quote section 12 of the Act of 1894 as under: "12.—(1) Such award shall be filed in the Collector's office and shall, except as hereinafter provided, be final and conclusive evidence, as between the Collector and the persons interested, whether they have respectively appeared before the Collector or not, of the true area and value of the land, and the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested. (2) The Collector shall give immediate notice of his award to such of the persons interested as are not present personally or by their representatives when the award is made."

23. From the above section, it appears that the award filed in the Collector's office shall be final and conclusive evidence as between the Collector and the persons interested. It is immaterial whether the persons interested appeared before the Collector or not and the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested. Section 16 of the Act of 1894 states that when the Collector has made an award under section 11, he may take possession of the land, which shall thereupon absolutely vest in the Government, free from all encumbrances. In the case in hand, the plaintiffs stated that the Collector assessed the compensation of the acquired land at Taka 11,592 and that the plaintiffs' grandfather took Taka 5001 on 15-2-1943 with objection and that the remaining amount was kept in the revenue department which plaintiffs did not withdraw.

24. The Act of 1894 in part-Ill provides for "Reference to Court and Procedure Thereon". Section 18(1) occurring in part-III provides that any person interested who has not accepted the award may, by written application to the Collector, require that the matter be referred by the Collector for the determination of the Court, whether his objection be to the measurement of the land, the amount of the compensation, the persons to whom it is payable, or the apportionment of the compensation among the persons interested. Part-III of the Act contains sections 18 to 28 which provide for addressing the grievances of the persons whose properties have been acquired by the Government. The plaintiffs could not produce any paper showing that their predecessor-in-interest had made attempt for a reference to the Court for the reliefs contained in sections 18 to 28 of the Act of 1894. Therefore, it appears that the plaintiffs' grandfather received Taka 5,001 with objection was not proved and nothing was produced by them showing that their grandfather made any attempt to vindicate his grievances before the Court as provided by Part-III of the Act of 1894.

25. In the light of the findings, we are of the view that the Government validly acquired the suit land along with other land for establishment of District Headquarters of Noakhali and that the acquired properties vested in the Government free from all encumbrances as provided under section 16 of the Act of 1894.

26. Once the property is validly acquired there is no scope for releasing the same. But as owner of the acquired property, the Government is at liberty to lease out the suit land to anybody. In the case in hand, the trial Court, the appellate Court and the High Court Division found that the plaintiffs had been in possession of a portion of the suit land and that their dwelling houses, garden, and tank are on the said land.

27. Admittedly, the Government took decision to lease out 3.06 acres of land to the Jalal Uddin Mohila College, Begumgonj, Noakhali. The college was given recognition by the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Cumilla and also by the National University. The college has also been included in the Monthly Payment Order (MPO) of the Government and as part of its development scheme Government constructed a building of the college. The Government has decided to lease out `Kha' schedule land measuring 3.06 acres of land out of the suit land to the said college for imparting education to thousands of students of that area. The plaintiffs do not have any right to challenge the decision of the Government to lease out the 'Kha' schedule land to the college. Moreover, they have not acquired any right in the suit land till date. If 3.06 acres of land shown in schedule 'Kha' are deducted from 'Ka' schedule land measuring 8.10 acres then 5.04 acres of land remain in possession of the plaintiffs.

28. Having gone through the records and the judgments of all the Courts, we find that the remaining 5.04 acres of land belonging to the grandfather of the plaintiffs before acquisition may be leased out to them as their grandfather was stated to have withdrawn 50% of the lease money.

29. In the light of the findings made before, we are inclined to set-aside the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division and allow the appeal with the direction that 5.04 acres of land may be leased out to the plaintiffs considering their prolong possession thereof.

30. Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3203 of 2015 is disposed of in the light of the findings and decision made in the body of the judgment of this appeal.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:

Tabarak Hossain, Senior Advocate, instructed by Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 4-3-2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.7820 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman, J.: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 4-3-2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7820 of 1997 making the Rule Nisi absolute.

2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that: The writ petitioner filed the above mentioned writ petition before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the case property being House No.16/8, Block-B, Babor Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, was allotted to one Md Raisat by registered deed of lease dated 15-9-1964 for a period of 99 years. While he was in possession as owner, he entered into an agreement on 05-1-1971 for selling the case property to Most. Jahurunnessa. In pursuance of the said agreement, he also handed over the physical possession of the case property in her favour. However, ultimately, when Md Raisat refused to execute and register the sale deed in favour of Most. Jahurunnessa, she filed Title Suit No.343 of 1981 in the First Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka for specific performance of contract which was decreed ex-parte on 30-6-1983. In pursuance of the said decree, a deed of sale being Deed No.14197 dated 06-9-83 in respect of the case property was executed and registered in favour of Most. Jahurunnessa through Court. Subsequently, the said Jahurunnessa while being owner in possession of the case property transferred the same to the writ petitioner by a deed of sale being Deed No.15921 dated 20-4-85 and also handed over possession of the case property to the writ petitioner on that date. The writ petitioner on 7-9-85 filed an application to the Commissioner of Settlement, Mohammadpur praying for mutation in his name. However, at that time it was discovered that the case property was included in the "Kha" list vide Gazette Notification dated 23-9-86 in pursuance of Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985. The writ petitioner to release the property from the list of the abandoned properties filed Settlement Case No.31 of 1994 before the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka. The writ respondent-Government did not file any written statement in the case but at the time of hearing of the case only made verbal submission. The First Court of Settlement, by its judgment and order dated 19-6-97 dismissed the case. Hence, the writ petitioner finding no other alternative efficacious remedy moved the above mentioned writ petition before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule Nisi.

3. A Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule Nisi absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-3-2001. 4. The Government of Bangladesh and another feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-3-2001 of the High Court Division preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1191 of 2001 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal.

5. Mr Murad Reza, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf .of the appellants submits that the High Court Division sitting in writ jurisdiction being not a Court of appeal was not competent to set-aside the findings of facts arrived at by the Court of Settlement, the suit for specific performance of contract having no bearing on the abandoned character of the property and the writ petitioner having failed to discharge the onus of proving that the case property was not an abandoned property and further the writ petitioner not having acquired valid and legal title over the case property by alleged transfer from a person having no title at all, the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside, and hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 6. Contrariwise, Tobarak Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. He submits that admittedly the case property was leased out by a registered Deed of lease in favour of one Mr Raisat. He handed over physical possession of the property to Mst. Jahurunnessa in pursuance of a deed of agreement dated 5-1-1971 long before the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972, even, before the liberation of Bangladesh. The possession of the said Jahurunnessa was not denied by the Government. The Government was also aware of the suit for specific performance of contract. Subsequently, the Government to set-aside the said ex-parte decree filed an application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But subsequently for reasons best known to the Government, the said miscellaneous case was not pursued. As such, the ex-parte decree remained in force and the Government rather impliedly accepted the decree of the Court with regard to the right of Mst. Jahurunnessa in respect of the case property and, as such, the Government cannot claim the property. Hence, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule Nisi absolute. Therefore, on above backdrops the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Division. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be dismissed.

7. We have heard the learned Additional Attorney-General and Mr Tobarak Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respective parties. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 8. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions: Firstly, the High Court Division sitting in writ jurisdiction being not a Court of appeal was not competent to set-aside the findings of facts arrived at by the Court of Settlement. Secondly, the High Court Division ought to have decided that the suit for specific performance of contract having no bearing on the abandoned character of the property and, as such, the petitioner and his vendor not having acquired valid and legal title over the case property by alleged transfer from a person having no title at all, therefore, the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute. Thirdly, the High Court Division ought to have discharged the Rule as the writ petitioner having failed to discharge the onus of proving that the case property was not an abandoned property.

9. In view of the submissions of the learned Additional Attorney-General, we have anxiously examined the judgments of both the Courts and perused the connected materials on record.

10. The Court of Settlement found that the writ petitioner failed to prove that the case property was not abandoned property by producing oral and documentary evidence. The Court of Settlement opined that "nothing on record to show that Jahirun Nessa got possession through Court after obtaining sale deed through Court.

11. It is apparent that the High Court Division in its judgment discussed the facts of the case regarding bainapatra, handing over possession, ex-parte decree of the suit of specific performance of contract, filing of miscellaneous case by the Government, failure to proceed with said miscellaneous case and consequently, came to conclusion that ex-parte decree of specific performance of contract obtained by the vendor predecessor of the writ petitioner becomes binding upon the Government and, as such, the judgment of the Court of Settlement was set-aside.

12. The High Court Division has failed to appreciate that in a writ of certiorari under Article 102 of the Constitution in exercising writ jurisdiction it cannot sit as a Court of Appeal over the judgment of the Court or tribunal for re-settling the disputed question of fact as discussed by it in the instant writ petition which cannot be sustained in law, we find substance and good deal of force in the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General.

13. We find support of our view to the case of Mostafa Kama! (Md) vs First Court of Settlement reported 48 DLR (AD) 61, the learned Advocate for the respondent could not rebut this legal proposition in his submission. We are, therefore, of the considered view that the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the judgment of the Court of Settlement.

14. The abandoned property Order 1972 i.e. PO No.16 of 1972 took effect from 28-2-1972, the day of PO No.16 of 1972 was promulgated. Abandoned property has been defined in Article 2(1) of PO No. 16 of 1972. Admittedly, the original owner Raisat got the lease of the property as refugee coming from India. The owner of the property Mr Raisat was untraceable till independence of Bangladesh. In the Court of Settlement the Vendor of the Zahurun Nessa, Mr Raisat never appeared admitting the fact of sale. The Settlement Court will not decide the title of the property. However, it will decide whether property in question vested in the Government as abandoned property or not.

15. On perusal of the record it is crystal clear that date of Bainapatra was 05-1-1971. However, title suit was filed on 13-7-1981. The suit property in question had already been enlisted as an abandoned property by dint of PO 16 of 1972 before filing of the suit for specific performance of contract. Therefore, the suit for specific performance of contract was hit by Article 6 of PO No.16 of 1972. So, the ex-parte judgment and decree of the suit for specific performance of contract was not binding upon the Government, however, binding upon the vendor. It may be mentioned that before filing suit the vendor of Zahurun Nessa, Raisat had lost the ownership of the property by dint of PO No.16 of 1972. Furthermore, as per provisions of Article 4(b) and 7 of PO 142 of 1972 if any property is transferred in violation of those provisions the transfer would be void and null. Therefore, Zahurun Nessa by dint of the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 30-6-87 had not acquired any right, title and interest in the suit property. The High Court Division committed error of law in opining and deciding that the Zahurun Nessa, vendor of the writ petitioner had acquired right, title and interest in view of the ex-parte judgment. We are, therefore, of the firmed view that the High Court Division in this point committed inherent mistake in the judgment and order.

16. According to judgment and order of the Court of Settlement the signature of vendor in bainapatra was not genuine, but the High Court Division found the signature of vendor in the bainapatra is genuine, the High Court Division was not competent to decide the disputed question of fact in sitting writ jurisdiction. In exercising writ of certiorari, the High Court Division can only look into, if it can show that the judgment has been obtained by fraud, collusion or corruption, the Court of Settlement has acted contrary to the principle of natural justice or judgment based on no evidence or the decision is vitiated by malafide. On a careful reading of the judgment of the Court of Settlement, we do not find such error of law.

17. Rather, in the judgment of the High Court Division it is apparent that it's clearly misconstrued and misread the relevant law i.e. the provisions of PO No.16 of 1972 because property in question was abandoned first in 1972 as owner Mr Raisat was untraceable from 25th March 1971, after liberation he never took possession, control and manage the property. He also never claimed this property and, as such, the property in question was vested in the Government under Article 4 of the PO No.16 of 1972. Thereafter, Gazette dated 23-9-86 vide Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 the property was vested as an abandoned property in the Government. As per provisions of section 5(2) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 such vesting shall be the conclusive evidence of the fact that buildings included therein are abandoned property.

18. This Division has been held to the case of Shahidul Haque vs the Court of Settlement reported 69 DLR (AD) 241 which is as follows; "Writ of Certiorari—A writ of certiorari is maintainable only if it can be shown that the tribunal erroneously held that the property was illegally declared as abandoned property without admitting legal evidence or rejected the legal evidence or it has misconstrued the law". Article-6, "All the deeds and transfers were collusively made after PO 16 of 1972 came into force and these transfers are hit by Article 6 of PO 16 of 1972".

19. It appears that the Court of Settlement found that the writ petitioner was failed to prove that the property is not abandoned property but the High Court Division rebutted this finding as a Court of appeal without any basis as like as appellate Court and found that the writ petitioner was able to prove before the Court of Settlement that the property are not abandoned property. The High Court Division further erroneously found that ex-parte judgment and decree between the vendor and vendee Jahirun Nessa was binding upon the Government, because the Government appeared in the suit for specific performance of contract and also filed the miscellaneous case against that judgment which was dismissed for default. Such, finding of the High Court Division is misconception and misreading of the relevant settled principle of maxim of law as enunciated by this Division. In the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh reported 47 DLR (AD) 72 it has been held by this Division: "Section-5, Decree in a suit for specific perfor-mance of contract—Whether such decree can be pleaded as a bar for inclusion of a building in the list of abandoned property. The decree in the suit for specific performance of contract will show that it has only decided the controversy between the vendor and vendee and declared to Vendor to execute the necessary document in favour of the vendee. Such a decree is not the one which is mentioned in proviso (a) and, as such, the existence of such a decree cannot be pleaded as bar for inclusion of the building".

20. It has been held by this Division in the case of Government vs Md Abdul Mannan reported 71 DLR (AD) 338 which is as follows. "Section 5 and 10(5) "Suit for specific performance of contract-even if the decree was obtained legally the Government is not bound by the decree passed in a suit for specific performance of contract. In a suit for specific performance of contract the only issue to be decided whether the contract was genuine or not and, as such, though the Government is made a party to a suit for specific performance of contract as a requirement of law it is not bound by the decree. Ex-parte decree Ex-parte decree was obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court and, as such, the decree did not prove the writ-petitioner's claim over the property".

21. Regard being had and reasons stated hereinbefore, we find substance in the 3(three) grounds as noted earlier on which leave was granted.

22. Accordingly, this Civil Appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 4-3-2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.7820 of 1997 is hereby set-aside.

End.

case_source: (From the judgement and order dated 3rd of August,2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1031 of 2010).
full_judgment:
Md Inman Ali, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgement and order dated 3-8-2010 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1031 of 2010 discharging the Rule. 

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the respondents herein as plaintiffs filed Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh for setting aside the ex-parte judgement and decree dated 26-8-1977 passed by the learned Mimsif, 2nd Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No.199 of 1976 which had been filed for specific performance of contract. In the present suit they also prayed for cancellation of sale deed No.8964 dated 19-4-1979 which had been executed and registered in consequence of the said ex-parte decree, and Other Class Execution Case No.27 of 1978. The present plaintiffs also prayed for declaration that the aforesaid deed is not binding upon the plaintiffs and for declaration of title of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The plaintiffs contended, inter alia, that the suit land under CS Khatian No.413 CS Plot No.783 is in the name of Narayan Datta. 60 decimals land was recorded under SA Plot No.2390 under SA Khatian No.130 in the names of Brajeswar Datta, Biraswar Datta, Bimalaswar Datta and Biseswar Datta. Brajeswar, Biraswar and Bimalaswar died leaving behind their brother Biseswar Datta who got the land and was in possession. Biseswar Datta died leaving behind his son Ashok Kumar Datta and wife Ranuka Roy Datta. Ashok Kumar Datta sold 10 decimals land by deed No.7726 dated 2-11-1972 and 10 decimals land by deed No.8094 to Dr. Anwaruddin who died on 16-12-1975 leaving behind the plaintiffs as heirs. The plaintiffs are paying rents to the Government and municipal taxes. Ashok Kumar Datta and Ranuka Roy Datta did not sell the land described in the schedule No.3 to Syed Abu Sayeed predecessor of the defendant-petitioners and no bainapatra was executed and other Class Suit No.199 of 1976 was falsely initiated by Syed Abu Sayeed; no summons was served upon the defendants (present plaintiffs and Bhabesh Chandra Saha) in that suit and on 26-8-1977 obtained the ex-parte decree. Syed Abu Sayeed initiated Other Class Execution Case No.27 of 1978 and got registered sale deed No.8964 dated 19-4-1979 through Court in his favour; the deed is illegal. Dr. Anwaruddin was a bonafide purchaser. After death of Dr Anwaruddin the plaintiffs got the land by inheritance. On 24-4-1981 Bhabesh Chandra and plaintiff No.2 came to know about the decree dated 26-8-1977 and they clearly came to know about the decree on 28-4-1981, and filed Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Sadar, Mymensingh under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) for setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 26-8-1977, which was dismissed for default on 30-4-1982. Then the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 under Order IX Rule 9 of the Code which was dismissed on 26-9-1982 holding that the miscellaneous case was not maintainable and that an appeal should have been filed. Then plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No.106 of 1982 in the Court of District Judge, Mymensingh against the order dated 26-9-1982 which on transfer to the Court of Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Mymensingh was dismissed on 27-7-1987. The plaintiffs then filed Civil Revision No.1033 of 1987 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was discharged on 1-7-2008 and the plaintiffs filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1739 of 2008 before this Division which was dismissed on 8-4-2009. 

3. On 4-9-2008 the respondents herein filed the present Title Suit No.27 of 2008 claiming that Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 was not decided on merit and was dismissed for default on 30-4-1982 and the subsequent Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982, Civil Revision No.106 of 1982 and Civil Revision No.1033 of 1987 were all decided without going into the merits of the case. The plaintiffs claimed that Title Suit No.199 of 1976 was decreed ex-parte beyond their knowledge and without serving notice. Hence, they filed the present suit. 

4. The petitioners as defendants entered appearance and filed a written statement on 12-4-2009 and thereafter filed an application for an order of rejection of the plaint on 10-5-2009 stating that the suit is barred as res judieata and also by law of limitation. The learned Joint District Judge, Mymensingh after hearing the parties by the judgement and order dated 01-9-2009 rejected the application for rejection of the plaint. Being aggrieved the defendants filed Civil Revision No.61 of 2009 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Mymensingh, which on transfer to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh was disallowed by judgement and order dated 9-2-2010. Then the defendant filed Civil Revision No. 1031 of 2010 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was discharged by the impugned judgement and order dated 9-2-2010. The defendants then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2288 of 2010 before this Division and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners: 
"I. That the High Court Division did not consider that for setting aside the ex-parte decree miscellaneous case under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is the proper forum. The respondents for setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 26-8-1977 passed in Other Class Suit No.199 of 1976 filed Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 which was dismissed on 30-4-1982 and the respondents filed Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 in which the respondents lost up to this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1739 of 2008 which was dismissed on 8-4-2009. After filing the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1739 of 2008 and during its pendency, the respondents filed the Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008 on 4-9-2008 for setting aside the aforesaid ex-parte decree dated 26-8-1977 passed in Other Class Suit No.199 of 1976 and, as such, the Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008 is not maintainable and the plaint is liable to be rejected by the principle of res judicata and the suit is barred by limitation as per averments made in the plaint of the Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008." 

5. The appeal was heard by virtual means in accordance with the provisions of the আদালত কর্তৃক তথ্য-প্রযুক্তি ব্যবহার আইন, ২০২০।

6. Mr M. Qumrul Hoque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further submitted that the respondents deliberately dragged the dispute up to this Division earlier only to kill time to ensure that the evidence of service of summons of OC Suit No.199 of 1976 can be destroyed after willfully letting the Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 to be dismissed for default on 30-4-1982. He also submitted that the respondents deliberately dragged the issue to ensure that the suit goes to trial after death of the witnesses of the contracts for sale of land dated 31-7-1963 and 2-1-1972, so that the appellants cannot prove the contracts for sale of land. He also submitted that an application for setting aside ex-parte decree under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not a wrong forum. But the respondents willfully remained absent on the day fixed and got the miscellaneous case dismissed for default. Thereafter, knowing fully well, they did not file miscellaneous appeal against the order of "dismissed for default" rather filed an application under Order IX, Rule 9 of the Code and kept the matter pending up to this Division, which was not bonafide and, as such, they are not entitled to get benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act. He submitted that in paragraph No.10 of the plaint of Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008 the plaintiffs came to know of ex-parte decree of Other Class Suit No.199 of 1976 on 24-4-1981 and got certified copy of sale deed executed by Court on 28-4-1981 and Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008 was instituted on 4-9-2008. So, the question of fact is not disputed and hence, the Courts below erred in holding that limitation in this case is a mixed question fact and law. He submitted that the plaintiff respondents are not entitled to get any discount of time under section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908 because the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 under Order IX Rule 9, Civil Revision No.106 of 1982 filed in the Court of the District Judge, Mymensingh and the 2nd Civil Revision No.1033 of 1987 filed before the High Court Division were not bonafide/ in good faith. 

7. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appeared on behalf of the respondents. Since no concise statement was filed on behalf of the respondents, we are precluded from hearing any submissions as per Order XIX, rule 3 of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988. 

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

9. The High Court Division upheld the rejection of the application under Order VII rule 11 for the reason that the earlier attempt to set-aside the ex-parte decree was not decided on merit. It was observed that the plaint could not be rejected on the ground of limitation and res-judicata which can only be decided by taking evidence. 

10. We note that the High Court Division acknowledged that the present plaintiffs fought up to the Appellate Division but failed to establish that they were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the said ex-parte decree was passed. If that is the case, then clearly the present plaintiffs are having a second bite at the cherry, which is not permitted by law. When the earlier suit was decreed ex-parte, the present plaintiffs had the choice of one of three avenues: to file an application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code, to file an appeal or to file a separate suit. In this case the present plaintiffs chose to file a miscellaneous case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code. He cannot now try again through a different avenue having exhausted his first choice all the way up to the Appellate Division. 

11. When the matter was before the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1033 of 1987, it was observed that the petitioners (respondents herein) filed an application under Order IX, rule 9 read with section 151 of the Code which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 for restoration of Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 filed under Order IX, rule 13, which had been dismissed for default on 30-4-1982. 

12. Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 was dismissed stating that although the petitioners were present in Court with witness but the clerk of their learned Advocate filed their hazira after of the case had been dismissed for default due to their non-appearance. It was held that dismissal of Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 was appealable under Order XLIII, rule 1(d), accordingly Miscellaneous Case No.119 of 1982 was rejected as not maintainable. In spite of the finding that the application under Order IX, rule 9 did not lie, the present plaintiffs filed revision before the learned District Judge, which having been dismissed, they filed Civil Revision No.1033 of 1987 before the High Court Division. It cannot be said that the present plaintiffs were not aware that the dismissal of Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 under Order IX, rule 13 was appealable. The present suit was filed on 04-9-2008, about 26 years after Miscellaneous Case No.111 of 1981 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code was dismissed for default. It is abundantly clear that the present plaintiffs have acted with malafide from the very beginning. The present suit is hopelessly barred by limitation as well as the principles of res-judicata. 

13. In view of the discussion above, we find that the High Court Division and the courts below ought to have allowed the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code. 

14. We find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants. In view of the discussion above, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgement and order of the High court Division as well of those of the Courts below are set-aside. The application of the defendants under Order VII, rule 11 is allowed. The suit of the plaintiffs is dismissed. 

15. A separate suit was filed by Subash Chandra Saha and four others, being Other Class Suit No.11 of 2009. impleading as defendants Syed Rafiqul Islam and others, who were also defendants in Other Class Suit No.27 of 2008. The prayer in both the suits is identical. In Other Class Suit No.11 of 2009 also the defendants filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 which was rejected. Challenging that Civil Revision No.20 of 2010 was filed before the learned District Judge, Mymensingh. This was also rejected. Thereafter, Civil Revision No.4068 of 2010 filed before the High Court Division culminated in the Rule being discharged by the judgement and order dated 13-12-2010 which is impugned in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.545 of 2011, which has been tagged to be heard along with Civil Appeal No.101 of 2012. 

16. The reasons given in our decision in Civil Appeal No.101 of 2012 are equally applicable in the case of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.545 of 2011. 

Accordingly, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.545 of 2011 is disposed of in the light of the judgement of Civil Appeal No.101 of 2012. For the same reasons, the application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code filed in Other Class Suit No.11 of 2009 is allowed and the suit of the plaintiffs is dismissed. 

End.
