parties:
Mia Rezaul Haque -------- Appellant
VS
Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, Regional Office, Faridpur ------- Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Rezaul Hasan, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 13-3-2014, passed by the teamed District Judge, Faridpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 2013, arising out of Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 2013 rejecting the miscellaneous case, filed under 9 Rule 13A of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

2. The fact in brief, relevant for disposal of this miscellaneous appeal, is that, the respondent-Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation sanctioned credit facility, of Taka 6,55,000, in favour of the appellant, on 26-9-1980 and the appellant availed the said credit facility and, as security, mortgaged his property, vide registered mortgage deed No. 2061 dated 27-24981; that as per terms of the sanction letter, the appellant was under an obligation to repay the dues within 25 years in equal monthly installments, but he has failed to repay his entire liabilities within the stipulated period; that as on 31-12-2012, the liability of the appellant stands at Taka 3,28,256.47, out of which Taka 88,578.55 is principal amount and Taka 2,39,686.92 is interest; that in order to recover the said amount the corporation, as petitioner, filed a Miscellaneous Case before the District Judge, Faridpur, under Article 27 of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (PO 7 of 1973) and the said case was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 2013; that on 31-10-2013, the case was fixed for ex-parte hearing. But, on 28-10-2013, the present appellant filed a written objection and an application for withdrawing the case from the list of ex-parte hearing and the District Judge, Faridpur fixed the same for hearing on 31-10-2013; that in his written objection, the appellant contended that the claim of the Corporation is not correct; that by 3-2-2011 he repaid a sum of Taka 18,52,796.75 to the Corporation; that thereafter he made several verbal and written request to the corporation to provide him the statement of accounts, but the Corporation did not pay any heed to it; that due to such non-cooperation of the Corporation the appellant failed to deposit any money; that the claim of the corporation is imaginary and unreasonable; that on 31-10-2013, the opposite party i.e. the present appellant filed hazira, but the Corporation filed an application for adjournment which was allowed and the Court below has fixed the next date of the case on 23-1-2014; that on 23-1-2014, the opposite party i.e. the present appellant, due to sever illness could not appear before the court and even could not give any instruction to the his learned advocate and consequently the case was decreed ex-parte on 23-1-2014 against the opposite party i.e. the present appellant; that thereafter the present appellant filed an application before the District Judge, Faripur on 23-2-2014 under Order IX, rule 13 for setting aside the said ex-parte judgment and decree, but the said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 2014. That the Court below upon hearing the said miscellaneous case No. 2 of 2014 rejected the same by his impugned judgment and order dated 13-3-2014. 

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and order dated 13-3-2014, the opposite party-petitioner-applicant has filed this FMA, on the grounds stated therein. 

4. Learned Advocate Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that, the findings of the learned District Judge, Faridpur is not based on correct appreciation of evidence, rather the same is contrary to the fact, as because the learned Court below, while rejecting the miscellaneous case, has come to a findings that, the present appellant did not take any step on the date fixed on 31-10-2013 and on 23-1-2014, respectively, but from the record, it is clear that on 31-10-2013 the present appellant filed hazira before the learned Court, but the respondent-corporation prayed for adjournment. Mr Razi next submits that, the appellant filed the application under Order IX , rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree within the prescribed time limit of 30 days from the date of the said ex-parte judgment and decree and offered sufficient reason for failure to appear on the date of petition hearing. He also submits that, the impugned judgment and order is neither proper, nor just one. Rather, that is an outcome of non-application of mind and that has resulted in serious injustice to the appellant. He prays for allowing the appeal so that the appellant can prove his case in the Court below. 

5. No one appeared on behalf of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. 

6. I have heard the learned. Advocate for the appellant, perused the materials on record. 

7. I find that, on 31-10-2013, the case was fixed for ex-parte hearing and before that on 28-10-2013, the present appellant filed a written objection and an application for withdrawing the case from the list of ex-parte hearing and the learned District Judge, Faridpur, fixed the same for hearing on 31-10-2013. It also appears that, on 31-10-2013, the opposite party in that miscellaneous case, i.e. the present appellant, filed hazira, but the Corporation filed an application for adjournment, which was allowed and the Court below fixed the next the date on 23-1-2014. That, on 23-1-2014, the opposite party i.e. the present appellant due to his illness; could not appear before the Court and even could not give any instruction to the his learned Advocate and consequently the case was decreed ex-parte on 23-1-2014; that thereafter, the present appellant filed an application before the learned District Judge, Fardipur, on 23-2-2014, under Order IX, rule 13A for setting aside the said ex-parte judgment and decree and the said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 2014 and the learned District Judge, Faridpur, upon hearing the said miscellaneous case No. 2 of 2014, rejected the same by his impugned judgment and order dated 13-3-2014. 

8. On query, as to the applicability of the Code of Civil Procedure in the instant case, it further appears to me that, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (PO 7 of 1973) is not a self-contained law and there is no non-obstante clause in the said law as well as the application of Code of Civil Procedure has not been curtailed by the said law, and there is no such debarring Article in the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (PO 7 of 1973). Moreover, Article 27(9) of PO 7 of 1973 has made provision that, the Code of Civil Procedure applicable for the attachment and sale of the attached property. 

9. Since, the miscellaneous case filed by the House Building Finance Corporation (under PO 7 of 1973) is a proceeding of civil nature, therefore, Code of Civil Procedure will apply, in view of the provisions of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

10. It further appears that the last two days of that month was Friday and Saturday and, therefore, the said application was filed within 30 days i.e. within time, in view of section 10 of the General Clauses Act. 

11. Moreover, having gone through the ex-parte judgment, it appears that the same has been passed very mechanically violating the provisions of Article 27 and also violating the settled principles of law that, even in an ex-parte cases, the onus to prove is not to be disregarded, nor becomes lesser than the required standard of proof. 

12. In view of the discussion made above, I find merit in this appeal and accordingly the same should be allowed. 

13. In the result, the appeal is allowed. 

14. The impugned ex-parte judgment and decree dated 23-1-2014 passed by the learned District Judge, Faridpur, in Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 2013 is hereby set-aside. 

15. The learned District Judge, Faridpur, is hereby directed to give the opportunity to the borrowers to contest in the original suit/ miscellaneous case. 

Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Courts below at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Bikash Paul, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Bivuti Tarofder, Advocate—For the Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Suruj Molla (Md) and another ---- Petitioners
VS
Artha Rin Adalat and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: At the instance of the judgment debtors in Artha Execution Case No. 23 of 2018 and that of the defendants in Artha Rin Suit No. 7 of 2014, this Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms: 
"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 18-11-2020 passed by the respondent No. 1 in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2020, arising out of Artha Rin Suit No. 7 of 2014 recalling the order dated 16-9-2020 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2020 shall not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and /or pass such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this court also stayed the operation of the impugned order dated 18-11-2020 passed by the respondent No. 1 in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2020 for a period of 6(six) months. However, on the date of issuance of the Rule, this court also fixed the matter for passing further order fixing it on 12-12-2021. Record shows that, no further extension was taken of the operation of the impugned order. 

3. The precise facts so have been figured in the writ petition are: 
The present respondent No.2 as plaintiff originally filed a suit being Artha Rin Suit No. 7 of 2014 against the present petitioners impleading them as defendants in the said suit claiming an amount of Taka 6,67,011 as of outstanding dues. As the defendants did not appear the suit was ultimately decreed ex-parte on 26-8-2014 (decreed drawn up on 31-8-2014). Since the defendants did not repay the decretal dues, the present respondent No. 2 then filed an Execution Case being Artha Execution Case No. 33 of 2014 which was subsequently renumbered as Artha Execution Case No. 23 of 2018. Near about 6 years of decreeing the suit, the present petitioners on 16-9-2020 filed an application under section 19(1)(2)(3) and (4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (precisely "the Ain") for setting aside the ex-parte decree claiming that, they came to learn about the said decree on 15-9-2020 and on the following day they filed the application which gave rise to Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2020. On the very date of filing the said Miscellaneous case, the learned judge, respondent No. 1 allowed the same (dated 16-9-2020). After that, the present respondent No. 2 on 29-10-2020 filed an application for setting aside the said restoration order for ends of justice. Against that very application for setting aside the restoration order, the present petitioners on 4-11-2020 also filed written objection. The learned judge however vide impugned order dated 18-11-2020 allowed the application of the bank and thus set aside the restoration order passed by him on 16-9-2020. 

4. It is at that stage, the petitioners came before this court and obtained the instant Rule and order of stay. 

5. Mr Bikash Paul, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners upon taking us to the writ petition and all the annexure so appended therewith at the very outset submits that, since under the provision of section 19(2) of the Ain the petitioners filed the application by depositing 10% of the decretal amount through pay order so the court has nothing to do but to restore the suit and in the instant case, the learned judge vide order dated 16-9-2020 rightly restored the suit to its original filed and number by setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree passed on 31-8-2014. 

6. The learned counsel next contends that, since under the provision of section 41 of the Ain any order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat can only be challenged through preferring appeal and in case of preferring appeal, the bank is not required to deposit any amount, so without exhausting that alternative and efficacious remedy it field the application for setting aside the restoration order in the pretext of ends of justice which cannot be sustained in law. 

7. The learned counsel next contends that, soon after restoration of the suit to its original file and number the present petitioners initiated mediation and arbitration process under the provision of section 22 and 23 of the AM and when the suit was being proceeded with that stage, the present respondent No. 2 filed the application for setting aside the restoration order with a malafide intention not to dispose of the suit on merit and contest. 

8. The learned counsel next contends that, the respondent No. 2 filed an application for setting aside the restoration order without mentioning the relevant provision of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain just claimed for ends of justice which does not come within the ambit of any provision of the Ain and therefore the impugned order is ex-facie illegal. 

9. The learned counsel next contends that, in the meantime the petitioners have repaid 50% of the claim amount to the respondent No. 2 yet the respondent No. 2 kept on proceeding with the execution case for realizing the decretal dues which is totally illegal illogical and cannot be sustained. With such submission the learned counsel finally prays for making the Rule absolute. 

10. On the flipside, Mr Bivuti Tarofder, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent No. 2 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition very candidly opposes the submission so placed by the learned counsel for the petitioners and contends that, since the petitioners entered appearance upon receiving summons and took adjournment for filing written statement so there has been no occasion to claim that they came to learn about the ex-parte decree through information slip which is barefaced untrue and adopted for delay the disposal of the execution case. The learned counsel by annexing entire order sheets of Artha Rin Suit No.7 of 2014 draws our attention to order nos. 5 and 6 dated 4-6-2014 and 1-7-2014 respectively further submits that, from those two orders it is crystal clear that, having every knowledge about the proceedings of the suit, they have cooked up a story in their application filed under section 19 of the Ain for setting aside the ex-parte decree and therefore the learned judge has rightly exercised his inherent jurisdiction under section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and set aside the restoration order he passed earlier on 16-9-2020. 

11. The learned counsel also contends that, since the petitioners claimed that they came to learn about the said ex-parte decree through filing a "mention slip" so heavy burden lies upon them to prove the date of knowledge by adducing and producing evidence but it has not been done still the learned judge on the following date of filing the miscellaneous case set aside the ex-parte decree on 16-9-2020 which was ex-facie illegal. 

12. Insofar as regards to application of section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain in setting aside the restoration order the learned counsel further contends that, since a gigantic fraud has been committed by the petitioners upon the court concealing the truth about the knowledge of the decree of the suit, the learned judge has rightly exercised his prerogative authority under section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and accordingly while passing the impugned order the learned judge has rightly mentioned the provision of section 57 of the Ain which is sustainable in law. In that connection, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 22 BLC (AD) 139. 

13. The learned counsel has also placed his reliance in the decision reported in 66 DLR 1 and by placing the relevant paragraphs of that cited decision submits that, since the petitioners based on the date of knowledge so they must have produced evidence to prove the date of knowledge. 

14. With those submissions the learned counsel finally prays for discharging the Rule with costs. 

15. We have considered the submission so placed by the learned counsel for the petitioners and that of the respondent No. 2. Only point-in-issue revolves around to dispose of the instant Rule is, whether the provision of section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain will be applicable in setting aside restoration order passed by the respondent No. 1 and whether against the order of setting aside the ex-parte decree, the respondent No. 2 ought to have preferred an appeal under section 41 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. To address those two vital issues, we at the first place feel it expedient to see the application filed for restoration which has been annexed as Annexure-'F' to the writ petition. On going through paragraph No. 4 as well as paragraph No. 8 thereof, we find that, it has been alleged therein that, no notice or summons has ever been served upon the petitioners and they just came to learn about the ex-parte decree by filing information slip on 15-9-2020 and on the following day i.e, on 16-9-2020 they filed the Miscellaneous case. In that aspect we feel to examine the order sheets of Artha Rin Suit No. 7 of 2014 which has been annexed by the present respondent No. 2 as of Annexure-'2' to its -affidavit-in-opposition. On going through the orders being orders dated 4-6-2014 and 1-7-2014 we find that, the summons had duly been served upon the petitioners and the petitioners entered their appearance by filing a new power. The petitioners can not claim that they were not aware about the said orders passed by the Artha Rin Adalat because when they filed the Miscellaneous case under section 19 of the Ain they got the opportunity to go through the order sheets. Had it been so, then the alleged assertion so made out in the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree is proved to be totally untrue and on that score we genuinely assume that, fraud has been practiced upon the court for getting the ex-parte order set aside. Moreover, on the date of filing the Miscellaneous case the learned judge did not feel it bothered to issue summons or notice upon the respondent bank enabling it to appear and contest the case rather on the very date of filing the Miscellaneous case it was allowed which sounds totally unusual. 

16. We have also very meticulously gone through the decision so have been reported in 66 DLR 1 and in paragraph No. 13 thereof, it has clearly been spelt out that, in case of basing on date of knowledge while filing Miscellaneous case, the defendant petitioner must adduce and produce witness to prove the date of knowledge. But in the instant case it has not been done and the learned judge restored the suit in its original file and number even without bothering to inform the respondent No. 2 bank. In such a circumstances, it can easily construe that, the petitioners have misguided the learned judge of the Artha Rin Adalat in obtaining the order setting aside the ex-parte decree. In such a situation it is our considered view that, the provision of section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain will come into play and the respondent No. 1 has perfectly exercised his inherent jurisdiction in setting aside the restoration order of the suit apparently fraud has been practiced in obtaining the order. Now let us address the point in regard to preferring appeal claimed to be filed by the respondent No. 2 against the order setting aside the restoration order but we don't find any iota of substance in the said submission so placed by the learned counsel for the petitioners. Because, that very provision for preferring appeal under section 41 of the Ain is only applicable if it is against any judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat not against any interim order. And for that obvious reason, the provision of section 44(2) has been incorporated in the Artha Rin Ain which runs as follows: 
৪৪(২) উপ-ধারা (৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, এই আইনের অধীনে কোন আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত কোন অন্তবর্তীকালীন আদেশকে উচ্চতর কোন আদালতে আপীল বা রিভিশন আকারে বিতর্কিত করা যাইবে না।

17. So, the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioners that, against the order of restoration dated 16-9-2020 the present respondent No. 2 ought to have preferred appeal does not hold water. 

18. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we don't find any iota of merit in the Rule. 

19. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs resulting in the impugned order stands. 

20. The learned judge respondent No. 1 is hereby directed to proceed with the Execution Case No. 23 of 2018 and dispose of the same as expeditiously as possible preferably within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this order. 

21. At any event, the order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands recalled and vacated. 

Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the respondent No. 1 forthwith. 

End.

parties:
Moslehuddin Ahmed ------ Appellant
vs
Abdul Gafur being dead his heirs :1(a) Nuruzzaman (Rotan) and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 2-8-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4949 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman, J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 2-8-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4949 of 2001 making the Rule absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and order dated 10-7-2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Chandina, Comilla in Decree Execution Case No. 5 of 2000 dismissing the suit with a direction to the trial Court to proceed with the execution case in accordance with law and disposed of the same preferable within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the judgment.

2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the decree holder respondent Abdul Gafur instituted Title Suit No.166 of 1967 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Comilla against one Balaram Sarkar for specific performance of contract claiming that the defendant Balaram Sarkar entered into an agreement with him to transfer 56 decimals of land at a consideration of Taka 500 on first Ashar, 1370 BS. He paid Taka 48.75 to the said Balaram Sarkar for purchasing stamp paper; on 12-1-1964, he and Balaram Sarkar went to Chandina sub-registrar Office, therein a kabala was written and the defendant Balaram Sarkar received the rest of the consideration money amounting to Taka 1,500, Balaram Sarkar duly executed the kabala, but it was not present for registration on that date; he took immediate possession of the suit from Balaram Sarkar; the defendant Balaram Sarkar avoided registration of kabala by instituting criminal case against him; that he obtained necessary permission to sue the defendant Balaram Sarkar since he was a member of minority community. Thereafter, he filed suit for specific performance of contract. 

3. The defendant contested the case by filing written statement contending that he intended to execute a deed of usufructuary mortgage in favour of the plaintiff in respect of 16 decimals of land on receipt of Taka 200 as loan from him, but the plaintiff in collusion with the deed writer got the kabala executed by him, being aware of the same he brought a criminal case against the plaintiff, he denied delivery of possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by him and claimed his own possession. 

4. After hearing the parties the suit was decreed by the learned Munsif by his judgment and decree. As against the said judgment and decree Balaram Sarkar preferred Title Appeal No. 96 of 1973 in the Court of District Judge, Comilla, on transfer it was heard by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Second Court, Comilla, who by his judgment and decree dated 28-7-1973 set-aside the decree passed by the trial Court. Against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred Second Appeal No. 169 of 1974 before the High Court Division and by a judgment dated 2-9-1985 the High Court Division allowed the Second Appeal on setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate judge and restored the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. During pendency of the said Second Appeal in the High Court Division on 2-9-1980 the opposite party No.1 of the revision (appellant herein) and his father Mohammad Ali Miah filed an application to substitute them as respondents in the Second Appeal claiming that they purchased the suit land from Balaram Sarkar, and on the same date Balaram Sarkar also made similar prayer by a separate application, accordingly the High Court Division by an order dated 4-11-1980 substituted the said two persons as respondents in place of Balaram Sarkar in the said Second Appeal. 

5. The trial court in decreeing the suit directed the defendant Balaram to register the kabala within 30 days from the date of preparing the decree and in the Second Appeal the High Court Division gave similar direction to the substituted respondent/defendant in the following words; "As the purchaser respondents have put themselves in the shoes of defendant Balaram, they are also directed to execute and register sale deed in favour of the plaintiff" 

6. Since the said Balaram Sarkar or the substituted defendants did not comply with the court's direction by executing and registering any kabala in his favour he filed Execution Case No. 4 of 1990 for execution of the decree, the said execution case was dismissed for default on 6-6-1992.

7. The decree holder again, for execution of the said decree, filed another application on 13-11-2000 being registered as Title Execution Case No. 05 of 2000 against the substituted defendants. After filing such application for execution the decree holder respondent herein filed 4 (four) applications (i) dated 4-4-2001 under section 14 of the Limitation Act, (ii) dated 4-4-2001 under section 5 of the Limitation Act, (iii) dated 17-4-2001 under section 48(2)(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure and (iv) dated 25-6-2001 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the aforesaid application made under section 48(2)(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure the decree holder respondent stated that as per the provision of section 48(2)(a) of Civil Procedure, he is entitled to proceed with the execution case which he filed with delay for a period of 5 years, 5 months,14 days which require to be condoned. 

8. In another application made section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure he made the similar prayer asking to invoke the inherent power of the court to execute the decree obtained by him. 

9. In another application made under section 5 of the Limitation Act he also made prayer for condonation of delay. The contentions of his another application made under section 14 are also similar. 

10. One of the substituted debtors namely Moslehuddin Ahmed (the respondent No.1 in the High Court Division) filed a written objection in the execution proceeding denying the contention of the plaintiff/decree holder in his application for condonation of delay made under section 5 of the Limitation Act and stating that after obtaining the final decree on 2-9-1985 from the High Court Division the said decree was put into execution by filing execution 13-11-2000. The decree holder filed the subsequent execution case beyond the period of 12 years from the date of final disposal of the suit, as such the instant execution proceeding is not maintainable and the provision under section 5 of the Limitation Act is not applicable in the instant case as it appears from the decisions of the Appellate Division reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 and 16 BLD (AD) 73, hence the execution proceeding, is liable to be dismissed. 

11. All the aforesaid 4 (four) applications of the decree-holder as well as the aforesaid written objection of the judgment-debtor were taken up together for hearing. After hearing by a judgment and order dated 10-7-2001 the learned Senior Assistant Judge rejected the applications filed by the plaintiff/decree holder and dismissed the execution proceeding as being barred by limitation with the finding that he came to know that Mr Shahidul Islam the learned Advocate for the petitioner died in 1999 who could file the subsequent execution case within 3 years from the date of dismissal of the first execution case. Moreover the application of the decree holder made under section 14 of the Limitation Act, reveals that the plaintiff could file another suit being Title Suit No. 35 of 1992 which is pending and he has been proceeding with that suit as such he was able to come to the court after dismissal of the first execution case, his contention in the application under section 48(2)(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure appears to be false. 

12. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order the plaintiff-decree holder as petitioner moved the High Court Division in revision and obtained the Rule. To oppose the Rule a counter affidavit sworn on. 22-3-2006 was filed by the opposite-party No.1 Moslehuddin Ahmed wherein he reiterated his above mentioned written objection filed before the Senior Assistant Judge. 

13. The High Court Division after hearing the parties in Civil Revision No. 4949 of 2001 by a judgment and order dated 2-8-2007 made the Rule absolute thereby setting aside the judgment and order dated 10-7-2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Chandina, Comilla in Execution Case No.5 of 2000. 

14. The appellant, as petitioner filed civil pe.ition for leave to appeal No. 514 of 2008 and after hearing the same obtained leave, which, gave, rise to the instant appeal. 

15. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant has submitted that the law of limitation provides period of time for filing of execution case in Article 182 of the Act as well as in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the decree-holder, after obtaining the decree, did not file the first execution case within 3 years as per the provision of Article 182 of the Limitation Act. Moreso, the first execution case was dismissed for default, and even then, the decree-holder did not file the instant execution case within next 3 years from the date of dismissal of the first execution case, rather, he filed the same after expiry of 8 years 4 months from the date of dismissal of the first one. He has specifically pointed that the decree holder did not file the instant execution proceeding within 12 years from the date of decree in accordance with law, and, as such, it is hopelessly time barred, hence, not maintainable. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, in accordance with law, correctly dismissed the execution case which occasioned no failure of justice in view of the law laid down in the cases reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 and 16 BLD (AD) 73. The High Court Division erred in law in not following the decisions of apex Division as referred to above. He has further submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in applying sub-section 2(a) of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, maintaining the execution case, even after, expiry of 12 years although execution proceeding not having been kept alive by filing successive application within 3 years from the date of the last proceeding application as required by Article 182 of the Limitation Act. So, the instant application cannot be filed after 12 years as the first execution case was barred by time. The trial Court having found that the decree-holder was not prevented from executing the decree as described the story in the application for condonation but the High Court Division without appreciating the provisions of sub-section 2(a) of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the Code) in its true perspective of the case upon misinterpreting the provisions made applicable in this case. He has finally submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the decree-holder was prevented to file execution case within time which removed the bar of limitation to proceed with the execution of the decree, and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. 

16. Per contra, Mrs Qumrunnessa, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos.1(a) - 1(g) has submitted that the High Court Division as revisional Court did not commit any legal error, hence, rightly made the Rule absolute. Therefore, she prays for dismissal of the apgeal. She has further submitted that the High Court Division considering the provisions of sub section (2)(a) of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure opined that the decree holder satisfactorily was able to assign the reason of delay in filing the execution case, as such, make the Rule absolute setting aside the impugned order of the execution Court which does not call for interference by this Division. The learned Advocate-on-Record in a same breath next submitted that the objection raised by the purchaser defendant is beyond the provisions of law. She has pointed that after omitting of section 47 of the Code, in execution of decree, none can raise the objection regarding executing the decree which was affirmed upto the Apex Court. She has very candidly apprised the Court that the precedents referred by the Senior Counsel for the appellants are not applicable for the present case because those decisions were pronounced before the omitting of the section 47 of the Code. She has finally approached that this Division to apply Article 104 of the Constitution to do complete justice for the respondents. 

17. We have heard the learned senior Advocate and the learned Advocate-on-Record for the respective parties. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials available on record. 

18. The High Court Division found that the judgment-debtor was prevented by filing criminal cases one after another, practicing fraud in the name of compromise, those pretexts were not considered lawfully of the executing court, although the plaintiff-petitioner was able to assign legal cause according to sub-section 2(a) of section 48 of the Code. It was further observed by the High Court Division that the plaintiff-petitioner never cause to show the death of his learned Advocate but the executing Court had brought such extraneous matter in rejecting the application which occasioned failure of justice, further view of the learned Judge of the High court Division is that the justice demands the decree obtained by the petitioner being contested up to the apex Court of the country should to be executed, since the said decree of specific performance of Contract has mostly been performed accept registration moreover after transfer of the suit land to the decree holed by the original owner Balaram Sarkar as it proved in the title suit there is no scope to claim or establish the subsequent purchase by the opposite parties from the said Balaram Sarkar. However in the prevailing circumstances I hold the view that the execution of the decree cannot be restrained. Reading the two decision mentioned above I find that those are not applicable in the instant case. In both the decisions it appears that the judgment-debtor raised abjection by filing application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure on such objecting raised by judgment-debtor respective Miscellaneous case well initiated after formal disposal of the respective case the fate of the execution proceedings were decided. But in the instant case there was no scope to initiate any such miscellaneous case since section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure had already been repealed by Ordinance No.48 of 1983. After such repeal of section 47 I find no scope to entertain any objection as raised by the judgment-debtor in the instant case. My such view got support from the decision of a Division Bench of this Division in the case of Tripura Modern Bank Ltd. vs Sunil Kumar Rajgharia and others reported in 1991 BLD 479 = 43 DLR 460. 

19. It is, however, not denied, rather, admitted fact that at the time of filing the Execution Case No.5 of 2000 on 13-11-2000, the decree holder filed four applications two for condonation of delay under section 5 and 14 of the Limitation Act, amongst other two applications one under section 48(2)(a) and another under section 151 of the Code. The Executing Court at the time of hearing of the applications heard the respective Advocates and rejected the same by its judgment and order dated 10-7-2001. The High Court Division, however, upon hearing both the parties was pleased to allow the application under section 48(2)(a) of the Code by the impugned judgment and order. 

20. Now the question is, if, the executing Court found that the execution case is barred by law of limitation and in the other applications reasons have been offered therein were not satisfactory and untenable that is the decree holder could not proved the facts of fraud or force as per provisions of section 48(2)(a) of the Code, such applications can be rejected after elaborate discussions. 

21. The Executing Court in rejecting such applications opined that the decree holder filed the decree execution Case No.4 of 1990 which was dismissed on 6-6-1992 for want of steps. On 13-11-2000, 2nd decree execution case being Case No.5 of 2000 was filed, which was admittedly delayed by 8 years and 4 months. The decree holder took the pretext to condone the delay in an application under section 48(2)(a) of the Code. The Executing Court found that decree holder had filed another suit being other Suit No.35 of 1992 and proceeded well ahead without any hindrance for the same time. Furthermore, some criminal cases were not at the period of limitation but later like GR Case No.32 of 1998, non GR Case No.33 of 1998 and CR Case were out of period of limitation, however, execution case was dismissed on 6-6-1992, hence, the Court disbelieved the aforementioned pretexts to allow the aforementioned applications. 

22. Thus, such discussions according to us are legal and lawful to its true perspective. We observed that High Court Division without discarding the findings based on strong inferences reversed the order of the Executing Court. 

23. On perusal of the impugned order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge it is found that his order is sound on point of law as well as fact and it is a speaking order. The executing court found the execution application dated 13-11-2000 was hopelessly barred by limitation under the concerned legal scheme enshrined in the section 48 of the code of civil procedure, 1908 read with Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which were further affirmed by the Apex Court in the cases reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 and 16 BLD (AD) 73. We found the findings of the Executing Court as factual and rational. On appreciation and sifting of facts Executing Court disbelieved the decree holder's version of case as claimed that fraud or force, which prevented the execution of the decree at some time within twelve years immediately before the date of the application. 

24. However, the contentions advanced by the learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondents, referring repealed section 47 that no objection can be raised by the judgment-debtor or title claimer through the judgment-debtor, if, such arguments are accepted in toto, then the execution proceeding if suffer from any legal impediment like the present case, the executing Court would not be able to look into that impediment either factual or lawful in disposing the execution case. 

25. We are, therefore, further, of the view that the executing Court itself can look into if it is found in a execution proceedings that such execution proceedings are not maintainable due to any factual and legal impediment. Therefore, such arguments are devoid of merit. 

26. We have anxiously thought as regard the application of Article 104 of the Constitution, as prayed by the learned Advocate for the respondents, nevertheless, we are unable to apply this article because of legal impediment as it appears in this matter. We have already viewed that the decree holder in filing both the execution cases admittedly were delayed due to his own fault. Therefore, other side appellant has accrued a valuable right in accordance with law due to fault and latches of the decree holder the predecessors of the respondent No.1(a)-1(g) in not executing the decree in time according to law. However, the plea taken by the decree holder according to us unsuccessful. Therefore, our considered view is that in violation of the specific provision of law, one side cannot get the complete justice depriving the other side from his valuable right obtained under the law. 

27. Concerning the execution proceedings this Division observed in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank Ltd. vs Sangbad Daily Paper and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 as follows: 
"It is well settled that 12 years is to be counted from terminus quo mentioned in clauses (a) and (b) of section 48(1).
Although the period of 12 years has been fixed which has been termed as an "outside period" the decree must be kept alive under the Limitation Act and Article 182 requires the first application for execution to be made within 3 years of the decree and each successive application to be made within three years of the final order passed on the last application. In Pingle Venkata Rama Reddy vs Kakaria Buchanna & others AIR 1963 Andhra Pradesh FB page 1 it was held that section 48 deals with the maximum limit of the time for execution. This includes the "out side period" after which no execution could be granted. It was considered that section deals with the maximum limit of time for execution and no application would be entertained after this period, notwithstanding that the last application was filed within three years of the final order made on the previous application as required by Article 182 of the Limitation Act. It was further noticed that the section requires the decree-holder to be diligent in realising the fruits of the decree. Even if successive applications are filed within three years of each order, it will not avail the decree-holder if the last one is not put in within the period-specified in section 48. It was considered that the judgment-debtor is under no obligation to establish that the earlier petition was out of time. It is enough for him to show that the execution proceeding which was the subject matter of enquiry is hit by section 48 CPC. In LaIji Raja and Sons vs Firm Hansraj Nathuram, AIR 1971 (SC) 974 the Supreme Court of India considered that section 48(1) of the Code indicated that the period is a period of limitation not a bar as was a judicial opinion at one time. The opinion that has now crystalised is that section 48 is controlled by the provision of the Limitation Act. In India by Limitation Act, 1963 section 48 of the Code is deleted and its place has now been taken by Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963. In this view the contention of Dr. Kamal Hossain that the execution proceeding is hit by Article 182 of the Limitation Act has considerable force. 

28. This view has been expressed in 27 DLR Dac. 72 Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo where it was observed: 

29. Both prescribe the period of limitation for the execution of the decree. The Civil Procedure Code fixes the longest period, whereas the Limitation Act the earliest period to take the first step in execution and the subsequent steps known as steps-in-aid. 

30. It was further observed: An application for execution has therefore to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code which prescribed the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail. 

31. This is a correct approach and it is interesting to note that the learned Judges commented that these two provisions though expressed in different language "create anomaly." "The removal of the anomaly is the function of the Parliament and not the court". Precisely for this reason, in India section 48 has been deleted by the Limitation Act, 1963 and the .period of limitation is now governed by Article 136 instead of the previous Article 182." 

32. The same view was reiterated by the Appellate Division in the case of Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property (Vested and Non-Resident) (L and B) and ADC (Revenue), Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 73 = 48 DLR (AD) 141 as follows: 
"In support of his submission that the last Execution Case was barred by section 48 CPC. Mr Moksudur Rahman has relied upon some decisions all of which are not relevant. This Court has, however, already pronounced itself on this point in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank Ltd. vs The Sangbad, Daily Paper and others BCR 1983 (AD) 418. The said decision was given on consideration of the cases of Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo, 27 DLR (Dhaka) 72, Pingle Venkata Rama Reddy vs Kakaria Buchanna and others, AIR 1963 Andhra Pradesh (FB) 1 and Lalji Raja and Sons vs Firm Hansraj Nthuram, AIR 1971 (SC) 974. This Court approved of the approach of the then Dhaka High Court in the afore-cited cases in 27 DLR (Dhaka) 72 and affirmed that both section 48 CPC and Article 182(2) of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act provide the period of limitation for the execution of a decree. The Civil Procedure Code fixes the longest period whereas the Limitation Act fixes the earliest period to take the first step in execution and the subsequent steps known as steps-in-aid. This Court also affirmed further view of then Dhaka High Court that an application for execution has therefore to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act being the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 CPC which prescribes the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail." 

33. Though the above mentioned principles were enunciated through the procedures of miscellaneous case which rightly mentioned by the single Judge of the High Court Division. Therefore, according to learned Advocate-on-Record, those precedents are not applicable in the present case because the miscellaneous cases were arose out under section 47 of the Code which now not in existence as repealed amending the Code. The contentions of the learned Advocate-on-Record cannot be sustained because the principle enunciated by this Division not according to the provisions of section 47 of the Code, though miscellaneous cases were filed on the procedure under section 4 of the Code, rather, it was enunciated regulating the provisions of the Limitation Act and section 48(2)(b)of the Code. So, it is squarely applicable in the present case. 

34. As a result, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants and the reasons elaborated above we find that the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division do call for interference. 

In the result, the Civil Appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is set-aside and the order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge is hereby restored. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J: On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 29-11-2017 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 5 of 2009 restoring the case to its original file and number should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts in brief are that, the opposite-party, as applicant, filed Money Execution Case No. 5 of 2009 on 30-9-2009 under Order 21 Rule 11 of the Code read with section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka as decree-holder, against the opposite-party, as judgment-debtors, for enforcement of a foreign award passed by Singapore International Arbitration Centre in Arbitration Case No. 52 of 2005 and Arbitration Award No. 40 of 2006. Application for execution was admitted by the Court and notices issued upon the judgment-debtors. Finally, the Executing Court amongst other dates vide Order No. 47 dated 21-3-2017 fixed the case for return of notice. On the date fixed decree-holder filed hazira. The notices were not returned after service, but judgment-debtors entered into appearance by filing Vokalatnama, consequently, next date was fixed on 4-5-2017 for hearing of the case. On the date fixed for hearing the decree-holder did not take any step either by filing hazira or application for adjournment. When the case was taken up for hearing the decree-holder was found absent consequently, the Court below, by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-5-2017 dismissed the case for default. Thereafter, the decree-holder filed an application on 11-5-2017 serving copy of the application upon the judgment-debtors, praying for restoration of the execution case. The application was opposed by the judgment-debtors by filing written objection on 29-11-2017. Learned District Judge after hearing both the parties by the impugned judgment and order dated 29-11-2017 allowed the application and restored the execution case awarding costs of Taka 5,000 (Taka five thousand) to be paid to the judgment-debtors. 

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the learned District Judge, Dhaka the judgment-debtor-petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application and obtained the present Rule and order of stay. 

4. Mr AKM Alamgir Parvez Bhuiyan, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the execution case was filed by the decree-holder for enforcement of an award under provision of Order XXI, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. There is no provision in law to restore an execution proceeding dismissed for default, but the decree-holder can file fresh execution case for enforcement of the decree subject to provision of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that though the application for restoration was filed within week after dismissal of the execution case, but the court has no power or jurisdiction to allow the application for restoration of the execution proceeding, as such, the order passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka apparently suffers from lacking jurisdiction as well as contrary to the provisions of law. 

5. Mr Md Sagir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite-party submits that the execution case was fixed on 21-3-2017 for return of notices. On the date fixed the decree-holder filed hazira and the court noted that notice after service have not yet returned but order shows that the judgment-debtors entered into appearance on that date and the case was fixed for hearing on 4-5-2017, but in the cause list, it was posted mentioning service return which led the decree-holder to understand that the case was not ready for hearing, consequently, the decree-holder failed to take step on the date fixed for hearing, however, after coming to know about order of dismissal, the decree-holder hurriedly filed the application for restoration of the case. The court below fixed the application for hearing on 29-11-2017 and on that date the judgment-debtors filed objection against the application. The court after hearing both the sides, restored the execution case awarding costs of Taka 5,000. He further submits that the court in restoring execution case committed no illegally or error of law as the court has inherent power to be exercised for the interest of justice, notwithstanding, the fact that the applicant had another remedy, accordingly, the court restored the execution case. He argued that because of restoration of the execution case by the court below the other party has not been prejudiced in any way rather they will get opportunity to get the case disposed of within a shortest possible time. In support of his such submissions he has referred to the case of Nemi Chand and other vs timed Mal reported in 1962 AIR Rajasthan 107. 

6. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, have gone through the revision application, application in execution case, application for restoration of the execution case, objection filed by the judgment-debtors and the impugned judgment and order. 

7. The execution case arises out of an foreign award passed by the Singapore Inter-national Arbitration Centre. The award holder put the award in execution by filing Money Execution Case No.5 of 2009 on 30th September, 2009 before the court of District Judge, Dhaka. 

8. From perusal of order sheets (Annexure-B series to the application), it appears that the case was fixed for taking steps on the part of the decree-holder and return of notices on 47 dates and it took more than 8(eight) years time. Order sheets show that the decree-holder on all dates before dismissal of the execution case took steps either by filing hazira or by putting requisites for service of notices upon judgment-debtors. In usual course the case was fixed on 21-3-2017 for return of notices. On that date decree-holder filed hazira and the court noted that notices not returned after service, but the judgment debtors entered into appearance by filing vokalatnama. Because of appearance of the judgment-debtors on 21-3-2017 the court below fixed on 4-5-2017 for hearing of the case, but on that date the decree-holder took no step either by filing hazira or seeking any adjournment consequently, the court below dismissed the case for default. Thereafter, on 11-5-2017 decree-holder filed an application for restoration of the execution case, copy of which was received by the judgment debtors on 22-11-2017. The learned District Judge fixed on 29-11-2017 for hearing the application. On the date fixed the judgment debtors filed written objection against the application for restoration. The Court after hearing both the sides allowed the application and restored the execution case in its original file and number on condition of payment of costs of Taka 5,000 (Taka five thousand) to be paid the judgment-debtors. 

9. Now, the question is whether the court can restore an execution case dismissed for default under any provision of law. It is true that there is no provision for restoration of an execution case dismissed for default in the Code of Civil Procedure, in particular, under Order XXI. It is well settled that after dismissal of an execution case the decree-holder can file a fresh execution case subject to the provisions of section 48 of the Code and Article 182 of the Limitation Act. In the present case, the decree-holder did not take recourse to such provisions of law but filed an application simply praying for restoration of the execution case in its original file and number and the court below allowed the same. 

10. It is to be looked into whether by allowing an application for restoration of the execution case the court below has committed any illegality or error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The petitioner contended that the execution court has no jurisdiction to restore the execution case in the exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Civil Procedure Code admittedly contains no express provisions for restoration of the execution case dismissed in default or for re-hearing of the execution matters heard ex parte. 

11. From the impugned order, it appears that the Court below did not specify the precise provision under which the execution case was restored as well as the application filed by the decree-holder also mentioned no provisions of law. In the absence of mentioning any provision of law in the application as well as dismissal of the execution case and restoration of the same it can be construed that the impugned judgment and order was passed by the execution court under its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In pursuing the case the decree-holder was not so vigilant, but from order sheets it appears that they took steps on all the dates fixed, except on the date of dismissal of the execution case and there was no gross negligence on the part of the decree-holder. The court below in passing the impugned order though did not discuss or decide the applicability of section-151 of the Code to the restoration of execution applications dismissed for default and has not assigned any reason for restoration of the case but the judgment-debtors could not satisfy the court how the order of restoration prejudiced them from getting justice, rather they will have all the weapons in their armoury available to wreck out the execution case on any point of law, as held by the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank (Shimabadha) vs Shafiqur Rahman and another in Civil Appeal No. 39 of 1980, arising out of Civil Rule No. 309 of 1969 (Ref: 53 DLR 78, wrongly quoted as Civil Revision No. 309 of 1967 and Civil Appeal No. 30 of 1980). 

12. It is now well settled that the courts have wide discretionary power and they have to be exercised according to the exigencies of the particular cases. In the present case, we find that on 21-3-2017, in the daily cause list of the court below, subsequent date was posted on 4-5-2017 for service return inadvertently instead of hearing which is mistake of the court and for correction of its own mistake the execution court exercised its power under section 151 of the Code for securing justice and for speedy disposal of the execution case and by the order of the execution court no injustice has been done to the judgment-debtors. 

13. Apart from this there is another aspect to be mentioned that the award in Arbitration Case was passed on 2-10-2006, Money Execution Case No.5 of 2009 was filed on 30-9-2009 i.e. within 3 (three) years, the execution case was dismissed for default on 4-5-2017, the application for restoration was filed on 11-5-2017 within a week and within 12 years from the date of award/decree dated 2-10-2006, therefore, the proceeding is not barred both by special provisions of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure and general provisions of Article 182 of the Limitation Act. 

14. Had the court below rejected the application on the ground of maintainability, the decree-holder could have filed a fresh execution case within 10 months from the order or 12 years from the decree, but because of restoration of the case by the court below, in one hand, the decree-holder had no necessity and or scope to file a fresh execution case and on the other hand, because of elapse of 12 years by this time, the decree-holder has lost such opportunity to file a fresh execution case within the said period from the date of dismissal of the present case under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, moreover, by filing an application for restoration of the case instead of filing a fresh execution case it appears that they did not adopt indirect method to achieve the goal to avoid other legal consequences of the case. 

15. Had the decree-holder filed fresh execution case instead of filing this application it might have taken more time for the process of service of notices upon the judgment-debtors again. For speedy disposal of the proceeding by filing an application for restoration and allowing the same in exercise of inherent power of the court, in our view, has caused no injustice to the judgment debtors, moreover, it is not a case of inherent lack of jurisdiction but at best it can be said to be a case of an inappropriate decision restoring the case. This by itself does not justify interference by this Court in the exercise of revisional jurisdiction at this stage in the facts and circumstances of the case. Mere restoration of an execution case by exercising inherent power of the executing court has not occasioned any injustice to the judgment-debtors, hence, we do not find any reason for interfering with the order passed. This is an exception to the principle of generality and shall not be applicable in every cases, like the present one, unless the dismissal of the execution case was caused by the mistake of the court or because of any strenuous circumstance arises beyond the control of the decree-holder subject to the provisions of section 48 of the Code and Article 182 of the Limitation Act. 

16. In view of the above, this Court finds no merit in the Rule as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. 

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to costs. 

18. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated. 

19. The court is hereby directed to dispose of the case within shortest possible time. 

Communicate a copy of the judgment to the Court concerned at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J. This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 21.03.2005 passed by a single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.101 of 1992 making the Rule absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 17.09.1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court, at Khulna in Title Appeal No.120 of 1986 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 31.03.1986 passed by the Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dacope Upazilla, Khulna decreeing the suit. 

2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiff instituted the above mentioned suit being Title Suit No.259 of 1985 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dacope, District-Khulna for declaration that enlistment of the suit land as vested and non-resident property and the purported lease of the said land are illegal, malafide and void stating, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands as described in the schedule of the plaint by successive devolution devolved upon one Monindra Bachhar. He died in 1963 in Bangladesh without any issue and wife. After his death, the plaintiff got the suit land as his cousin and since then has been possessing the same. On 15.08.1981, when the employees of local Tahshil Office threatened to dispossess him, he came to know about creation of lease in respect of the suit land as vested and non-resident property. There was no valid reason to declare the suit land as vested and non-resident property. Hence the suit. 

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement and denied the material allegations made in the plaint. The case of the defendant is that Monindra left for India before 1965 and consequently the suit land became vested and non-resident property and the Government has been managing the same and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. On conclusion of the trial, the trial Court, considering the evidences and documents on record, decreed the suit by the judgment dated 31.03.1986. 

5. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.120 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Khulna. On transfer, the said appeal was heard by the learned Sub Judge (now Joint District Judge), Commercial Court, Khulna who by the judgment and decree dated 17.09.1999 allowed the appeal and thereby set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit.

6. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree dated 17.09.1999 passed by the learned Sub Judge (now Joint District Judge), Commercial Court, Khulna, the plaintiff as petitioner preferred Civil Revision No.101 of 1992 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. 

7. In due course, a Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the par-ties made the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 21.03.2005 and thereby set aside the judgment and decree dated 17.09.1999 passed by the learned Sub Judge (now Joint District Judge) Commercial Court, Khulna in Title Appeal No.120 of 1986 and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree dated 31.03.1986 passed by the learned Munsif now Assistant Judge), Dacope Upazilla, Khulna in Title Suit No.259 of 1985. 

8. The defendants as petitioners herein feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 21.03.2005 of the High Court Division preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1721 of 2005 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

9. Md. Jahangir Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the plaintiff prayed for only relief in Title Suit No.259 of 1985 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Dakope, District-Khulna that is for declaration that the enlistment of the suit land as vested and non-resident properties is illegal, void, and without jurisdiction and did not seek any declaration of title, as a result the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and, as such, the High Court Division and the Courts below ought to have dismissed the suit on the ground of maintainability but the High Court Division failed to do so and hence, there has been miscarriage of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

10. No one appears on behalf of the respondent. 

11. We have heard Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellants. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

12. Leave was granted to examine the following submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellants-defendants as to that the plaintiff prayed for only relief in Title Suit No. 259 of 1985 of the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Dakope, District Khulna that is for declaration that the enlistment of the suit land as vested and non-resident properties is illegal, void, and without jurisdiction and did not seek any declaration of title, as a result the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and as such the High Court Division and the courts below ought to have dismissed the suit on the ground of maintainability ground but the High Division failed to do so and hence there has been miscarriage of justice. 

13. Crux point of this case is that whether the predecessor of the plaintiff-respondents left for India prior to 1965 or not. It is the defendants who claim that predecessor of the plaintiff-respondents left for India prior to 1965, as such, by operation of law his properties became enemy property and vested to the government. So, the onus of proving these facts lies absolutely with the defendants. To that effect, defendants miserably failed to adduce any sort of documents or witnesses. As he was a citizen of this country, in absence of any superseding proof it shall be presumed that he died in this land. 

14. Rather, the plaintiff side established these facts on firm basis that Manindra Bachhar died in this land prior to 1965 leaving the plaintiff as sole heir with the oral evidence of all of the P.W.'s specially, with P.W. 2, who was a physician and treated Manindra Bachhar at the time of his death by diarrhea in this land. 

15. Consequently, as it is proved that Manindra Bachhar died in this land prior to 1965 then enlistment of his property as vested and non-resident properties is illegal, void, and without jurisdiction for sure. 

16. It is admitted that the Manindra Bachhar's name was rightly recorded in the SA and RS Ithatians of the suit land. Consequently, the question as to whether the suit was maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 as the plaintiff prayed only for declaration of the enlistment of the suit land as vested and non-resident properties is illegal, void, and devoid of jurisdiction without seeking any declaration of title over the suit land, depends on whether the plaintiff is in possession over the suit land or not. 

17. P.W. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 corroborated with P.W. 1 as to that P.W. 1 got the suit land as heir of Manindra Bachhar and possessing the same since his death. Government side was not able to extract contradiction with their statements concerning possession. 

18. On the other hand, though the Government did not assert in their pleading that they possesses the suit land through anyone, nevertheless, D.W. 2 claimed that he possesses the suit land by leasing out from government and D.W. 3 affirmed D.W. 2's possession. However, D.W. 2 failed to submit any such lease deed and no proper witness appeared to prove his DCR's regarding the suit land. As such, we concur with the findings of the learned Munsif that it is the plaintiff not the defendants possess the suit land. 

19. The following conditions are to be satisfied for seeking declaratory relieves under Section 42 of Specific Relief Act, 1877 are (1) the plaintiff must be entitled-to a legal character at the time of; the suit, or (2) to a right to property (3) defendant should have denied these or be interested in denying this character or right, and (4) the plaintiff should not be in a position to ask for relief consequential upon declaration sought. On perusal of the plaint it is found that in the present case the plaintiff side fulfills all the first 03 conditions. Side by side, as the suit land's inclusion in the list of Enemy Properties, at present, Vested Properties is illegal; Manindra Bachhar died in this land leaving behind the plaintiffs predecessor as sole heir prior to enforcement of Enemy Properties laws (The Defence of Pakistan Ordinance 1965 and The Defence of Pakistan Rules of 1965) and the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land, then it is not a sine qua non to include consequential relief such as declaration of title for getting decree in the instant suit as it's plaint was framed. 

20. It materializes that the High Court Division, on scrupulous appreciation and sifting of the evidence, both oral and documentary adduced by the plaintiff and defendants and also the other facts and circumstances on record found that the plaintiff's case that they are the owner of the suit property by way of inheritance from Manindra Bachhar, has been proved sufficiently. Appellate Court below erred in both factual and legal aspects of the suit in dismissing the suit. 

21. Accordingly, we don't find merit in submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellants-defendants. 

22. The reason elaborated above, we find that the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is immune from any sort of interference. 

23. Accordingly, this Civil Appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. 

End.
